"I'LL BE A BACHELOR." Said our bright-eyed boy, with hair of gold, "I'll be a bachelor when I'm old, cf: And always stay with mamma and you, As sure as sure, and as true as true,"— But he fell a prey to Cupid's dart, For tiny Bess stole his tiny heart, • Next day he announced with solemn air, "He loved dear Bessie, he did, so there— Bessie was pretty, Bessy was good— He'd marry Bessie—yes, he would." • - Reminded of what he had said before, He pondered a moment the problem o'er, Then softly said, in his bashful way, "I hadn't seen Bessie yesterday." • Oh, boy of mine, 'tis vain to plan "I'll be a bachelor when a man." Some fairy creature with golden hair, And sweet blue eyes, like your mother's there, With rippling laugh, like the song of a bird, ler' Or voice the sweetest we ever heard, makes us forget the words long spoken, m Half unconsous their spell is broken, fr And then, like you, we simply say, "I hadn't seen Bessie yesterday." —Leeds-Tlercury Weekly. Eprni K. PERRY.

div.p: Tarittio.

Virtue and a trade are the best portions for children. Life is so short that it is the worst of stupidities to Waste an hour of it. Wind up your conduct like a watch every day, exam- ining minutely whether you are fast or slow. Any man may do a casual act of good nature, but a Continuation of them shows it is a part of his tempera- ment. The power possessed over us by those we love is nearly always greater than that which we possess over our- selves. True politeness is perfect ease and freedom. It con- sists simply in treating others as you love to be treated

yourself. The Lest, best fruit which comes late to perfection, even in the kindliest soul, is tenderness towards the hard, forbearance towards the unfortunate, warmth of heart towards the misanthropic. Under no circumstances, if you can avoid it, ask a nvour, not even from your nearest and dearest friends. Give as many as you can, and if they are freely offered i it is not necessary to be too proud to take them; but never ask for, or stand waiting for any. An amateur named Plunkett was acting in Dublin as Richa,rd 111. The audience were in fits of laughter from the beginning to the end. When he said in Gloster's soliloquy, "Why, I can smile, and murder while I smile," the response from the pit was, "Oh, by the powers, you can !" To his question, "Am I, then, a man to be be- loved ?" voices answered, "Indeed, then, you are not." Lord Wm. Lennox records what he calls an admirable saying of one of the wittiest men of our ago, perhaps of any age, who, when Sir John Paul's bank stopped pay- ment, was met coming out of it by a friend. "So Sir John has failed?" said the friend. "Yes," replied the lawyer, "and I've been victimised." "Really !" con- tinued the other, "the news must have quite upset you." "Not at all; I was not upset, although I lost my balance." FETCHING THE BLACK-COUNTRY Foree—A poor woman who had been accustomed to beg with two children in her arms at a well-known corner in London, was seen the other day, down in the Black Country, by a gentle- man who had givqp her many a penny. Remarking that she had four infants in her charge, he exclaimed, " Why, how is this ?" " Ah, Sir," was the reply, "two .are enough to fetch Londoners; but they are very hard people down here !" Many a child goes astray, not because there' is a grievance at home, but simply because home lacks sun- shine. A child needs smiles as much as the flowers need sunbeams. Children look little beyond the present moment. If a thing pleases, they are apt to seek it; if it displeases, they are apt to avoid it. If home is a place where faces are sour and words harsh, and fault-finding is ever in the ascendant, they will spend as many hours as possible elsewhere. It is not merely by conversing on serious subjects that you promote serious thoughts, nor by seeking directly to obtain influence that you really influence others—it is by being good that you do good—it is by kindness and thoughtfulness for other's feelings, by sufferings or disappointments cheerfully endured, by advantage of intelleet or fortune humbly borne, by adherence to fixed principles or duty, by the princely heart of guileless innocence, whose vary look is the best rebuke to vice. A man who had seven daughters wearing out shoe- leather for IS m went to the cave of a wise old character and besought his advice as to how to bring them up. "Marry them off," said the sage, "as soon as possible, and you can then break up housekeeping and go board- ing among them." After a few months the father re- turned to the cave, and his face had such a lonesome expression that the sage cried out, "All, youmust fol- low my advice to learn wisdom." "The trouble is that -1 did follow it; but instead of having seven places to board at, I have seven sons-in-law to board on me." AN EXTINGUISHER.—One of the neatest retorts ever made was a brief responce given by a young lady to a young fellow who offered her, the other day, with some hesitation, his seat in the tramcar. She got in with an older companion. The car was crowded, and two young men sat near. One man gave his seat at once to the elderly lady; the other kept his place. His friend asked him—disguising it, however, in German—why he did , not give his place to the young lady. He answered in , the same language, "Because she is not pretty enough." But, after a little reflection, he rose and surrendered his seat. The lady took it, and thanked him—in German! THE RAVAGES OF SLAVERY ON THE UPP:2R NIGER.— To read the accounts which Clapperton gives of Northern Nup S some 50 years ago, and contrast those with the facts of its present condition, is most melancholy. He speaks of great towns, inhabited by tens of thousands and astir with intense commercial activity, of villages which greet you at every mile, ever enlivened with the dance, the song, and the feast; for the land teemed with plenty. All that is now changed. 'Thu still pass the sites of great towns and numerous villages, but their in- habitants have been:killed, sold as slaves, or driven from the country. You see still where were the gardens and rich fields, but now they are become as the surrounding wastes. Civil war has been the cause of it, and Maliktl and his Fillani supporters have taken care that, in their day, they will hear no more about rebellion. A new era has, however, commerked for the down-trodden people. Only a month ago -Sup() was placed under a British pro- tectorate, and some day doubtless a strong arm will be stretched forth to shield the people from their oppres- sors.—Good Words. LUCKY HITS.—It would be a stupid misreading of events to say that the famous duel to which David owed his rapid rise was a single lucky hit—a chance shot, in which success redeemed what would otherwise have been a foolhardy venture. Men rarely owe their success in life to chance shots of any kind. But they often do take their start from some single act which serves to disclose what manner of men they are, and to foretell to the sagacious what their career must prove. It was not in reality the slinger's skill, which aimed cool and fair at the giant's forehead when an older hand might have swerved for fear—not that alone which revived the de- caying ardour of Israel, bound Jonathan to his friends:in life-long admiration, and made David the hero of the war He became the man he was just be- cause he carried this same devout reliance upon an arm unseen into all his affairs, acted ever as in Jehovah's sight, and knew himself to be, by day and night, beneath Divine protection. . . . . The qualities which made 'Aim the conqueror of Goliath were the very qualities which made him the founder of the Hebrew Empire, and the type as well as ancestor of the Messiah.—Sunday Jraga:lize,for April. BIS3IARCK AS A TABLE TALKER.—The most character- istic part of the feast is reserved, however, until late in the evening, after the ladies have been dismissed. Cigars are then handed around, but the Chancellor prefers a long Turkish pipe, which a discerning lackey will bring him at the right moment, filled and ready for use. The Tobacco Parliament is opened. Debate there is, indeed, none; for, although suggestions and inquiries may now and then be thrown out timidly by the listeners, the pro- ceedings consist practically of a sustained monologue, which the Prince addresses to the group sitting near him in chairs, or standing farther away in a semicircular ...fringe about the chairs; nor are any formal conclusions adopted. There is nevertheless a well-considered method in the programme. linable to speak without entertain- ing, the Prince has the art and the privilege of blending instruction with entertainment, the useful with the pleasant; and thus compels the most frivolous guest to pause at some grave practical truth, while laughing at incomparable jokes. Indeed, the kernel ef the discourse is perhaps to be found only half-concealed, in the jokes themselves, or the stories. With him, these are some- thing besides a mere rhetorical device. He not only puts his hearers in good humour by pleasantries, thus gaining a favourable ear for his cause, but he actually combines precept and illustration with such art and in such proportions, that his hearers are already convinced, while they think they are only amused. That anecdote was not the setting of his proposition; it was the pro- position itself. This pun is not an insignificant jeu &esprit, but a vital truth, or a sophism which the Prince i wishes to be accepted as a truth. And thus the last hour ; of the evening passes away. A score or more of admiring guests, in full evening costume, dimly visible through the smoke, listen to the words of a very unrailitary- looking giant in military clothes, who discourses of the tariff or the currency in a delightfully varied stream of humour, wit, and story; of illustrations from history- and incidents from his own experience; of shrewd com- mon sense, lofty political reason, and fallacies made attractive and almost respectable, until the morning hours begin to strike, the lackeys dare to yawn, and with a parting joke, washed down with a final libation, the circle is broken up, and the lights extinguished. Two FAULTS.—A gentleman once bought a horse of a country dealer. The bargain concluded, and the money paid, the gentleman said, "Now, my friend, I have bought your horse; what are his faults ?" "I know of no faults that he has except two," replied the man, "and one is that he is hard to catch." "Oh, never mind that," said the buyer; "I will contrive to catch him at any time, I will engage. But what is the other ?" "Al, sir, that is the worst," answered the fellow. "He is good for nothing when you have caught him." A detective went down to Aldershot to search the ranks of a militia regiment for a criminal who was "wanted." Up and down went the investigator, till at last he stopped opposite the left-hand man of the rear rank and looked hard at him. "Come," said the colonel, his dignity and esprit de corps not a little offended, "this can't be the man you want, surely? He's the best man I've got in the regiment. You don't mean to say you know him?" "No" replied the detective, after a pause, "I don't. He's the only man in your regiment I don't know, and I was wondering where he came from." How A MAN DOES THE SHOPPING.—" You'd better put them on a piece of paper," said Mrs. S.' when about to give her first order. "Oh, no," said Mr. S., "my memory is good." "Well, then," began Mrs. S., "a spool of 60 Coates's black thread." "Yes," said Mr. S. "A yard of not too light and not too dark calico." "Yes." "A small hammer, a can of peaches of the Passadena brand, a dozen small pearl buttons, two yards of cardinal rib- bon silk on one side and satin on the other." "Yes," said Mr S., thoughtfully. "A pair of slippers for baby. a dozen lemons, a good tooth-brush, a pineapple, two ounces of sky blue German yarn, an ounce phial of homceopathic flux voroica pellets, a—" "Wait a second," said Mr. S., counting on his fingers and looking perplexed. "And a bottle of vanilla extract, and a yard of triple box-pleated crepe lisse ruching, and three yards of small-checked nainsook, and —" But Mr. S. had seized his hat and was running for the station. What the Door man brought home was a yard of bed-ticking, Ithree yards of black crape, a bottle of vinegar, eight yards of nankeen, a scrub brush, a pound of green yarn, sixty spools of "coat thread," a yard of very black calico, and a pint bottle of homceopathic pills. "There, my dear," he said, triumphantly throwing down his numerous packages; "I don't think you'll find a thing missing. Who says a man can't do shopping? My memory never played me false yet." THREE MORE THAN FOUR.—In many of the Southern States the negro farm Lends work on what is known as the share system. The landowner furnishes the land, mules, and farm implements, and advances the supplies. At the end of the crop season the labourer usually gets one-third of the product, corn, cotton, &c. A farmer in Sunflower county, Miss., in re-contracting the first of the present year with his labourers for the year 1886 found several of them who were unwilling to remain with him for one-third of what they produced. "How much more do you want ?" inquired the farmer. "We wants a forf ; dat's what Mister Mitchell's gwine to gib hes han's dis yearh." The farmer laughed, and, calling to his wife, asked her to bring out a couple of apple pies she had just baked, and when the pies were produced lie cut one of them into three equal parts, and the other into four, and invited the darkies to help themselves each to a piece. It is needless to say that the pie that had been cut into three pieces was the one first attacked. "Now," said the farmer, pointing to the thirds, "that is what I propose to give you, and that," pointing to the fourths, "is what you say Mr. Mitchell is going to give you; which had you rather have ?" The darkies opened their eyes and stared at one another, when the spokes- man exclaimed, "Well! dat pie business do prove dat a free is biggeen a fo'. Whar dat contract, Marse Bob?" The contract was produced and signed. BISMARCX AS AN ORATOR AND A WRITER. —As an orator, Bismarck may be compared with Cromwell. He has no rhetorical action, his motions are not graceful; im posing. He voice, a husky tenor, is neither musical nor He stammers, he coughs, he often stops for a word—it is always the right one when he has found it—while some of his sentences are terribly involved, and (when printed) nearly a foot long. But, as a writer, he may be compared with Luther or with Schiller. Few living Germans can write their mother speech more clearly, more idiomatically, more gracefully, more expressively, than their great political Chief. Frederick the Great raised high his native country, but he very nearly ruined his native tongue. The creator of the German Empire has penned some things which must rank as master- pieces of the German languages. Of this class were the despatches he wrote to Count Arnim, after the war, on the relations of the Empire and the Republic; and to this class also must be added many of the reports which lie drew up at Frankfort, and which so good a judge of style as Professor von Sybel pronounced to have "a classic worth unsurpassed by the German prose-writers of any age." As the Marquis of Salisbury, when a young man, trained himself for the composition of eloquent State papers by writing for the Saturday Review, so did Bismarck's steady contributions to the Kreuz-Zeitung, in his early parliamentary days, enable him to develop that literary power which is stamped with exceptional brilliancy on all his despatches.— Prince Bismarck. By Charles Lowe, JILA. A SHORT CHAPTER ON FEET.—Women are much oftener too short than too tall, and they try to gain height by high heels. These de undoubtedly, as long as their wearers stand still, give dignity; but they are most graceless for walking, even in a room, and deform the feet. Thus they administer to a very short-lived vanity, and we cannot recommend them. American women have very often their feet too small, and this is no beauty. The better shaped a foot is, the smaller it will look; but that it should really be too small involves an awkward gait. Again, it should be remembered (though it is usually forgotten) that the foot of a tall woman should be large—not large in proportion to her size—but it is no beauty that it should be as small as that of a small NVO man. A heavily built woman should have a large foot than a slenderly built woman' and usually, to her unnecessary sorrow, she has. The foot should be as lone as the ulna, or chief bone of the forearm; that is, from the small head of the bone to be seen at the wrist to the point of the elbow, should be the length of the foot. Where the forearm is too short, the foot will be found to be also too short; where this is too long, the foot will be too long. Most people are surprised that the foot should be as long as the forearm, and are inclined to dispute the fact till they prove it by experiment; but an experiment will easily show that a straight line drawn from one point to another will appear a great deal longer than the same space filled by a line divided into curves. Large women pinch their feet in tight shoes because they are ashamed of having them in proportion to their bodies; thus in time they deform and swell them until they are out of proportion to their bodies, but in the direction that they did not intend. Small women pinch their feet because they are vain of their smallness, and would em- phasise it Now, in many cases they are not so small in proportion as the feet of tall women; but the public eye being not critical of proportion, will, without their going to the pain of pinching their feet, consider them small because they are abstractedly so; therefore they seem to us to make a poor exchange for a graceful motion and a dignified carriage—two essentials to the greatest beauty. In fact, anything else had better be sacrificed to ease of motion, and yet this is what one sees most frequently disregarded. kIARRISTIERB—wDose professional laboars necessitate long In- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted nate as Cadbury's latitationS.C°c"4-- ifAive.tlaranteed absolutely pure. A travelling man, noticing a pretty girl alone in the car, went over in her direction, and smilingly asked, "Is this seat engaged, miss ?" "No, but I am, and he is going to get on at the next station." " Oh—ah—indeed —thanks—beg pardon—" and lie picked up his feet, after stumbling over them, and went into the smoking- car to be alone awhile.

Those who are in the power of evil habits must con- quer them as they can; and conquered they must be, or neither wisdom nor happiness can be attained; but those who are not yet subject to their influence, may, by timely caution, preserve their freedom; they may effectually resolve to escape the tyrant, whom they will very vainly resolve to conquer. A gentleman lately, boasting of the neatness and regu- larity of his wife, said, "If I get up in the night, pitch- dark, I can find my clothes, down to my very gloves, all in their proper places. I was up this morning before daylight," he continued, putting his hand into his pocket for his handkerchief, "and —" Here he pulled out, not his handkerchief, but his wife's nightcap! Georgia has a post-office named "Talking Rock," which acquired its title in the following manner :—Some one in the vicinity found a large stone, upon which was painted the words, "Turn me over."lt required great strength to accomplish this, and when it was done, the ntan was confronted with the legend on the other side of the stone, "Now turn me back, and let me fool someone else." tn,

Probably there is not one of us who has come to middle age who does not often have moods in which he would gladly lay down his own old self and be literally born again—a new man, unfettered by past obligations, un- injured by past mistakes. We dream about what we would do if we could begin anew; but dreaming is only dreaming, and wishes are not horses for any of us to ride. Such as we have :made our own; lives we must live them.

It is not merely by conversing on serious subjects that you promote serious thoughts, nor by seeking directly to obtain influence that you really influence others—it is by being good that you do good—it is by kindness and thoughtfulness for other's feelings, by sufferings or dis- appointments cheerfully endured, by advantage of in- tellect or fortune humbly borne, by adherence to fixed principles or duty, by the princely heart of guileless in- nocence, whose very look is the best rebuke to vice. THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE FRENCH BREEDS OF POULTRY.—(Continued.) Du MANS.—This is another breed of fowl coming from the Department of La Sarthe, and it has many of the good qualities of the other natives of that district, where, as has been already stated, poultry breeding and rearing is carried on to an enormous extent, and from where much of the very best poultry which is seen in the Paris markets is sent. This breed has never advanced to any great popularity in France, but there are signs that it is growing in favour. It is, however, noted for its table qualities, from its being made the renowned dish with epicures, "ponies De Mans." The plumage is entirely black, like that of the La Fleche and the Creve ; but, whilst like the former in many points, the shape of the Du Mans is less upright, though broad and massive. A distinctive feature is that the small ear feathers are white; the comb is triple, and there is no chest. As will be seen from M. Lemoine's tables, the hen of the Du Mans is a very rare sitter. It will also be seen that it has the smallest quantity or rather weight of bone in proportion to the meat when six months old. Number of eggs per annum lll Average weight of egg 2 oz. 113 grs. Weight of food consumed per day 7 oz. Quality of flesh fine and white. Weight of meat on fowl at six months old 4 lb. 6 oz. 64 grs, Weight of bone on fowl at six months old 2 lb. 11 oz. 11 grs. Characteristics Rather tame; suitable to all clhnates ; develops rapidly; very rare sitter. Colour of chicken when hatched Black; under-colour grey. Weight of chicken when hatched 1 oz. 257 grs. Increase of weight for first 20 days, per day 123 grs. COITRTES PATTBS.—The Courtes Pattes is not unknown in this country, though it has never become popular, but there are a few breeders of this quaint variety of fowls. It is undoubtedly related to both the La Fleche and the Du Mans varieties, owing its origin to the same district. It is much smaller than either of these breeds, and the legs are very short indeed, little more than an inch in length. From this cause the birds are inactive and quiet, never attempting to scratch, for which reason they can be kept in gardens without the slightest fear of their doing any harm. The appearance of the cock bird of this variety has been described by M. Lemoine as fol- lows :—" The Courtes Pattes cock, notwithstanding his lowness, holds his head upright, as though he had a de- sire to increase his steNture. He is like all the fowls of the department of La Sarthe—the eye large and open. His plumage is entirely black, with greenish reflections. Each feather is very full, especially on the neck. The body is horizontal, wide, and long; the comb fleshy, straight, single, indented regularly with high spikes, and very thick at the base. The beard feathers are long; the ear feathers white and long; the legs thick, of a direct gray, and very low, not very much more than an inch in length. The tail is fully furnished, and the plumes carried high. All these eccentricities give to the Courtes Pattes cock a truly singular appearance." The hen does not look quite so peculiar, and often is rather longer in the leg, sometimes being much longer. The Courtes Pattes are very hardy, and fairly good layers. Early in the season they are ready for the market; when they are made by the great French cooks into a most delicious dish called "Poulets aLa Reine." It will be seen from M. Lemoine's figures that the hens are prolific layers of a good sized egg : Number of eggs per annum l5O Average weight of eggs Weight of food consumed per day 6 oz. 391 grs. Quality of flesh good. Weight of flesh on fowl at six months ..... 3 lb. 10 oz. 99 grs. Weight of bone on fowl at six months 2 lb. 8 oz. 316 grs. Characteristics :—Very tame; suitable to all climates; de- velopes moderately; good sitter and mother, ha slow. Colour of chicken when hatched—black, under colour yellowish white. Weight of chicken when hatched 1 oz. 117 grs. Increase of weight for first twenty days—per day 77 grs. BARBEZIEUX.—This variety has been called the Minorca of France, and so far as appearance goes it is the most like the English Minorca of any French breed. It has pretty much the same outline, but from the specimens we have seen there is a very evident want of care in the breeding. If the two came originally from the same place, it is very probable that the Barbezieux has been crossed. Fine and coarse legs appear to be admissible, for both were to be seen at the Paris Show. If we care- fully examine M. Lemoine's table, a greater difference will at once be apparent. The Minorca is a non-sitter, is very hardy, and can be kept almost anywhere, but the Barbezieux is the reverse of all this. The table is— Number of eggs per annum l5O Average weight of eggs 2oz. 208grs. Weight of food consumed per day 6oz. 391grs. Quality of flesh fine Weight of flesh on fowl at six months 4lb. 10oz. 92grs. Weight of bone on fowl at six months 4lb. 15oz. Characteristics —Requires mild climate and dry soil ; develops
lowly: good sitter and mother. Colour of chicken when hatched :—Black, yellowish under-

colour. Weight of chicken when hatched loz. 257grs. Increase of weight for first twenty day., per day l23grs. GOURNAY.—The Gournay is one of the smaller races of French poultry, but is highly spoken of as a good layer, the eggs being rather above the average in weight. The breed is not very true to type, but they may be charac- terised as strongly built, single-combed, non-crested birds, with Houdan plumage, but only four toes. It will be seen from the table that the Gournay is an ad- mirable fowl for all districts, and that it is rapid in its development. From what we have seen of this variety, we should judge that it is a breed well worthy of atten- tion, and as it reproduces itself fairly true to colour it would give satisfaction to anyone who took it up. With the warmer weather which has come to us the fowls will begin to be greatly troubled with fleas, and something should be done to keep them down. These pests breed during the spring and summer in immense numbers, and often so irritate hens that they desert their nests, besides being a great cause of gapes in the chickens. They may be in large measure prevented by providing a good dust bath, in which plenty of carbolic powder has been mixed. Hens can be allowed off their nests about fifteen or twenty minutes if the weather continues mild, and when it is warmer, half an hour, so that these times will give the hens plenty of opportunity to dust themselves. To preventinsects becoming very troublesome in the nest the following plan may be adopted .--Some of the nest straw should be saturated with paraffin, taking care to have clean straw on the i top, so that no harm s done to hen or eggs. In America sulphur eggs are sold, and there are breeders who use

NOTES,b-N AGRICULTURE, HORTI- D CTL TOBACCO GRUM-NO.—The Irish Farmers' Gatttte does not encourage the idea of tobacco growing being a profitable undertaking, even In Ireland, which is better , fitted for the crop than England or Scotland, because there is less liability to frost. "There is just one county in Ireland," a contemporary says, "that could grow really good tobacco, namely, in the neighbourhood of Gorey, co. Wexford, where the soil is admirably suited for the particular crop." That is to say, there is only one district of a single county in which good tobacco could be grown. COLOUR IN 13urrEn.—A correspondent asks about the relative quantity of white and coloured butter, and if artificial colouring is advisable. Professor Long says: —" There is a popular belief that white butter is not so good as that which is a rich yellow, but this is not a fact. On grass, a cow gives butter of the highest colour peculiar to her; on hay and roots it becomes much lighter. There is no doubt that oolouring is a superflu- ous habit; in addition to being useless, it interferes with the flavour, and it takes both time and 'money away. Makers are not all so good as to use the best' annatto, while some who make their own mix it with melted butter and pour it on during the process of making—a most objectionable plan. If we were required t o use a large quantity of colouring matter regularly, we should prepare it from carrots; if not, we should prefer to pur- chase annatto from a respectable maker." " HoosE."—Yorkshireman would like to know the best treatment for " hoose" in calves under four months old. There are several ways of treating hooso" in calves. One of the best remedies to give per mouth is Friar's Balsam one drachm, and balsam of Peru half a drachm, given in about three ounces of good linseed-oil, every alternate day; and it is a good plan to substitute a dessertspoonful of turpentine for the balsam of Peru and Friar's Balsam occasionally. (These doses are for a calf between a fortnight and a month old.) Some advocate fumigating them with sulphurous acid gas, which can readily be done by placing the calves in a close place, lighting some sulphur (brimstone), and then setting the vessel containing it, which must be of earthenware or iron, in the place with the calves. In doing this care must be taken that the fumes are not too strong for the animals; and, should one or more begin so show signs of distress take them at once into fresh air.; CALI? MEALS.—" A Practical Farmer," writing to the Agricultural Garette. asks :—"Why are the manufacturers of cakes and meals—substantial cattle foods—poked away in a corner of the agricultural showyard—neg- lected, disregarded, snubbed in the general scheme of the Society— treated as one with Messrs. Biscuit, Spice, and Condiment, with whom they really have no necessary connection whatever? Let us all be submitted to the society's judges, and have careful, elaborate comparisons and trials, and adequate official recognition." Comment- ing on this, the Editor says-f--Societies have long since given up mere inspection as a test of merit in tier ma- chinery department. They are at great expense to put all implements to a sufficient trial before an award is made. Let makers of our cattle foods be similarly , treated. The one great point would be to have well- authenticated comparative experience officially recorded and declared. Let the trials be conducted by the society's own officers, and the establishment of such atrial, annu- ally conducted, would set all our cake and calf meal makers on the gui vire, and so benefit the customers one and all.—ln the same issue a very interesting description is given of a visit to the mills and experimental farm of Messrs. Bibby, the calf meal manufacturers, of Lancaster. :NORTH LANCASHIRE NOTES.—Grass lands are now showing growth; and, as the rains are on the whole what may be called warm showers, both ewes and lambs are rapidly improving. So far, we have an average of lambs equal to double the nuLtber of ewes, and have lost but one of the latter, which succumbed to weak- ness, and a couple of lambs at the beginning of the lambing season. The lambs are still living, being; brought up by hand. The latter was a common experi- ence this season, as the ewes were so short of milk when the lambing time set in. Lambing is now general, and, although the pastures certainly are looking better than in the long period of frost and snow, and the ewes are milking better, the cold winds and the heavy rains are very trying to the lambs, and great care is needed. Boon Ploughs.—Owing to the late spring, incoming tenants have been bothered to get their ploughing done. To the credit of northern farmers, be it said, they will at any time leave their own work to give a new neighbour a lift. Thus, on Wednesday no less than 75 teams as- sembled at Mountbarrow to assist the incoming tenant, and before nightfall the 70 acres of plough land on the farm had been turned over in a workmanlike manner. On the Friday the scene of operations was the Edgehill Farm, and 20 acres were ploughed; and on the Saturday a boon plough was held at the Nook Farm, and 11 acres ploughed.—R. Mint SETTlNG.—Writing on this important subject, Mr. Primrose Mc.Connell says :—" The question of deep versus shallow setting has advocates on both sides. The most natural solution one would think to be that the cream would rise most quickly and thoroughly through a thin stratum, but the regulation of the temperature is a matter which has really the most influence on it. Both heat and cold will cause the cream to rise more quickly and more of it. Fat is a substance which takes up or parts with its heat very slowly, and which has a corres- pondingly large expansion and contraction. If the milk is set at 65 degrees, and kept at that, the fat of the cor- puscles is expanded, their specific gravity is less, and they rise more quickly. If, on the other hand, the milk is suddenly cooled, the butter globules retain their heat and expanded state longer, are thus relatively lighter, and again rise more quickly. The former is the principle of ordinary setting, the latter that of the Schwartz and Cooley systems, and of setting refrigerated milk. In deep setting there is a larger bulk, which thus retains its heat longer. Of recent years we have adopted the cream separator, which is far and away the best method of extracting cream from milk. The milk is spun round at an enormous speed; the heaviest part of the milk (the skim milk) tends to go furthest outwards in the recep- tacle, aad the cream (the lightest) keeps nearest the centre from the so-called 'centrifugal force;' the two are then led off in tubes into separate vessels. In ordi- nary hand-skimming as much as one per cent. of butter fats may be left in the milk, but with the separator less than one-fourth of this."

Rnunann.—Where,from old age or other causes, this vegetable has made weakly growth a fresh planting should be made in the following manner :—lf only one row is to be planted, throw out the soil 31t. wide and 2ft. deep if the nature of the ground will permit, and on the bottom place a few inches of manure, and on that double the quantity of soil, which should be well mixed by turning them over with the fork. Continue this pro- cess till the soil is all replaced. When completed the ground will be several inches lower; but this is of no consequence, as the trenched portion will in time sink to its level. Moderately fresh manure should be used, and not the black decayed stuff that has had all the virtue washed out of it by the rain or driven out by fermentation. The kind of manure we recommend will impart additional warmth to the soil, consequently the Rhubarb roots do not miss their move, and before half the season is over they will be in advance of established plants. Pieces cut from the side of permanent plants are suitable for planting, so that it is not necessary to dig a whole clump and cut it up. Plants that may have been lifted and forced as recommended in this column will also answer the purpose, and by the end of the year would be but little inferior to the others. The distance between the roots will depend on the varieties, and the largest growers require 4ft. or sft. the second or third year. The first year a crop of Cauliflowers may be planted between the roots, or the latter may be planted half the distance and alternate plants taken up the first year for forcing. Each root should be mulched with short littery manure, and in dry soil during dry weather a watering or two will greatly assist them. It may be necessary to warn our readers not to pull a single stick of this season's growth, as nothing tends ,to weaken the plants more than that. SOWING OP SERDs.—The billowing seeds should now be sown, which we prefer to do in shallow drills drawn with the corner of the hoe :—Broccoli, Savoys, Borecole, Cauliflowers, Cabbage, Cottagers' Kale, and Asparagus Kale. Those who planted the two latter in the past year will now be having abundance of tender and succu- lent shoots, for in ten days after the snow disappeared these vegetables were growing rapidly. In gathering the young sprouts they should be cut a joint or two from the bottom, so as to allow otheis to spring out. Broccoli are now coming in useful, but it is such a stranger to the cottager that he confounds it with Borecole, or the Scotch Kale which he is so fond of putting in his broth, which is quite a different thing from the Broccoli, which is really a handy form of cauliflower. Birds are most destructive to the germinating seeds of the above, and no sooner are the plants in sight than the birds pull them up, and as they are engaged early in the morning and evening, as well as during the day, it is all but im- possible to prevent them taking the seed if not protected by a piece of herring net or wire netting of the same mesh. Either of these materials should be nailed on a wooden frame made of four pieces about an inch thick and three or four wide, and for convenience the dimen- sion of the frame need not be more than 4ft. by sft. These frames are also useful during the season to pro- tect turnips and radishes, which require to be sown at short intervals in order to secure them sweet and crisp. Tun Fnow GARDEN. Most herbaceous plants are sufficiently high above ground to enable.us to determine the space they are likely to require to grow during the coming season, and measures should now be taken to reduce the size of those that are likely to encroach on their weaker neighbours. Perhaps the best plan is to cut with a sharp spade a portion of the plant on the tres- passing side, and fill the vacant space with soil. Many plants push themselves out of the soil, so that to have soil well up to their collars many of the smaller plants would be buried. When this occurs they should be taken up and placed deeper, and if practicable in a fresh spot, if only a few feet distant; and those requiring manure should be supplied with it. This material should also be dug into all the vacant spaces except those that are in- tended for the flowering sections of geraniums, as they are more disposed to grow than flower when in too rich a compost. Mignonette may be sown either in a row along the side of the border or bed, or in round patches; and where there is not sufficient space for sweet peas in the border, they may be sown so as to be trained up the walls of the dwelling, except on the north side, or against a fence would be a suitable place. THE GaEENHOUSE.—Ferns, as a rule, do not look very happy in greenhouses. Being shade-loving plants, they are much exposed when elevated on stages in company with other plants; but if they were placed on the floor a little under the stage, and clear from drip that may occur from watering the other plants, they would ap- pear quite different in a few weeks. Many of them will be now starting to grow in the coldest of greenhouses, and if it is desirable to give them a shift into a larger sized pot, the operation should be performed without de- lay. The soil may consist of peat and loam, or the latter and leaf mould, with a fair admixture of sand. Pot moderately firm in well-drained pots, and place the plants after where they will be well shaded from the sun, and give a slight sprinkling overhead two or three times during the day.

div.head: HOME RULE BILL.
div.p: THE HOME RULE BILL.

The Government of Ireland Bill, introduced by Mr. Gladstone last week, is published. The bill is divided into two parts. The first consists of twenty-one Clauses, of which six deal with legislative authority, two with executive authority, three with the constitution of the legislative body, nine with finance, and one with the police. Part two consists of twenty clauses, of which one deals with the powers of her Majesty, two with the legislative body, one with the decision of constitutional questions, one with the Lord-Lieutenancy, four with judges and civil servants, one with transitory provisions, and ten with miscellaneous provisions. •

The following is the te.X't of the clauses of the bill which provide for the establishment of an Irish Legisla- ture and define its powers :- 1. On and after the appointed day there shall be estab- lished in Ireland a Legislature, consisting of her Majesty the Queen and an Irish Legislative Body. 2. With the exceptions, and subject to the restrictions, in this Act mentioned, it shall be lawful for her Majesty I the Queen, by and with the advice of the Irish Legisla- tive Body, to make laws for the peace, order, and good lgovernment of Ireland, and by any such law to alter and repeal any law in Ireland. 3. The Legislature of Ireland shall not make laws re- lating to the following matters, or any of them :—(1) The status or dignity of the Crown or the succession to he Crown or a regency; (2) The making of peace or war; (3) The Army, Navy, Militia, Volunteers, or other military or naval forces or the defence of the realm; (4) Treaties or other relations with foreign States, or the relations between the various parts of her Majesty's dominions; (5) Dignities or titles of honour; (6) Prize or booty of war; (7) Offences against the law of nations or offences committed in violation of any treaty made or hereafter to be made between her Majesty and any foreign State, or offences committed on the high seas; (8) Treason, alienage, or naturalisation; (9) Trade, navi- gation, or quarantine; (10) The postal and telegraph service, except as hereafter in this Act mentioned, with respect to the transmission of letters and telegrams in Ireland ; (11) Beacons, lighthouses, or sea marks; (12) The coinage, the value of foreign money, legal tender, or weights and measures ; or (13) copyright, patent rights, or other exclusive rights, to the use or profits of any works or inventions, that any law made in contraven- tiOn of this order shall be void.

4. The 'lrish Legislature shall not make any law (1) respecting the establishment or endowment of or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or (2) imposing any disability or conferring any privilege on account of religious belief; or (3) abrogating or derogating from the right to establish or maintain any place of denomi- national education, or any denominaticnal institution or charity; or (4) prejudicially affecting the right of any child to attend a school receiving public money without attending the religious instruction at that school; or (5), impairing without either the leave of her Majesty in Council first obtained on an address presented by the- legislative body of Ireland; or the consent of corpora- tion interests that rights, property, or privileges of any existing Corporation incorporated by Royal charter, or general Act of Parliament; or (6) imposing or relating to duties of Customs and duties Excise as defined by this Act, or either of such duties, or affecting any Act relating to such duties or either of them; or (7) affect- ing this Act, except in so far as it is declared to be alter- able by the Irish Legislature. 5. Her Majesty the Queen shall have the same preroga- tives with respect to summoning, proroguing, and dis- solving the Irish legislative body as her Majesty has with respect to summoning, proroguing, and dissolving the Imperial Parliament 6. The Irish legislative body whenever summoned may have continuance for five years, and no longer, to be reckoned from the day on which any such legislative body is appointed to meet. The following clauses define the Executive authority : , 7, (1) The Executive Government of Ireland shall I give or withhold, vested in her Majesty, and shall be car- ried on by the Lord L.ieutenant on behalf of her Majesty, with the aid of such officers and such councils as to her ' Majesty may, from time to time, seem fit; (2) subject o any instructions which may from thne to time be given by her Majesty, the Lord-Lieutenant shall give or her Majesty to bills passed by the Irish and shall exercise the prerogative loelgidstllaiteivaessbenodtyo,f of her Majesty in respect of the summoning, prorogu- ing, and dissolving of the Irish legislative body, and any prerogatives the exercise of which may be delegated to him by her Majesty. 8. Her Majesty may,,by order in Council, from time to time place under the control of the Irish Government, for the purposes of that Government, any such lands and buildings in Ireland as may be vested in or held in trust by her Majesty. The next three clauses deal with the constitution of the legislative body in almost the same forms as those in which Mr. Gladstone described it. Clause '9 provides that the two orders shall sit and vote together, except on questions arising in relation to standing orders or rules of procedure when each shall, if a majority of either denial:., a separate te vo were separa legislative bodies, give their votes as if they
order

and that if the result of the voting of the two orders I does not agree the question shall be resolved in negation. ' The term of office of an elective member would be ten years, and if a peerage member, the period of his life or until the expiration of thirty years from the appointed day. At the expiration of thirty years the offices of all peerage members should be vacated, and their places filled with elective members of the first order. The offices of members of the first order should not be, vacated by the dissolution of the legislative body. The second order of 204 members would be chosen by the existing constituencies, except Cork, which would be divided into two districts, each returning two members. It would be in the power of the Irish Legislature, after the first dissolution, to alter the constitution or election of the second order. Finance is the next question dealt with, and to this are devoted nine clauses thiprincipal of these referring to the question of Customs and Excise as affecting Ire- land, as distinct from Great Britain. Clause 12 provides that "for the purpose of providing , for the public service of Ireland, the Irish Legislature may impose taxes other than the duties of Customs and Excise as defined by the Act, which duties shall continue to be imposed and levied by and under the direction of the Imperial Parliament only. On and after the ap- Ipointed day there shall be an Irish Consolidated Fund separate from the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom. _ _ __

Clause 13.—A1l taxes imposed by the Legislature of Ireland and all other public revenues under the control of the Government of Ireland shall, subject to any pro- visions touching the disposal thereof contained in any Act passed in the present session respecting the sale and purchase of land in Ireland, be paid into the Irish Con- solidated Fund, and be appropriated to the public service of Ireland according to law." Then follow the state, meats of the annual contributions from Ireland to the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom. Clause 14 provides that the moneys collected in Ireland from the Customs and Excise shall be applied, under the Treasury regulations, to payment of cost of collection, management of duties, the annual contributions to the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom, the sums re- quired towards the reduction of the National Debt, of all moneys declared by the Act to be payable out of the Customs and Excise, and all sums due to the Consolidated Fund for interest for sinking fund or loans. Under Clause 17, the Irish Land Commission shall con- tinue to exist, the officers being paid by the Treasury out of the Irish Church Fund, the balance of which would be carried to the Customs and Excise account. All charges on Church property guaranteed by the Treasury shall, if not paid out of the property, be paid out of the Customs and Excise receipts, or, failing that, out of the Consolidated Fund of Ireland. All charges on Church property not guaranteed by the Treasury would be charged on the Consolidated Fund of Ireland. Subject to any existing charges, the Church property should be- long to the Irish .Governmerit. Interest and principal due to the Public Works Loan Commissioners or Com- missioners of Public Works would become payable to the Government of Ireland, the latter paying the same I to the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom by half- yearly instalments. Clause 18 provides that in case of war on a declaration from the Queen it shall be Lawful for the Irish Legisla- ture to appropriate a further sum out of the Consolidated Fund of Ireland in aid of the Army or Navy, and to raise money for that purpose payable into the Conso- lidated Fund of the United;Jiingdom. The Irish legis- lative body could not raise or appropriate any part of the public revenue without a recommendation of the Queen through the Lord-Lieutenant. Vacancies in the Exchequer Division will still be filled up by appointment by the Queen, and its sittings regulated by the Lord Chancellor of Great Britain. Then follow the provisions for the regulation of the constabulary. The second part of the bill contains supplementary provisions, the first of which reserves power to her Majesty to erect forts, magazin.es, arsenals, dockyards, and other buildings for military or naval purposes for, the defence of the realm. The next provides for the ex- ercise of the veto by the first order of the legislative body, and how it may be overruled, and the following for the cessation of Ireland to send either peers to the House of Lords or members to the House of Commons. It is then provided how questions arising as to the powers conferred on the Legislature of Ireland under this Act shall be determined, and the powers of the Lord- Lieutenant are next defined, it being expressly stipu- lated that "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any Act of Parliament, every subject of her Majesty should be eligible to hold and enjoy the office of Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland without reference to his re- ligious belief." It is provided that judges shall be re- movable only on address, and that those at present hold- ing office in the Civil Service shall continue to do so.

div.head: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening in the Lecture Room at the Museum. The chair was occupied by the president, Mr. T. G. Rylands, and there were was a Rood attendance of members..—The PREBIDENT said as that was the last meeting of the session he desired to show some recognition of the services of two gentlemen to whom that society owed at least its health and activity, if not its existence. He wished them to pass a cordial vote of thanks to the secretaries of the society. (Hear, hear.) He had often said they might have a stick for their chairman, but they must have a man for their secretary. He congratulated the society that it had two gentlemen as secretaries who had acted so effi- ciently that, he thought he could say, they had never had a more successful session, than the one which concluded that night. (Hear, hear.) He moved a vote of thanks to the secretaries, Dr. White and Mr. J. R. Young. Mr. BROADBENT seconded the proposal, which was heartily agreed to. Dr. Macxr.s moved the re-election of the following officers :-.—President, Mr. T. G. Rylands ; vice-presi- dent, Rev. Canon Dodd;. treasurer, Mr. John Dan; secretary, Mr. W. 0 wen ;. committee, Rev. Morley Stevenson, Rev. G. Smith, and Messrs. R. Davies, C. Broadbent, W. D. Jeans;. secretaries, Dr. White and Mr. J. R. Young.—Mr. D. W. FINNEY seconded the proposal, which was agreed to.—Mr. R. DAVIES moved a voted to the president. He did not know, he said, whether they should thank the chairman most for his astronomical, geographical, geological, or genial qualities. (Hear, hear.) They were all satis- fied he had made an admirable president. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Davies then exhibited some beautiful specimens of the daffodil 117-arcisw4T Horsfeldi which he said grew in this district very rapidly. He hoped that they might be celebrated in Wairington for the culture of that valuable daffodil, which he believed was first raised by a Lancashire man named Horsfield. —Mr. You's() seconded the proposed vote of thanks to the chairman, and made a Dressing request to the members to pay up their subscriptions. From the number of members of the society, he said, they ought to have an annual income of £.33, but in point of fact it VMS only about one half that amount, or in other words only one half of the members of the society paid their subscriptions. (Laughter.)—The vote of thanks to the president was. then carried, and was ap- propriately acknowledged by 111 r. Rylands. The PRESIDENT then exhibited a volume of that huge I Halliwell's Shakespeare, which contained the play of Hamlet. That volume was one of sixteen'and contained three plays.—Mr. Joust Dust then read .an interesting paper:entitled "Remarks on the character of Hamlet," in the course of which he recited in an effective manner several passages from the Play.—After the paper, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Dun, on the motion of Dr. Adams, seconded by Mr. Broadbent, and supported by Alderman Webster, Dr. Mackie, and the Chairman.—Mr. Dun having responded, the proceedings.terminated.

FOREIGN NEWS. ASSASSINATION OF THE BISHOP OF MADRID. , MADRID, MONDAY.—The Bishop of Madrid, who was shot °Y a priest yesterday morning on the steps of the Church of San Isidro, died at five o'clock this afternoon. The Republican journal El Progreso publishes copies of 24 letters which the priest who shot the Bishop of Madrid forwarded to the editor of the journal. The correspondence explains motives far the crime. It appears that some months ago the prisoner was dismissed from his appointment by the rector of one of the churches in Madrid. He repeatedly applied to the Bishop to be reinstated, then employed threats to gain his object, and finally determined to kill the pre- late. The crime has produced an extraordinary sensation in the city. The Bishop, who lay in a dying state in the Church of San Isidro, with the bullet lodged in his spine, 'was visited by many distinguished personages, and the Queen has sent several messages to inquire regarding his condition. The Pope telegraphed his benediction to the dying man. MADRID, MONDAY Niffirr.—The collapse of the Bishop Was rapid. In the afternoon delirium was soon succeeded ' bY prostration. and then consciousness was lost. The dying' raan did not hear the last prayers of the Church repeated I J)3l' his Canons, nor the pontifical benediction the Nuncio gave just as he breathed his last, at fire o'clock. The body !rill be embalmed and laid out in state at the Episcopal . Palace, after the post-mortent examination required by law. The Queen sent repeatedly to express her concern and sym- , Palle'. The Bishop was 55 years of age. Senor Castelar Promoted him to the See of Salamanca in 1873. King Alfon- so held him in high esteem after he pronounced the funeral oration on the late Queen Mercedes in 1878. The Bishopric of Madrid was only created in 1885. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—The Bishop of Madrid was buried in the San Isidore Cathedral this afternoon. A large Congregation witnessed the ceremony'. THE 'EASTERN QUESTION.—REFUSAL OF GREECE TO DISARM. CONSTANTINOPLE, SA.TuRDAY.—The Governments of Eng- , Land, France, and Italy have replied to the Forte's Circular' regarding Greece in the same sense as Germany, Russia, , and Austria, and all the Powers are thus in accord as to the necessity of Greek disarmament. The Hellenic Go- vernment has, however, to-day declared its refusal to die- ; aem. ATHENS, SUNDAY.—It is not yet known what steps the , Powers intend taking in presence of the unconciliatory tePIY of the Greek Government to their last collective .. Note. ATHENS, MONDAY.—The Russian Minister here left to- ilaY for Livadia, havine been summoned by the Emperor to Proceed there with all baste. The Minister of War left to- day for Thessaly, in order to review the troops now at the front. A steady advance of battalions from all parts of the country to the frontier continues, and the war fever shows n 0 sign of abatement. MOVEMENT OF GREEK TROOPS. ATHENS, TUESDAY—The Greek Government kas char- tered four Greek steamers to convey troops to Vole, whence lithey will proceed to the frora. Three battalions, number- ' lag together over 3,000 men, now quartered here will ; Shortly join the army in the field. The order has been re- salved with enthusiasm by the men. Part of the troops stationed on the Turkish frontier are now leaving their win- ter quarters and camping out. It is intended to move up the Bret line nearer to the frontier. The second line will be strengthened by fresh detachments of reservists. The semi- official press continue writing in a warlike tone. ' EXCHANGE OF SHOTS BETWEEN OUTPOSTS. r' ATHENS, THURSDAY —Last night shots were exchanged between the Greek and Turkish outposts on the frontier, near St. Clias, the firing lasting half an hour. There was 140 casualties on either side. The Turks retired from their Position, which, being on Turkish territory, they were in- vited by the Greek commander to reoccupy. All is quiet at Present. BUCHAREST, THURSDAI.—Prince Ouroussoff, the Russian Minister here, left yesterday for Livadia, whither General iOrghelesco, the Minister of War, will proceed on Saturday next. CANDIA, THURSDAY —fier Majesty's torpedo vessel, Poly- Phemus, has arrived in Suda Bay. A TOWN DES raoYED BY FIRE. VIENNA, SATURDAY.—A fire broke out yesterday in the town of Stry, and is still raging this morning. Telegraphic communicatioa is interrupted, the telegraph office having been destroyed by the conflagration. The railway station is also burning. , VIENNA, f:UNDAY —lntelligence fron Stry announces that the whole town has been destroyed by the conflagra- tion. Six hundred houses have been burnt down, and many persons were killed. ,teeveral hundred families are now , homeless, and great destitution prevails. LEmBERG, MONDAY.—The conflagretion at Stry is still . raging, and the state of affairs is appalling: Thousands of persons have lost all their property and even their money, barely escaping with their lives. The charred remains of , the victims are being dug out of the ruins. , DISASTROUS FLOODS AT MONTREAL. MONTREAL, SUNDAY.—This city has been visted by floods of a character more disastrous than any experienced in its previous history. The loss of property, which is very large, is seriously estimated at from three to six million dollars. bir All the English newspaper offices have been flooded. It is feared that there has been much loss of life. MONTREAL, TnESDAY.—The floods here are slowly sub- siding. The merchants in this city now estimate the loss of property at ten million dollars. THE STRIKES IN BELGIUM. CHARLEROI, MONDAY.—The strike has extended in a cer- tain degree to-day among the miners in the collieries near this city, but perfect quiet prevails everywhere. At a meet- ing held yesterday at du net the men on strike decided to send a petition to the King. The speakers recommended peaceful action, and urged the men not to resume work Until the result of the petition was known. The court today Passed sentences varying from fifteen days' to six months' imprisonment upon thirty prisoners convicted of attempting to prevent other men from continuing to Work. THE AUSTRIAN BUDGET. Ittlik"-,' VIENNA, MONDAY —The Upper House of the Reichsrath to-day adopted the Budget. In the course of the debate Dr. bunajewski, Minister of Finance, declared that there was ample evidence that all the European Powers having autho- rity were desirous of maintaing peace. The fact that there eras no deficit in the Budget was evidence of the continued tievelopment of the financial condition of the country. FRANCE AND THE VATICAN. Rome, MONDAY.—Negotiations, which are expected to have a successful issue, have been proceeding daring the last three days between France and the Vatican with the ob- ject of coming to an agreement on pending questions, in- cluding the maintenance of the concordat. THE RAILWAY STRIKES IN AMERICA. NEW YORE, Moe-rms.—A strike is announced of the employes on all the New York surface railroads with the exception of two. The strike of switchmen on the Balti- more and Ohio Railway at Chicago has been amicably ad- justed.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT
HOUSE OF COIMONS.7MoNDAy.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. GOVERNMENT LEGISLATION.—Mr. CHILDERS gave notice that on the 4th May he would move for leave to introduce a bill to provide compensation for losses by riot applicable to the whole country; and on the 11th May a Coalmines Regu- lation Bill. TRADE ON THE RIO DEL REY.—Mr. BRYCE, in reply to a question said that the territories on the right bank of the Rio del Rey fell within the area over which British juris- diction extended, and British traders there would have the benefit of any British jurisdiction which might be con- stituted. THE IRISH RESIDENT MAGISTRATES..—Mr. TREVELYAN inquired whether the position of resident magistrates would . be governed as regarded their tenure of office and personal prospects by the provisions applied to civil servants in Ire- land under clause 29 of the Government of Ireland Bill.— Mr. J. MORLEY said his answer must be in the affirmative. The bill distinguished between those persons, such as judges and county chairmen, whose salaries were by law charged on the Consolidated Fund, and ordinary civil' ser- vants, paid out of moneys voted by Parliament. The resi- dent magistrate belonged to the latter class, and were dealt with, like other civil servants, by clause 29 of the THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.—Mr.CoBB asked whether, looking to the neglect of the trustees of parochial charities to carry out the provisions of the Allotments Extension Acts, 1882, the Government could approximately state when they would be in a position to introduce the Lecal Self-government Bill.—Mr. STANSFELD, in reply, remarked that the hon. member correctly assumed that the subject of allotments would be dealt with by her Majesty's Govern- ment in the Local Government Bill, and they were fully conscious of the importance of dealing with the subject in the interests of ' the agricultural population. Be regretted that he was not at that moment in a position to make any statement as to the time when it would be possible to ask leave for introducing the Local Government Bill, but he could assure his hong. friend that there should be no una- voidable delay in the matter. ASSIZE SITTINGS IN LANCASHIRE.—Mr. BADEN POWELL asked the Attorney-General if he could inform the House whether the Lord Chancellor had come to any decision in reference to the representations which were made to him by the deputation which waited upon him in reference to the Continuance Sittings Bill.—Tho ATTORNEY-GENERAL, who was very indistinctly heard, was understood to say he had received a communication from the Secretary of the Lord Chancellor to the effect that the Lord Chancellor had been in communication with the judges with regard to the depu- tation from Lancashire on this subject, and with the assent of the judges he had it in contemplation to alter the exist- ing rules by removing the restrictions which limited facili- ties of trial in Lancashire affected by those rules. The Lord Chancellor also had under consideration, and hoped to be able to provide, a scheme by which the administrative business of causes proceeding in the district registries of Manchester and Liverpool might be transacted locally, and not necessarily in London. TEE LAND PURCHASE BILL.—Mr. JOHN MORLEY in- formed Mr. W. O'Brien that the Government had been un- able to see their way to include the question of the claims of purchasers of Church lands in Ireland in the provisions of the Irish Land Purchase Bill, and at present he would rather not commit himself to say that these claims would be taken into consideration. TEE CnorrEets Brer...—The House went into Committee on the Crofters Bill.—Clause 14 was added to the bill.—On clause 15, Dr. MACDONALD moved an amendment providing that the three Commissioners should be able to speak the Gaelic language.—The LORD ADVOCATE admitted that one or more of the Commissioners oneht to be able to speak Gae- lic, but thought that this need not be made a statutory quail- fication.—The amendment was withdrawn, and a provision inserted that one of the Commissioners should be able to ' speak Gaelic.—On clause 16, Mr. MACFARLANE moved an amendment to provide that the measure, instead of apply- ing to certain portions of the counties stated in the bill, ' should apply to the whole of those coenties —The LORD ADVOCATE opposed the amendment.—After discussion, the Committee divided and rejected the amendment by 152 to 95. —Mr. HUNTER moved the omission of the words providing that the measure should apply to every crofter who was the tenant of a bolding at the passing of the Act, and to his heirs, in the same manner as if the tenancy were a lease.— The LORD AnvoceTE could not accept the amendment, holding it to be inconsistent with the theory upon which the second reading of the bill had been agreed to.—Mr. BARCLAY and Mr. MACFARLANE maintained that the bill as it stood would not satisfy the crofters, and that whilst disturbing the past relations between landlords and tenants, it would not settle future relations.—On the division the amendment was lost by 89 to 70.—Dr. CLARK moved to re- port progress. The bill was distinctly a delusion and a sham, and the members interested in the well-being of the crofters would be no parties in the future to the carrying Aut of the measure. The bill would not be a solution of the question, and it would be a pare waste of time proceed- ing with it.—Mr. BARCLAY declared that the bill would • not apply to more than one or two thousand out of 4,000 crof- ters. He supported the motion for reporting progress.—The motion was negatived without a division.—The 16th clause was then agreed to, also clauses 17 to 23.—Certain amend- ments in successive clauses being agreed upon, clauses 24 to 28 inclusive were added to the bill. On clause 29, contain- ing definitions and specifying that the crofter should reside linen his holding.—Mr. BARCLAY moved to add "or in the vicinity."—The LORD ADVOCATE opposed the amendment. —Upon a division it was negatived by 133 to 84.—The LORD ADVOCATE moved to extend the definition of the term" Crofter" so as to include the tenant from year to year of a dwelling-house situated in a crofting parish who resides therein, and who pays to the landlord therefor an annual rent not exceeding £6 in money, whether with or without garden ground, but without arable or pasture land. —This was agreed to. Some fur- ther verbal alterations were made in the clause, and clauses 29 and 30 were then added to the bill.— On the motion of the Lord Advocate a new clause provid- ing for reduction from rent in case ef lands held for sport- ing purposes was agreed to.—The clause was then added to the bill.—A new clause providhag for loans to assist in the . purchase and equipment of fishing boats was on the motion of the Lord Advocate. adopted.—The Lord Advocate moved a clause enabling a person to bequeath his right to his hold- ing to a member of the family, which was added to the bill. —The bill passed through committee. The House adjourned at ten minutes past three o'clock , on Tuesday morning till Monday, 3rd of May.

As regarded the town of Warrington,"' there was no town in England of its number of inhabitants that was so well cared for in its improvements towardsl health and sanitary affairs. For that be would give all credit to our councillors, for health meant wealth. If, in- stead of grumbling at depressed trade, Englishmen would work out and improve their various trades, England would as hitherto beat the world. He respected Warrington and ,its people as much as he did the place where he was born, and hoped Warrington would succeed and prosper as well as it had hitherto done. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN prowled "The Warrington Football Cup Team, winners of the West Lancashire and Border Towns Challenge Cup"—(cheers)—coupled with the name of Mr. Ashton. (Renewed cheers, and " He's a jolly good fellow.") When the cheering bad subsided the Chairman said that the players, he was sure, must be delighted with the hearty reception that they had,received. When he ac- cepted the office of president he never expected that the football team would come to the front as they had done. He could not have dreamed that they would have beaten so many good teams as they had done. There were people, and in Warrington, who said that the game was a dangerous one and were very timid about it. Of course, there was danger attending all our national sports. The greatest noblemen hunted, which was a much more dangerous sport than football play- ing. The national sports of a country had a wonderful effect upon the character of the people in after life. As Mr. Davies had said, the battle of Waterloo was won on some of the fields at Rugby. He could well believe that in twenty or thirty years from now, some of their forwards would he forward in the ranks of life, and prominent amongst their fellows. (Applause.) The pled; and the determination that they had learnt on the football field must stand them in good stead in after life, and must have an excellent effect upon them both physically and morally. He had watched nearly every game during the last season and must say that he never saw more determined pluck and heroism than bad been shown with the football team. At Widnes they fought a splendid game against Runcorn. When they met the same team again at Southport every man went there deter- mined to win—(Applause)—and when be told them that one of their team (Massey) fought for 75 minutes with a broken collarbone, he thought they would say there was some- thing in it. (Cheers.) That player could have honourably walked off the.field invalided, but instead of doing so he re- mained, made one or two excellent runs, and secured two minor points for his team. He would ask them to drink the health of the winning team, and could assure them that when he saw the cup handed over to the keeping of Warrington it was one of the proudest moments of his life.—Replying to the toast, which was enthusiastically drunk, Mr. ASHTON, captain of the cup team, thanked the company for the honour paid him and the team. When that trophy was first organised the War- rington F.C. was one of the first clubs to come forward with the needful to establish it on a firm basis. (Applause.) The Yorkshire Challenge Cup was contended for on the same afternoon that Warrington met Aspull, and Halifax and Bradford took £6OO, which was a record for that part of the country. When Warringten met Runcorn and Widnes they also had a record in that way, taking £1.20 at popular prices, which showed the popularity that Rugby football was gaining in this part. To win the cup Warrington had fought the best clubs of the union. (Applause.) They had had no favour shown thein—(hear,bear)—but had won by sheer skill and science. He fully believed that they could have beaten the Runcorn "15" at Widnes, which was exemplified when they met them again at Southport. That game was about the best form Warrington had shown in the competition. They had to struggle bard to win the cup when they met Aspall. Their players now, in additioa to holding the cup for twelve months, were each to be presen- ted with a gold medal, whicn was a great encouragement to them to strive to win the cup. (Applause.) To get pos- session of it they had worked like Trojans—(applause)— each one, as it were, being imbued with the feeling that the i success of the team deptoided upon himself. He trusted , that the club would win the trophy again next year. They had met some of the best clubs in the north of England I land acquitted themselves well. Before they finished their 1 season they would have an opportunity of meeting Brough- ton Rangers and Wakefield Trinity, two of the finest expon- ents of Rugby football in the north of England. He hoped that they would continue to work together with good feel- ing, that they should stick together ae a body like bees in a hive, and never sting each other. (Laughter and cheers.) He again returned thanks for the hospitable manner in which they bad been received.—Mr. POVEY, sub-captain, also responded in suitable terms Mr. FRANK ROBERTS gave the health of the' Warring- ton Football Club," remarking that there were many more members of the club than the" prize 15." He had great pleasure in proposing the health of the nursery which bad produced such a splendid team. He denied that the Rugby game was attended with the roughness attributed to it by some, and claimed that the game was naturally a scientific one when properly played. He was glad to couple with the toast the name of the captain, Mr. Warren. (Cheers.) He believed he was right in saying that Mr. Warren's absence from the "15 " was a matter of disappointment to him and to the remainder of the team. He hoped that Mr. Warren's success would be equal to the success that had attended the team of which he had been so able a member, and for which he had done so much to help to bring it to its present state of efficiencv.—Mr. WARREN, responding, said that the success of the club for the past two years had been remarkable. Prior to then they had the greatest difficulty to get together a team, and now they could with success turn out three. Whereas before they had difficulty in pay- ing their way, now they had a„ balance at the bank. (Ap- plause.) With perseverance they bad succeeded in getting together a team which he believed could hold its own against the best organisations in the country. No matter what detractors and critics might say, there was a great deal in the game of football, and he believed that there was no game more calculated to bring out the determination of Englishmen. It was not a game for the weak, the delicate, or the timorous, but it was of sterling worth for all that. (Applause.) Mr. WILLIAM PIERPOINT, who was received with cheers, said that he was pleased to hear from Mr. Ashton that the Warrington (elub was one of the first to join in helping to promote the contest for the cup, and he was pleased indeed that the cup had been brought to Warrington. Be had as much gratification as Mr. Davies when be beard at Liver- pool that the cup \ was won, though he was afraid he had not the same pleasure as Mr. Davies in receiving the news at the general election. (Laughter and applause.) He was glad that they were going to encounter Yorkshire clubs, but he was sorry that they had not got a fixture on with Swinton, which be thought was one of the best clubs in this part of the country. He then gave the health of " The West Lancashire and Border Towns Union," coupled with the names of Mr. Parry and Mr. Hall, who were mainly instrumental in forming the union.—Mr. PARRY first re- sponded. He congratulated the Warrington team on their success. Warrington should be proud of them. (Applause.) He especially mentioned the full back Buxton, Jolley, Massey, and the centre three-quarter Barnes, who, in his opinion, won the cup by dropping the goal. (Cheers.) At first he fancied Runoorn for the cup, but when he saw Warrington play St. Helens he was really sur- prised at the combination of .the Warrington team. He then made up his mind that Warrington would take a lot of beating. (Applause.) The union was formed in November, 1884, and Mr. Hall was the father of it. He congratulated Warrington on winning the cup, from the bottom of his heart.—Mr. HALL also responded. He also referred to the formation of the union to keep up the pres- tige of the Rugby game in Liverpool and the neighbourhood and to the stimulus thus given. He could not tell them how much they had to contend against in Liverpool. It was a difficult matter for young and struggling clubs to get engagements with a certain class of clubs, and unless they could, by an organisation of this kind, rise to a superior standard of excellence they would not be able to rank with them and compete withthem. It was a wise saying that if the people of France had engaged as much in national pastimes as we did in England, there would be less of revolution in France—there would have been a levelling up of the people who would have understood each other better. He was glad that the competition had been so successful. They had founded the trophy by the hard work of their members, and he thought that, in addition to having paid their way, they would finish the season with almost £lOO in hand. (Applause.) Councillor MACKIE congratulated the guests on their ex- cellent appearance. He proposed the health of the "visi- tors," coupled with the name of Mr. Wilcox.—Mr. WILCOX, acknowledging the compliment, said that as umpire for the winning team he thought he should have been included in the team. When he was a boy, he said, and played Rugby football, there were b‘ 20" on a side. The backs in a game of that kind generally looked on and urged the forwards to go at each other's legs, for perhaps twenty minutes before the scrimmage broke up. (Laughter.) Evidently Rugby foot- ball bad become more scientific. He did not doubt that those who had not seen it before need only go once or twice to become infatuated with the game. When the Warrington team went to Liverpool many members of the aristocratic Liverpool club went there expecting to see little better than a free fight. The reverse took place, and a promiaent member of the club referred to, a most determined oppo- nent to cup contests, said to him, "Wilcox, another game of this description and I shall be converted into believing 1 in cup contests." (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN, on behalf of the club, then presented a heed tome timepiece to Mr. E. (Laughter and ap- plause.) Mr. MORRIS proposed the health of the "Chairman," who, in responding to the cordial reception his name re- ceived, referred to the success of the gathering, and spoke of the interest taken in the club by the vice-presidents. (Applause.) . Mr. ASHTON proposed .a vote of thanks to the hosts' and to Mr. J. L.
