THE DISTRESS IN WARRING-TON. I The Mayor, the Revs. R. Filcher, S. Wilkinson, and E. C. TIIE GENERAL COMMITTEE. Carleton, Messrs. Monks, Litton, Smethurst, Whitham, and R. Davies; the Mayore ' ss, Miss C. Harvey Mrs Carle- The weekly meeting of the General Relief Corn- ton, Mrs. Fox, Mrs. Liiton, Mrs. W. Dutton, Miss Kendrick, mittee was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday after- and Mrs. S. Reynolds. This concluded the business. noon. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there was a large attendance of ladies and gen- tlemen. The Hon. Sec. (Mr. P. Monks) read the report of the Executive Sub-committee, which stated that during the past week £2O 16s had been ex- pended for food, and £2O 19s 10d for clothing; total £4l 15s 10d. The applications for the week had been 185, of which 164 had been renewals; number of cases relieved, 3,345; number of cases visited, 219, and 59 of these had been refused. The sub-committee recommended that in consequence of the change and improvement in the weather and increase of employment, the necessity for having relief was greatly diminished, re- lief in food be discontinued after Sunday next. He (Mr. Monks) moved the adoption of the report.—Mr. SUTTON seconded the proposal.—ln answer to the Mayor Mr. MONKS said he believed there was now more work at the forges.—The Rev. N. C. E. CARLETON said he had heard that the workmen at Whitecross were only employed some- thing like two or three 'days in the week.--Mr. H. WHITHAM said it was just possible Mr. Monks' remarks might make a wrong impression outside. He thought the statement of Mr. Monks, in so far as it related to the trade of the town having im- proved, was a rather strange statement. As far as the works he was employed by, Rylan.ds Bros.,was concerned the workmen had been " playing " all the week before last, a great portion of last week, and that afternoon he should not have been at that meeting had they been working. He thought it advisable that the fund should be kept open a little longer, especially for those who were depending on the mills and factories for work, and he moved a re- solution to that effect.—The MAYOR said he had some reason for saying that there was still a very great amount of terrible distress existing in the town. He was afraid there were a great many people literally eating themselves out of their houses. (Hear, hear.) That did not indicate that things were looking more favourable than they had been do- ing. There were a great many houses which were I kept scrupulously clean, but which had not chairs ' to sit dbwn upon in them, and such was the praise- worthy independence of their occupants that rather than trouble any relief organisation or go to the parish for relief they were content to eat them- selves out of their houses. He was told that a good many people were entirely dependent upon the bread they got from the drill shed.—Mr. BEAMONT said that as far as the immediate cause which led to the opening of that relief fund was concerned it had been answered, and he thought the report made by Mr. Monks was a satisfactory one. Mr. Beamont then alluded to the excellent service which was being done by several relief organisations already in existence in the town, which, he said, might all become admirable centres for providing people against pressing wants. A little providence and a little forethought, and that instruction which the ladies were so able to give to their own sex might bring about quite a different state of things. He was sorry to see that amongsu the working classes a great many labourers, honest in many respects, were too apt to think that if they gave their wives a certain sum they were at liberty to spend the rest. He thought that by the system adopted by the ladies they might very soon bring about a chanae in these habits. He was of opinion that instead of establishing a permanent relief fund of any kind they might set about some work of the kind he had referred to.—Mr. BROADBENT said it was quite true that there -was a very great deal of distress in connection with the great manufacturing concerns, that was to say the works were generally very unprofitable to the masters, and consequently there was not full employment. Mr. Carleton men- tioned one works, but he very much under-estimated the amount of work given at those works. He thought those works were much more employed than three days a week.—Mr. Moxics mentioned that the total number of cases relieved during the time the relief had been given was 56,229.—Mr. PARR having supported the recommendation of the committee, the minutes were passed.—This was all the business before the committee. THE PROPOSED RELIEF SOCIETY. The adjourned meeting for the purpose of considering the advisability of establishing a permanent relief society in Warrington was held in the Town Hall en Tuesday after- noon. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also prerent the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, J. Drum- mond, R. Filcher, Messrs. W. Beamont, J. C. Parr F. Monks, C. Broadbent, T. Sutton, H. Whitbam, W. Roberts, J. Smethurst, S. Davies, W. Diggle, Womarsley, J. L. Whittle, Major Litton, J. Fairclough, R. Davies, R. Gar- nett, J. Greening, and a large number of ladies.—Tbe Mearceii having explained the objects of the meeting, gave some particulars as to societies of the kind proposed to be established in Warrington which exist in Hull and Roch- dale. From these particulars he gathered that the expense incurred in conducting organisations of the kind was under all circumstances heavy in comparison to the amount sub- scribed.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said they might adopt some device for working the society more economi- cally than in some other towns. There were men in the town who took various agencies into one office' and they might find a man of that kind who in his spare time might undertake the work of the society for £2O or MG a year.—The alesoa said a good deal of time was spent in correspondence, and he thought they would hardly be able to find a person who could perform these duties efficiently in conjunction with other duties. At the previous meeting Mr. le. Davies had remarked about the large working expenses of the Bolton Relief Society in comparison with the relief afforded. He (the Mayor) had received 'a letter from one of the committee of that society, in which that gerttleman stated that there was considerable correspondence which entailed an expence of about £2O, and in addition to what appeared in the balance sheet the society distributed a large amount of cast-off clothing, coal. &c so that the amount distributed might be averaged at £3OO. The society were also obliged to be ready for any excep- tional distress when they obtained a special fund not mixed with the ordinary accounts.—Mr. Monies said the working expenses of such societies as were referred to would average at least 50 per cent.—Mr. SUTTON proposed that an associa- tion be formed for the relief of necessitous cases. He pointed out that at present a certain number of charitable persons were continually being applied to for relief, and he thought it was better that charity of this kind should be dispensed by an association than by a few individuals. He did not see that there should be any very great working expenses.—Mr. SMETHURST seconded the proposal.—Mr. R. DAVIES referred to the mode in which relief was ad- ministered in Paris, where there was no poor-law relief. Paris, he said, was divided into districts which were pre- sided over by ladies and gentlemen, and all cases of distress were examined by them, and relief that was worth being called relief was administered. It seemed to him that if they simply elected an officer they were almost destroying the Christian character of the relief that would be given. They would be creating an organisation that would supplement the poor law, but which would, nevertheless, be a hard organisation unless supplemented in some way by the efforts of ladies and gentlemen who could spare time. He proposed that a com- mittee be appointed to make inquiries as to the work done by relief societies in a large number of other towns.—Mr. Roomette/4.r thought it was desirable that some permanent organisation should exist to meet emergencies such as that of the past winter. He supported Mr. Davies' proposition. —Mr. R. GanesErr said that a charity organisation to be satisfactory would have to ba conducted on very different lines from those he had ever seen before. As a rule 50 per cent went to pay a secretary or visitor and very often 75 per cent went in that form. (Hear, hear.) He should feel very much disposed to oppose such an institution, because the result would largely be that people would shelter them- selves behind the society ; they would say to applicants " Oh, I contribute to the charity organisation, eou go there." He should very much object to an organisation on the lines of that in Bolton.—Mr. WHITHAM said he was cer- tainly at a lose to know what sort of permanent relief fund or organisation could be established In this town. The class of people who had received help from the organisa- tion that was just closing its work differed very much from the class who he thought, in this and most other towns, they were likely to be troubled with in the future. He thought himself that bad trade was becoming the normal state of things, and the man who was likely to want relief in the future would be the man who is called the respectable artisan. But he would not come to any charity organisation to ask for help; he would stand very much upon his dignity. What that man wanted was to be helped to help himself; he wanted work. He (Mr. Whitham) thought the greatest mistake any society or organisation could make would los to give money that had not bean earned. It something could be done towards carrying on improvements in the town, same committee formed to work along with the Corporation so that men might apply for a bit of work and get it, he was confident a good thing weuld be done. There was also a class the ladies might devote them- selves to, and that was the girls and women and children who had been left without any male members of the family. Mr. Whitham then referred to the distress that was beginning to be felt amongst the workmen who had before the bad times set in saved same of money, and he said that whilst their organisations were in- quiring into the cases of men of this kind the men themselves were quietly slipping through, starving to death. He supported Mr. Davies' proposal.—Mr. Mcesics urged the necessity of wives of poor men being taught domestic economy, so that they might make better use of the means placed at their disposal. He agreed with Mr. Whitham so far as to say that if they were to hold their own with foreign competition wages must be rednced.—Mr. W. ROBERTS supported the proposal of Mr. Davies.—The ISIA.Yon, with regard to Mr. Whitham's remarks said it would no doubt be better to give employment if they could, but where were they to get it.—The Rev. R, PILCHER having seconded the amendment proposed by Mr. R. Davies, it was agreed to and the following committee of inquiry was appointed, viz.;
LIBERAL COUNCIL AT RUNCORN.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., ON HOME RULE. A meeting of the Council of the Northwich Divi- sion Liberal Association was held on Saturday after- noon in Runcorn Public Hall. Representatives were present from all parts of the Division. Mr. S. C. Beckett, was voted to the chair. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., was present. The first business was the consideration of the new rules, which were unanimously adopted on the motion of Mr. JAE HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. J. 0. GLEAVE. The Government proposals with regard to Ireland then came up for discussion. The CHArnaux said that in order that they might per- haps understand the matter somewhat better, the secretary (Mr. W. Handley) had drawn up a resolution which he I would submit, and then the subject would be open for die- oussica. The SECRETARY Said the resolution, which could be adopted or rejected, read WS follows That this meeting of the General Council of the Northwich Liberal Associa- I

tion, specially convened to consider the Home Rule pro- posals of the Government, is of opinion that they contain the basis of a settlement which is calculated to promote the freedom, prosperity, and contentment of our fellow subjects in Ireland, and especially thank the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone—(applause)—for the bold, just. and statesman- like character of the proposed legislation." (Renewed ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN said he was authorised to state that Mr. Brunner was not afraid to express his views upon the sub- ject, and it was hoped there would be perfectly free discus- sion. (Hear, hear.) Mr. THOMAS GIBSON (Winsford) supported with all his heart and soul, and energy, the Grand Old Man on this question—(loud applause)—because he knew that if he could not do the work no mortal man could. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Gladstone had put his hand to the plough, and he would stick to it until the furrow had gone right to the end, until be had accomplished the great object. (Hear, hear.) Every true hearted Englishman desired that Ireland should have justice, and have control over her own affairs. (Hear; hear.) The fact that all the Tories were against the measure was sufficient guarantee for him that Mr. Gladstone was right. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. DAVIDSON (Acton Bridge) said he would yield to no man in his admiration for Mr. Gladstone, but considering the great depression in agriculture in England he was not in favour of opening the national purse and endangering the ' British taxpayer in favour of the Irish landlord. (Hear, hear.) Land legislation in England was overlooked, and Ireland attracted too much attention because of the crimes enacted in that country—(a voice: "No. no ")—and he did not know whether he could support Mr. Gladstone's whole scheme as it stood. _ _ _

The Rev. F. CARTER (Northwich) considered that Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill, with some modification, was the Bill which would settle the great question of Irish •wants. (Hear, hear.) He was not a financier, and had hardly an opinion on the Land Purchase Bill, but it cer- tainly seemed that the price to be paid to place the land in the hands of the Irish was an exceedingly large one. The Irish landlords have held the land under the protection of 'English law, and the land ought not to be taken from them without fair and just compensation. So far as he could see at the present, he would support both bills. (Ap- plause.) Mr. G. KING (Northwich) spoke of the enormous amount of coercion that bad taken place in Ireland, and said he did net suppose that a Liberal Government would every again try that method of governing the Sister Isle, and he did not believe that a Conservative Government would ever be allowed to do. (Laughter and applause.) The qt.estion then arose had anyone yet.fonnd a better plan for solving the difficulty better than Mr. Gladstone. (Cries of "No, no.") In his opinion, it was possible to give Ireland con- trol over her domestic relations, and yet maintain the in- tegrity of the empire. and Mr. Gladstone had not drawn hard and fast lines in matters of detail ; but if he thought the matter had to be settled without an appeal to the country, he did not think he should look with favour upon it. Mr. B. KNIVETON (Runcorn), alluding to the amount of money to be paid the landlords, said we were in a position that we could afford to be generous, and he did not think it was wise to push their pecuniary views too far on a ques- tion of this sort. During the debates Mr. Healy had said that it was the wish of the Irish party to hold out their hands over the wrongs of centuries, and become the Mena of the English. (Hear, hear, and applause.) That was what we wanted, and he firmly believed this measure of Home Rule would accomplish that object. It gave to Ire- land full control of their domestic affairs. while England had every possible guarantee for the maintenance of the integrity of the Empire. He heartily supported the pro- posals of Mr. Gladstone, and he hoped that meeting would cordially support Mr. Gladstone in his great work of eman- cipation. (Applause.) Mr. S. POPE (Runcorn), while disagreeing with the ex- , elusion of the Irish members from Westminster as proposed in the bill, gave his support to the resolution, as he be- lieved that Mr. Gladstone's scheme offered a basis for the settlement of the question. Mr. JAMES WILLIAMS said the feeling in Middlewich, which he represented, was in favour of the bill. Mr. Gitoneis BELLAMY (Runcorn) and Mr. J. D. JONES (Runcorn) made a few remarks, the latter gentleman con- tending, in reply to some obeervatiovs made by a previous speaker, that the question of Home Rule was before the constituencies at the general election, and he predicted that if the House of Lords threw out the measure, the question before the electors on the next occasion would not be Home Rule but the House of Lords. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) He supported the resolution. Mr. JAMES HANDLEY, 3.1'., then proposed the resolution, and in doing so expressed the opinion that some modifica- tion wauld be brought about with the discussion of the measures introduced by Mr. Gladstone that would unite the whole Liberal party—(hear, hear)—and then we should have that domestic legislation they were so ardently longing ' for in this country. Until the Irish question was out of the way we should have nothing done for temperance and other important matters in England. (Applause.) Mr. S. POPE seconded the resolution.

Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., on rising to support the proposition, was greeted with a prolonged round of applause. He said the last time he had the pleasure to appear before them the formal business took up so much time that there was little left for him, and he had been given to understand since that the curtness of his address to them was looked upon as indicating on his part a want of respect. He asked them not to believe it. (Hear, bear.) That day their friends from Runcorn had very little time to catch their train, and he did not think it wae respectful to them to go on speaking after they had been obliged to leave. (Hear, hear.) That day he was happy to think no man could get out of Run- corn until after six o'clock—(laughter)—and he did not think many of them would want to make many cells on the way to the station, so that that day he was not limited. The chairman was quite right when he said he (Mr. Brunner) was not afraid to declare his opinions. He had been a Horne Ruler for many a day gone by—(hear, hear, and applause) —but he was extremely anxious to hear their opinions and especially the opinion of those who were not exactly opposed to the proposal of Mr. Gladstone, but had objec- tions ; for the reason that as a rule objections to these pro- posals were founded upon misapprehensions, and when they were not founded upon misapprehension but upon perfect information, it was his duty to reprezent them. His friend, Mr. Davidson, was afraid the national purse would suffer from the proposals that Mr. Gladstone made. Now, unlike Mr. Carter, he could with all modesty say that he was somewhat of a financier because he bad been doing noth- ing else for the last quarter of a centery—(hear, hear)—and he could assure them that there was not a shadow of fear that the English taxpayers would loose one penny. (Loud applause.) We had lent to Irishmen in times gone by many many millions of money. We had lent money to the landlords and to the tenants in times of the greatest distress when hundreds and thousands of people were dying of star- vation. We had remitted some of the loans to the tenants, but beyond those remissions we had never lost one penny by the tenant. (Hear, hear, and applause.) But when we considered the landlords the matter was different—(laughter and applause)—and he would not advise them to lend any money to the landlords—(laughter)—because by them we had been losers indeed. The Irish landlords were amongst the most genial fellows on the face of the earth, and had been in the habit for more than a hundred years past of taking a great deal, and of spending a great deal more than they got—(laughter)—and if they would look around they would find that the men who spent other people's money always were jolly fellows. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Brun- ner than explained Mr. Gladstone's proposals with regard to land purchase, and said he considered that the landlords would make a very good bargain—(hear, hear)—cansidering how they had behaved in times gone by. (Hear, hear.) He told those present frankly that to give the Irish land- lords so good a bargain was a bitter pill for him to (Hear, hear.) The tenant would make a good bargain, he believed, and he was happy in that belief. (Hear, hear.) The Irish State would also make a good bargain,and nothing could please them better than that the Irish State should , make a good bargain—(bear, hear)—for in times gone by we had been quite as guilty as the landlords in our treat- ment of the people of Ireland. We had killed their trades, stopped their agriculture, and put taxes upon their produc- tions. There was a black load of sin lying upon our shoul- ders. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner considered the appoint- ment of the Receiver General 'very good security for the money to be repaid to England, and said on the previous night in the House of Commons he sat next to a baronet whose name was known all over the world—one of the Roth- childs, and when Mr. Gladstone was considering the financial effect of his schemes,and more especially the effect of his plan upon the money market of London he turned to him and said, "What a head he has." (Hear. bear, and loud ap- plause.) With regard to the Home Rule Bill, he did not think it perfect any more than he thought the Land Pur- chase Scheme perfect. He did not like the exclusion of the Irish from the Parliament at Westminster—(hear, hear,)— and he agreed with Mr. Chamberlain very strongly indeed in his reasons for disliking that exclusion; for he wanted the Parliament of Westminster to be the supreme—the im- perial Parliament. He agreed with Mr. Chamberlain too that it was a wrong thing for us to ask the Irish to pay money to us that we might spend it, and that they should not have

Loud applause.) He could not doubt that the great cherne of Mr. Gladstone, the misterpiece of constructive ; statesmanship, would receive the respectful and favourable consideration of his fellow-countrymen. (Loud applause.) ; The motion was enthusiastically and unanimously car* tied.

Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., who was received with continued applause, said :—Our frieed Mr. Handley has promised that I shall give you some account of my experience since that woeful night in Northwich. (Laughter.) My experience on that occasion is almost too sad to relate, for I hardly thought I should get home whole. (Laughter.) One moment it seemed to me that my right arm was coming off, and the next that the other was to be torn out of its socket. Fora full half mile I bad an enthusiastic admirer on one shoulder, another on the other, and another with his arms round me. I bad a powerful young man on each side of me, and it was just as much as they could do to keep me on my legs. When they got into the house they stretched their arms and said, "Now we know what it is to escort a popular candidate." (Applause.) Compared with that, i my times since have been "piping times of peace." Never. theless, stirring tino s indeed, and anxious times. We have I not known what a day may bring forth for our party and I for the welfare of our fellow-countrymen. Time and again has it seemed to us that the happiness of millions was trembling in the balance, and great has been the ! responsibility of those men who have ventured to ' disturb tlae unity of the Liberal party. I am thank- ful to say that Dever had I teen tempted for one moment to swerve from my loyalty to you and Bay loyalty to my leader. (Applause.) but the strain is over, and we shall lie down together, the lion and the lamb; or, as Sir Win. Harcourt said a night or two ago, "a fatling shall lie down with them—aye, and perhaps even a little child from South Paddington." (Applause.) The little child was on the other side of the table, the noble Lord Randolph Churchill. When I got to London on the 12th January I was as a sheep without a shepherd—(laughter)— for I did not know where to go nor when to be there; and you see I was in a difficulty. A general sort of an idea had that I had to get to the House of Commons, but to which door I had not the ghost of a notion. I made up my mind many years ago that I would not go there without a free right, and ask nobody any questions, but after all I had to ask questions. I went to these appointed guardians of law and order, the "bobbies"— (laughter)—and they put me right, and they "moved me on." (Renewed laughter.) So, by slots degrees, I found where to hang my coat and where to depcsit my het. It is rather a remarkaole thing that the place for your coat and the place for your hat are a very long way apart. A mem- ber entering the House of Commons has three doors to go through, and then he comes to the cloak room, round which there are hooks for coats, hut not for hats, and above each book is writteu a member's name, and the alphabet deter- mines where a man is to hang his coat; and I am not far from the door. Strange to say, my coat hangs between those of Mr. Bruce and Mr. Bryce. Mr. Bryce is my double, and I have been taken for Mr. Bryce over and over again; and am happy to say that he and I have agreed that neither of us will have any need to fear that the other will do some thing that the other would not like to have attributed to him—(applause)—for he is a decent sort, and he has come to the conclusion that I am too. (Laughter.) When the new member—they have a way of calling them- selves "young members "—and the thinner a man is on the top the oftener he calls himeelf a young member— (laughter)—goes out of the room he has a great many stairs to climb, and as some of the "young members" are over 80, they don't all get up. with great comfort. Mr. Brunner then described the mode of entering the House of Commons by members, the system by which the seats for the day were secured and the arriving of the declaration of the Queen's consent to a bine He said : When first I addressed the delegates in Runcorn I promised to do my business in a business-like fashion, and one way in which I thought of setting about it was to open an office in London, in which the business of the constituency could be done. That office is &pen, and the business is being carried on. I ventured not very long ago to say that I should be pleased during reasonable hours to see any gentleman from this division, and plucking up my ceurage, I ventured to add that the ladies might come to. (Laughter.) lam not very often ' there myself, but my secretary is a very good-looking young man. (Laughter.) Now, ladiesand gentlemen, honour me with a visit when you come to London. (Applause.) I have not had any local bills from this constituency to attend to. When it happens that any of your authorities have any local buslness to attend to, depend upon me. I have offered my services to the Salt Chamber of Commerce. promised when I was at Runcorn I should not be all salt, and this is the first time You have heard of salt this evening. I have done a little bit of work fer Runcorn. I presented a petition from the improvement Com- missioners in favour of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. (Applause.) I ought to have told you a little while ago that it is one of the first duties of a member of Parlia- ment who desires to act in accordance with the traditions of the House, to leave his card upon the Speaker. I left my card upon the Speaker, and in due course was invited to attend his levee, and my wife said very beautiful I looked when I went. (Laughter.) A velvet cut-away coat, a splendid cocked hat, velvet continuations, and silk stock- ings, and the loveliest buckles en my shoes that ever you saw. (Renewed laughter.) Thetis not all. Such a sword! I really must have been, though I aid not think so myself, perfectly beautiful. (Loud laughter.) I went to the levee, and was very much humbled to find that I was a poor grub amongst a lot of brilliant butterflies, for the men there were positively blazing with all sorts of colours and the most brilliant uniforms ; and Mr. Dillwyn, Radical amongst Radicals, had blossomed out until it was almost impossible to identify the man who sat in the House of Commons with a shockingly bad hat—(laughter)—in the brilliant speci- men who was present in the noble rooms. Round the walls of the reception room are portraits of former speakers, and amongst them was plain John Smith, who was speaker of the House of Commons in 1705. Well, I know John Smith as well as possible. (Laughter.) Electors of Runcorn, I have been trying to do my duty by you. I have been regu- lar in my attendance. I have got to the House early, and I have left early—that is early in the morning. (Laughter and applause.) Let me add one word of thanks to you, and to all my friends in the Nortlawich division, for giving me the privilege of sitting in the same house with William Ewart Gladstone. (Applause.) This I may venture to say will be his last Parliament, and I believe that my children and my children's children will look back with fondest I pride to the day when their forefather helped in the great work which that good man is doing te-day. (Ape please.) That work is one the echoes of witch will ring , down the roll of time, and not be forgotten as long as our children's children derive the benefit of the peace and good- , • will amongst the three nations. (Lout applaue.) ; A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Ghose on the motion of Mr. BRUNNER.

Mr. F. Scott sang "The Speaker's eve," which was en- thusiastically encored, and be responded. Mr. Clegg gave his experience of Mark Twain, and then the programme of miscellaneous items which had been arranged was aban- boned owing to the late hour, the speeches having occupied a longer time than was expected.

div.head: NEW POLLING DISTRICTS
div.p: THE NEW POLLING DISTRICTS

FOR WARRINGTON. The Town Council, by a unanimous vote at its meeting on Thursday evening week, adopted a scheme for the sub-division cf the borough into 15 polling dis- tricts. It will be of interest if we give a few par- ticulars as to its operation. To being with the electors in Latchford ward: Instead of the voters in this ward all polling as before at St. James's Schoolroom, those who live beyond Black Bear Bridge will vote at Wash Lane Schoolroom, and those on this side the bridge at St. James's Schoolroom. The South-west ward is divided into two polling districts—those voters residing beyond Bank Quay Bridge polling at the Working-men's Mission Schoolroom, and those resi- dent on this side of the bridge voting as before at Cairo-street School. The South-east ward is also divided into two polling districts—voters included within part of the ward bounded by Bridge-street. Buttermarket-street, Irlam-street, and one side of Napier-street polling at the Schoolroom, Lower Bank- street, and the remainder at the National Schoolroom, Church-street. The North-east ward is divided into four polling districts—voters living in Winwick -road, Orford, one side of Orford-lane and Pinner-brow, polling at the Catholic Schoolroom, Watkin-street ; those resident within that part of the ward bounded by Winwick-street, from the C?ntral Station to Pinners-brow, one side of Orford-lane and Orford- avenue, the Barracks and the Cheshire Lines Railway back t , the Central Station, polling at St. Peter's: those resident in the. ward within the part bounded by W inwick -street, Horsemarket- street, Buttermarket - street, Irlara-street, one side of Fennel street and Brick-street, to Battersby-lane bridge, returning to the Central Station by the Cheshire Lines Railway polling at the Old Wesleyan Schoolroom, Buttermar- ket-street ; and the remainder of the ward, which includes all School-brow, Church-street, Eoc.. at Brick- street Schoolroom. The North-west ward is divided into five polling districts—voters in Winwick-street and road, Dallam-lane, and one side of Bewsey-street polling at St. Anne's Schoolroom; those within the boundary of Sankey - street, Horsemarket- street. Bewsey-street, Bewsey-road, to the Bridge, and thence by the London and North-Western Rail- way to Bank Quay, polling at the Drill Shed; voters resident beyond Bewsey Bridge will most prob- ably have a temporary place erected until the district possesses some more permanent structure; one part of the voters resident beyond Froghall Bridge will vote at St. Mary's Schoolroom, Liverpool-road, and the remainder at St. Barnabas' Schoolroom, Lovely-lane. It can hardly be doubted that the operation of this scheme at future elections, 'both parliamentary and municipal, will be such as to fully justify the hopes of its promoters. One pleasant feature of the matter is that no additional emponse will be incurred, the number of officials at present required being sufficient to carry out the new arrangements. Both political agents have been consulted as to the working of the scheme. but Mr. H. Roberts, being a member of the Town Council, has been mainly concerned in pre- paring it.

div.p: a voice in the spending of it. (Hear, hear.) The Irish would be left in a position of subordination and degradation, and depend upon it they would not be proud of their con- nection with England, and we who put the shame upon them would not be proud of it either. He wished to do what in him lay to maintain the connection between Eng- land and Ireland as firm and as strong as it could be done and he wanted to bring it about that Englishmen and Irish- men should hold up their heads and be proud of each other. (Applause.) Alluding to the secessionists from Mr. Glad- stone, Mr. Brunner spoke of the Marquis of Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. Trevelvan in terms of appreciation. Then Mr. Heneage had gone. But did they ever bear of Mr. Heneage before? Believe him, they would not suffer very much if they never heard of Mr. Heneage again. (Ap- plause and laughter.) The man who looked after the Queen's horses had gone. (Laughter.) Mind, he gave up a thou- sand a year when he went. (Renewed laughter.) The man, too, who looked after the Queen's dogs had departed. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Brunner) did not suppose they ever heard the names of these gentlemen before, so that it was not worth while repeating them. (Laughter.) The Irish mem- bers were taking a very cool headed and very cautions posi- tion over this matter, and like the very good men of business they are had made up their minds to get as good a bargain as they possibly could for themselves. (Hear, hear.) There were some very fair men of business on the Liberal side, and when the bargain came to be struck both would be satis- fied. He was very much grieved to hear Mr. Parnell object strongly to the appoirtment of the Receiver-General of whom he bad spoken. Mr. Gladstone said, and he believed him absolutely, that it was not on account of any fears that he had with regard to the payment of the money, but it was to satisfy a very peculiar set of men, and that set of men was those who lend the money to the English Exchequer. And he advised the Irish people with the greatest earnest- ness to leave the provision as he proposed it, in order that I the men who lent the money should be perfectly satisfied that they were going to get their interest and the repay- ment of tbeir capital in due time, and so that Irish credit should be maintained at as high a point as possible. He (Mr. Brunner) yielded to no man, Irishman or Englishman, in his desire for the good of Irishmen, and the declaration of Mr. Parnell that the appointment of a Receiver-General would be felt to be offensive in Ireland was a declaration that gave him great pain. He intended to lay his views be- fore• Mr. Parnell, and he wanted to have their opinion about it. Did they believe that when Mr. Gladstone recommended such an appointment he intended to put a slight upon Ireland? (Cries of "No.") He could not believe it, and he was satisfied that no MAR who voted in support ef the proposal of Mr. Gladstone would have the ghost of an idea of putting a slight upon Ireland. (applause.) He was heartily pleased that they agreed with hini, and he would tell Mr. Parnell that they did. He had heard a good deal of talk ' since he had been in London doing their work about an idea that was alluded to by Mr. Pope, that a member of Parlia- ment was not a delegate. He agreed with Mr. Pope, that if men want to be worthily served they must leave their ser- vant's hand free. They must first pick the best man they can find, and then leave him free to do what he thought best in their interest. (Hear, hear.) With their permission he would keep his freedom. Although, as he had told them, neither one nor the other of theee billz is perfect, yet he in- tended to take this position, that if one or the other pre- sented to his mind a large balance of good he was going to vote for it. (Cheers.) He was very much obliged to them far their welcome that day, and extremely thankful to his friends who had given up to him two days which he had in- tended to devote to meetings in other parts of the con- stituency. (Cheers.) The resolution was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN intimated that it was thought desirable to appoint a permanent chairman of the Council. Mr. BRUNNER proposed that Mr. James Handley should be appointed to the position. There was no man in the copstituency to whom they owed more. (Applause.) Mr. Handley's services had been invaluable. He had a clear bead, a warin heart, and a civil tongue, and when those three things went together they made up a man who was not very far short of perfection. (Applause.) Mr. FLETCHER, in seconding the motion, said that the Council would derive great benefit by having Mr. Handley to preside over them. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried by acclamation, and the pro- ceedings concluded. THE EVENING SOIREE.

div.head: MR. BR-UNNEP.'S EXPERIENCES IN PARLIA-
div.p: MR. BR-UNNEP.'S EXPERIENCES IN PARLIA-

MENT. In the evening a soiree was held in the Public Hall. There was a good attendance of ladies and gentlemen, Mrs. BruEner being amongst the audi- ence. Mr. James Handley, J.P., presided, and on the platform were Mr. J. T. Brunner, &1.P., Mr. Lalma- hon Mose (Liberal candidate at Deptford last general election), Dr. O'Keeffe (Widnes), Messrs. Robert Shaw, S. C. Beckett, T. Handley. B. Kniveton, J. Morrison (Widnes), F. J. Norman, S. Pope, J. Bridge- water, and W. Handley (general secretary). The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said they, the huncorn Liberal Association, had thought it well to call them together that they might make a better ac- quaintance with their member, whom they were glad to see with them. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner had had almost three Months' hard work in the Homo of Commons, and that was the first time they had been able to get hold of him, and they wished him there to give an account of his adventures and experiences in that august assembly. He knew from what he had said that afternoon that he was very glad to be with them, and he felt that he deserved a holiday, and be felt it his duty as well as a privilege to see his constituents at Runcorn; and he (the speaker) was sure they would Rive him that evening, as they did that afternoon' a hearty wel- come. (Applause.) Alluding to tke Irish schemes, the chairman said he was sure their affection for Mr. Gladstone must have been increased from what they knew of him dur- ing the last few days. His physical ability and energy had ' shown rip to a wonderful extent, and they hoped that God , would spare his life for many years that he might put the crowning stone on his career, the pacification of Ireland.

(Applause.') Mr. KNIVETON moved a resolution similar in terms to the one passed at the Council in the afternoen. In doing so, he congratulated them upon the circumstances under which they were gathered together. For the first time, he believed, they had got a member of Parliament with them when there was no election pending. (Applause.) The resolu- tion spoke of thanking Mr. Gladstone for his bold, states- manlike efforts to pacify Ireland. He thought those thanks were well earned. (Cheers.) Had it not been for him he did not know when this Irish question would have been settled. The question was so vast and so complicated that it required the most penetrating and clear intellect, and a sympathetic heart. And that wee what they had in their noble leader, Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) The task might be a difficult one, but they were sanguine of success. They were confident of it. His past successes were a pledge of his future victory. He must triumph. He was werking in the cause of justice, and therefore it must eventually suc- ceed. (Loud applause.) Mr. ROBERT &Lew; who had a most cordial reception, seconded the motion. He said he did not think they ever met to consider any question fraught with greater conse- quences than the present. He felt sure that the people of Runcorn were not like some of the hasty persons who had long ago examined, as far as they were prepared to examine, and given a verdict upon the question before the country at the present time. He felt sure that it was a question that required an amount of consideration, and a question on which they would not be hasty in forming a conclusion off hand. One thing they might rest satisfied upon, and that was that the measure had been conceived with a desire to do justice to a down-trodden people—(hear, hear)—people who had for more than 100 years been striving against difficulties to secure a livelihood—(applause)—and who had scarcely been enabled to secure anything at all. He thought that the people of this country had come to this conclusion, that this world was intended by the Creator of it, by the Creator of man, that man should be as happy as it was possible to make him during the short period for which he inhabited it. (Applause.) He thought that the people of this country would assist the Government to do a simple act of justice by gitng the landlord what was fairly due, but no more, and not allow him to sell out at a big price because he wanted a big price. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that the landlord had been tak- ing from the country a great deal more than he ought to have taken—(hear, hear, and applause)—and he was sure they would easily understand the question Justice was all they wanted. (Applause.) They who were so magnanimous and so liberal when the question of oppres- sion and wrong was taking place in Europe and in different parts of the world felt it was a very hard case indeed if, when it came to their own doors, in their own cOuntry, their own flesh and blood—because Ireland was a part of the country, and had as much right to justice as any English- man there—if they could not help them ;an therefore he thought that one of the first coneitions was that they should manfully support the Grand Old Man. (Applause.) Don't let them be afraid of those false arguments that if they gave a Parliament to Ireland they would be separated. Why, they allowed the people in the Isle of Man to manage their own affairs, and nobody had ventured to say that they were a separate nation. They belonged to us and were part of us, and still made their own laws, and managed their own affairs, Why could not Ireland do a similar thing? His own impres- sion was that asto union they would be infinitely strengthened. He believed that without dipping deeply into the pockets of the British taxpayer the scheme that had been propounded would be carried, and the people of Ireland would be found in the end to be as honest and as upright as any of those who were assembled together. Therefore, he seconded the resolu ion heartily to support the present Parliament in carrying their measure. (Loud applause.) handful fLultd.oraf Irishoiiuie Glaunodsl onr,dws,hpoerwhaasp s receivedthew worst th classil ppl aoufset,h e said he, with the exception of ono or two questions con- nected with subordinate and minor details, had come to the conclusion, after all the impartial and earnest consider- ation that he was capable of devoting to this question, that the scheme proposed by Mr. Gladstone, on the whole, was ' a large, a just, and a wise measure, worthy of the respect- ful and favourable consideration of the country, and worthy, too, of the unrivalled genius and great fame of the illus- trious statesman by whom the proposal .was made. (Ap- plause.) The policy of continued coercion was only pos- sible as long as Parliament represented the views of a limited and privileged class. But now that the sceptre had passed away from a section to the whole of the nation, he, for himself, declined to believe that the democracy of Great Britain would be willing to coerce their brethren in Ireland in order to pander to the prejudices or to gratify the spirit of ascendancy of a bigoted minority for the benefit of a 1 human race, and for a handful of uureaucratic officials. \

THE EXAMINER.

div.head: SATURDAY APRIL 24, 1886.
div.p: SATURDAY APRIL 24, 1886.

MR. GLADSTONE'S Land Purchase Schemer is now before the nation; and instead having the effect that was predicted of namely, that of alarming and irritating all sections of the community, it must be con' fessed that it has found support where support was least expected. A few weeks ago Radicals like Mr. LABOUCHERE yen' tured to urge that the Prime Minister would do well to stick to his Houle Rule proposals, and abandon his Land Pur- chase project. But they knew not what MO said ; for Mr. GLADSTONE shows himself to., be much wiser than his critics. To-day, 11 there were a poll of the Radicals of the country on the question of expediency a 5 altogether apart from principle, the result would be an emphatic declaration in favour of standing by both great bills as neces' sary to the success of the one stupendous scheme. The other week we preached pa- I tience to those. who were condemning the Land Scheme before they knew anything about it, and we urged that it was safe to say it "would not violate any sound principle. of finance." While sincerely believing this, we had no conception that it would be pos- sible to formulate a measure for buying out the Irish landlords which would be so free from objections, so workable on the face of it, as the new Land Purchase Bill proves to be. The general impression has been that if Irish land was purchased with English gold for the benefit of Irish tenants, Englishmen, as Mr. TREVELYAN put it, would never again see the colour of their money;. tenants would not be willing to pay anything to. the Eng- lish Government when there was a bad sea- son; and they would be backed indirectly, if not directly, by a Home Rule Parliament. But Mr. GLADSTONE has foreseen and pro- vided against all this; he makes the Irish Parliament, which will provide what is to be known as the State Authority, responsible not only for the collection of the rent, but ensures that the fulfillment of contracts shall be matter, as it were, of life and death. The rents must be collected, or the Irish:, and not the Enalish, Government will be the sufferers. This is as it should be ; for if England is to lend money. at a low rate of interest for the benefit of Ireland there oughtAto be absolute security for it. And what is the security, it may be asked? We shall require from Ireland; as an annual Im- perial contribution for all purpcses, including interest on the money advanced under the Land Bill, a sum of £6;24.2,000 ; and, to, quote Mr. GLADSTONE, "that is secured upon Li 0,850,000, no portion of which can be ap- plied to any other purpose until the whole of our £6,24.2,000 has been liquidated." There is a margin, it will be seen, of £6,608,000t and if it were a question of a mortgage on ground rents that is a, margin which in any country would be accepted as ample security. The fact that under the Home Rule Bill the Prime Minister has safeguarded this country by our retaining control of customs and,ex- cise has well nigh disarmed; those who were disposed to object to the. Land Purchase scheme on financial grounds. As the matter stands, the Irish !Parliament will be 3ntirely dependent on the balance which accrues- (after paying "all dues and demaads " to, England) as a means of carrying on the civil Government of Ireland. Mr. PARNELL does not like the idea of the Irish State Authority having to collect the rent charges, and pour the money into the lap of aa English Receives-General.;, but it is just what we do like. If we are to find the money, we must have something to. do with fixing the secu- rity; and it will be as well for Irishmen to bear in mind that they themselves are inter- ested in establishing their creditupon a. sound basis. The man who goes into.businass with borrowed capital which he has received at a low rate of interest cannot afford to be too nice about provisions for "making, assurance doubly sure 't in the payment of interest, and the repayment of principal. And it is the same with new States; Ireland will do well to get the benefit of English credit upon such terms as the Prime Minister proposes; and Mr. PARNELL Will do well to show himself amiable and accommodating. A good deal has been said as to whether the total ad- vance should be FIFTY MILLIONS or ONZ HUNDRED MILLIONS; but for ourselves we do not think that is a matter of the first im- portance ; the great thing is to determine the bases upon which any sum, great or small, is lent; to see that they are such as give the debtor a fair opportunity of utilising it, and the creditor security of the soundest kind. We have dwelt sufficiently on the latter point; and, as regards the foxier-411

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: 'terms upon which Ireland will receive the 150,000,000 if the bill became law—we must say they are such as she could not possibly secure except in alliance with England. The English Government can obtlin money at three per cent; but if Ireland were cut adrift from this country, and left as a new State to make the best bargain she could in the open market, it is not unlikely that she vrot.ild have to pay five or even six per cent. This is a matter of vital importance to Ire- land at this juncture; and it is a matter, too, which those Englishmen would do well to con. sider who are so ready to suggest that Irish landlords should be left to make the best terms they can with the Irish rarlia• In.ent. It would be a sheer impossibility to either side to make such terms as Mr. GLAD- STONE can safely offer; and that, in other Words, is to say that the Irish landlords and the Irish Parliament would not be able to come to terms. Home Rule, without an equitable and workable Land Scheme, would be chaos come again; and it is because Mr. GLADSTONE sees this, and because he is not a make-shift politician that, once deciding to lake a new departure, he has grappled with 'the problem as a whole. With the Land Purchase Bill before us, we now perceive Illerits in the Home Rule proposals" which were previously hidden or obscured. We see how the PRIME MINISTER has acted on the theory that an Irish Parliament must have Power and authority legislatively as well as administratively in order to satisfy national aspirations. that the ties which bind must, with a view to their becoming silken cords love, be leading strings rather than chains. we see, too, how skilfully, and on every side, A. Ir. GLADsioNE has sought to protect every Interest, while opening the w 4 to changes which will revolutionise the Government of the country, The whole scheme is one Which, if it be loyally accepted by the Irish people, will go far to remove the causes of Misery, discontent, and disloyalty, and put Ireland at last on the highway to happi- Pess and prosperity. It is a scheme which Is noble in conception, which is just as well as genercus, and which is worthy therefore of a great statesman and a great nation.

THE result of the trial of ADELAIDE BART- '', Err for the murder of her husband being, as It Was, an acquittal, cannot have astonished anyone, and it is obvious from the cheering Which took place both inside and outside the court that it gave general satisfaction. 1)eoPle are governed a good deal in a matter Of this kind by feeling as well as by evidence, and from the moment the Rev. GEORGE bYSON was taken out of the dock and brought forward as a witness the feeling of the public set in favour of the female pri- soner. The conclusion come to was that the reverend but by no means revered gentleman was perfectly willing to sacrifice the woman, if he could only make sure of saving himself. This was the woman, too, he had professed to love ; and, as he admitted that he lied in ordEr to get possession of the chloroform by Which the deceased met his death, his conduct altogether was the reverse of commendable. If it be assumed, as it may be assumed, in view of the result of the trial, that Mrs. BARTLETT never had any intention of making an improper use of the drug, questionable as her conduct undoubtedly is in some respects, it is not so bad as that of Mr. DYSON himself. But with regard to the main issue, it will be noticed that the jury have been careful not to commit themselves to any affirmation of Mrs. BARTLETT'S innocence. Although bringing in a verdict of" not guilty," they say :—" We have considered the evidence, and, although we think there is the gravest suspicion attach- ing to the prisoner, we do not think there is Sufficient evidence to show how or by whom the chloroform was administered." This is What the Scotch would call a verdict of " not Proven ;" and we think it is the right view to take of the case. Granted that there is great force in the suggestion of the Judge that the deceased may have taken the chloroform himself whilst his wife slept, I there is also great force in the evidence bear- ing , upon the extraordinary relations of Mrs. BARTLETT and Mr. DYSON—relations which Were calculated to cause both of them to regard the death of Mr. BARTLETT as the best thing that could happen. A good deal has been said about the difficulty Mrs. BART- LETT would have in administering a fatal draught of chloroform; but there is one way in Which it might have been done quite easily. It will be remembered that the deceased ex- pressed himself on one occasion as not only believing in mesmerism, but as thinking that he was himself under mesmeric influence. What if he were subject to the mesmeric in- fluence of his wife, assuming she had such a power over him ? There would be no difficulty in that case in getting him to swallow chloroform or anything else, A " sub- ject" properly under " control " can be made to eat blacking in the belief that it is Custard; and would, if required, drink either Chloroform or vitriol as though it were cham- Pagne. There are people who dismiss mes- Merism as something ridiculous; but the Power of mesmerism is none the less a reality; and EDWIN BARTLETT, according to his own admissions, was just such a man as would be likely to make "a good subject." We have no proof, of course, that MTS. BARTLETT pos- sessed mesmeric power, or, if she possessed it, that she used it improperly, but since we are in the region of conjecture it is not un- reasonable to contend that an operation diffi- cult to an ordinary person might be easv to a tiesmerist. But the trial is at an end' and it is fitting that it should end as it has done—in giv- ing the prisoner the benefit of the doubt.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Mr. Brunner, M.P., has been giving an ac- count of his experiences in Parliament, and a description of himself as he figured in court dress. It is racy reading; it is as good as a Play.

The Warrington lads have done well in winning the cup, and their townsmen have (lone well in giving a dinner in their honour. Let them strive to stick to the cup—not their "cups," and they may win again.

The members of the Widnes Local Board know when they have got a good chair- man. Mr. F. H. Gossage has been elected :0 the post for the fifth time. Mr. Gossage s in point of service the "father "of the Board. He has served continuously since .867.

"The policeman's lot is not a happy one ;" tut it has its compensations. P.S. \Valley, now of Frodsham, has this week been pre- sented by the inhabitants of Runcorn with a gold watcb, good elbert, and purse of gold; and, what is better, it was accompanied with "golden opinions from all conditions of People."
More Protection ; the Russian Ministry of Domains is now granting a premium for the

export of meat from Libau and Reval to Eng- land. If foreigners go on in this way, Eng- land will be " ruined " by geting food for nothing; but we don't quite see how the foreigner is to grow rich in the meantime.

. Mr. Carvell Williams, M.P., calls atten- tion to the fact that the Home Secretary has expressed his regret at having misled the House of Commons in one or two details re- specting the Tarporley Burial case. Mr. Childers has found that it was not sufficient to depend upon the Rev. Canon Cooper's account of what happened. It is always as well to "hear both sides."

The authorities of the Corporation are tak- ing the right course in trying to put a stop to the obstruction of footpaths by butchers and others. It is bad enough to run against a townsman on the narrow footways; but worse to be shouldered into the street by shoulders of mutton. Of course, where tradesmen can prove their right, the right must be re- spected, and they must be bought out.

The Tories don't like the idea of Liberals making themselves gay with primroses on Primrose Day. But why not? The primrose was a pretty flower before Lord Beaconsfield was born, as it will be when, like last year's flowers, he is forgotten. Besides, as was remarked the other day to a puzzled Tory, there are Liberals who " rejoice " in the anniversary quite as much as the Conserva- tives.

It is stated that the Conservative party of the Clitheroe division have resolved, "in view of the probability of an early dissolution of Parliament," not to oppose there-election of Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth. It would be in- teresting to know whether their decision was in any way influenced by having also "in view " the licking they were likely to get. Sir Ughiredis majority at the General Elec- tion was 2,359.

The Liberals of the NorthwicV Division have been discussing Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule proposals at a meeting at Runcorn. Mr. Brunner's declaration in favour of Home Rule was cordially approved; and a resolu- tion was unanimously carried thanking Mr. Gladstone for "the bold, just, and states- man-like character of the proposed legisla- tion." In Runcorn, they do not do these things by halves; they are Radical go a-head electors.

When in doubt, please yourself. This seems to have been the rule on which one of the nominees of the Conservative party acted at the Board of Guardians election. ,As a party man, nominated by the party, he was expected to vote for all the party candidates. But it would seem that he had his doubts about five of the six official candidates; and so, as the story goes, when his voting paper was sent in it was found that he had toted for himself only. Oh, Number One, I love, I love but thee!

Sir William Cunliffe Brooks has been taking upon himself to speak of Mr. Glad- stone as "traitorous and treacherous" to England for taking measures to improve the government of Ireland. This is the way of grasping bankers and land-grabbing pluto- crats ; it is "traitorous " to lessen their chance of plundering the people. When Sir William ceases to talk nonsense about the Premier and Protection, he "may, perhaps, in such an hour "—as the song has it—be con- sidered fit to black Mr. Gladstone's boots.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Sr. AMBROSE SI7NDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.—An addition of 50 new books has recently been made to the library of this school.

CERTIFYINO SURGEON. Dr. J. O'Neil, of Farnworth' has been appointed certifying surgeon for Widnes under the Factory Acts, in place of Dr. Booth, resigned. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. On Sun- day morning the Rev. R. Yeatman, pastor of the above church, delivered a forcible and homely address to the young, and in the evening preached on the subject" Christ died foi the ungodly." CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. A meeting in connection with the newly-formed branch of the society was held on Monday evening in the boys' school- room, Woollen, the Rector, the Rev. G. H. Spooner pre- sided. The meeting was addressed by the Diocesan Secre- tary. ADDRESSES TO WORKING-MEN.—Tbe third of a series of Sunday evening addresses to working-men and their wives was preached by the Rev. R. G. Hughes, in the Milton Con- gregational Church, Simm's Cross, on Sunday evening, the subject being "The greatest plague." There was only a moderate attendance. THE WIDNES LIEERALS.—The following is a copy of a letter from Mr. E. W. Spencer Lyttelton to Mr. E. K. Mus- pratt:—" Mr. Gladstone desires me to acknowledge with his cordial thanks the receipt of the resolution on the subject of the Government of Ireland Bill, which you have done him the honour to forward to him on behalf of the Widnes Division Liberal Association." FAENWORTH CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SO- CIETy.—The members of this society gave an excellent en- tertainment in the National Schools, Farnworth, on Tuesday evening. Mr. James W. Davies presided. and there was a good attendance. A miscellaneous entertainment of vocal and instrumental music was admirably gone through, the Whines Church of England Temperance Society's Brass Band kindly assisted. TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. John Nolan, of Williani-street, Warrington-road, Widnes, has met with a terrible accident. About half-past ten at night, being under the influence of liquor, he went to a public-house near his home for some beer. As be was returning he slipped and fell upon the glass jug he was carrying. The broken pieces of glass cut his stomach open in a fearful fashion, and only slight hopes are held out of his recovery. NEW RATES FOR HALEWOOD AND DITTON.—On Thurs- day the Widnes magistrates sanctioned the laying of a poor rate of 2s Bcl in the for the township of Halewood to re- alise £3,031 ISs. There was £79 12s 4d recoverable ar- rears, principally owing by the railway company. Apoor rate of is 4d in the to produce £859 lOs was sanctioned for Ditton. The arrears amounted to £3l 35 2d, which was the subject of appeal. The sum consisted of tithes. ACCIDENT AT WlDNES.—Archibald McDonald, labourer at the works of Messrs. Mort Liddell and Co., and who lives in Gerrard-street, was admitted into the Accident Hospital, on Tuesday, suffering from scalded ancles. He was sitting on a plank placed across a lime-mud filter, in the act of eating his dinner, when the plank gave way and he fell into the filter, and his ancles were severely burned. Under the care of Dr. McDonnell he is progressing favour- ably. RUNCORN BOARD or CommissiorrEns.—A special meeting was held on Wednesday. Mr. P. Speakman presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Dobson, W. Fisher. H. J. Grine, E. Imison, W. Mellor, H. White, W. H. ',maker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and W. Baker (surveyor.)—On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Fisher, the seal of the Board was affixed to a new general district rate of 2s 2d in the for the year ending March 25th, 1887. DIPHTHERIA AT DITTON.—A serious outbreak of diph- theria has occurred at Ditton, in the family of a man named Cookson, who resides near the Ball Inn. Already two deaths have occurred, one on Saturday and the other on Monday, the victims being young children. There are still two other children in the family suffering from the disease, which is supposed to have been caused through defective drainage. As the unhappy parents are not in very good circum- stances, a subscription list has been opened, in order to help them. RuscoßN CIRCUIT WaSLEYAIf METHODIST SUNDAY ' Scnoor, Ihriox.—The annual meeting of the teachers and officers of the Sunday schools forming this union has been held in the Brunswick School-room. Tea was kindly pro- vided by Mr. R. Shaw, one of the visitors for the past year. After tea the chair was taken by the Rev. George Wood. The secretary read the statistical report, which showed that all the eight schools in the circuit are connected with the union—four town and four country. There are 223 teachers and 2,363 scholars en the books; 991 members of Bands of Hope; six libraries, containing 2,126 volumes. Mr. Alfred Harrison presented the visitors' report, which had been well prepared. It related an account of the visits paid to each school, and praise or censure was given where deserved or needed. Mr. Shaw followed with general remarks on school work. Several matters were then discussed by the meeting. Mr. A. Harrison and Mr. J. Unsworth were appointed visitors for the ensuing year, and Messrs. S. Pope and E. Taylor re- elected secretaries. KAY'S ComPourrn, a demulOent anodyne expectorant, for Coughs and Colds.
