ALBERT-ROAD WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.— The anniversary sermons were preached in the chapel on Sunday by the Rev. W. Cuthbert, of Didsbury. The e- lections amounted to about £2O. ON SUSPICION.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Frederick George Leach, 15 years of age, was nananded on suspicion of breaking into the Mill-brow Stone Delph Smithy. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE RAILWAY COMPANY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty sessions, on Thursday, James Murray. a youth, was summoned for having, on the 4th January, unlawfully travelled from Liverpool without hav- ing previously paid his fare. The prisoner, who absconded from the town at the time of the committal of the offence, pleaded guilty. The case was proved by Miss Atkinson and Alfred Rodgers, a porter, and the prisoner was tined I.os and costs. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Mr. (3. H. Danby, on behalf of the School Board, summoned the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school : Peter Riley, James Carr, John Bowyer, John Law, John Daley, John McCann, and Samuel Cartwright. Thomas Donovan, a boy, unmanageable by his grandfather, his ocly guardian, was sent to an industrial school. FOOTBALL.— Widnes v. Runcorn: A match between the second teams ef the above clubs was played at Widnes on Thursday. Widnes played a fairly representative second team, while Runcorn, through the absence of three of their second team men, played Woods, Speakman, an Wain- wright, of their first team. An excellent game resulted in a victory for Widnes by 1 try, 2 minors, to Runcorn 2 minors. The try was got by Parkinson. Wright attempted the kick, but failed. _

THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASH. - Joseph Houston, Pole, was brought up on remand at Widnes Petty Sessions charged with unlaw fully wounding Charles Meitchencavish also a Pole, at 56, Cromwell-street, on the 11th inst., by kicking him.—Superintendent Barker said he had seen the prosecutor in Whiston Workhouse Hospital that morning, and be was in a serious and dangerous condition, and un- able to attend court. The prisoner was therefore remanded for a week.

_ A FOREIGN TRIPP AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Annie Marcalis, an elderly Polish woman, was charged with stealing a sheet, value is, the property of James Bentham, of 48, Nelson-street. The sheet was missed from the house on the 12th inst., when the prisoner was there, and she was suspected. P.C. Liptrot made a search of the prisoner's house and found the stolen article.—The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. Mr. Frank Hopner, interpreter, in the employ of the Londonand North- Western Railway Company, officiated as interpreter. MR. GLADSTONE AND RUNCORN LIBERALS.—Mt. W. Handley, general secretary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association, has received the following letter with reference to the resolution passed at the Liberal meetings at Runcorn on Saturday last :—" 10, Downing-street, White- hall, April 21st, 188. Sir,-1 am directed by Mr. Glad- stone to inform you that he has received the communication which you have done him the honour to send him, and to convey to you his thanks for the expression of approval , and confidence in her Majesty's Government which it con- tains.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, G. W. SPENCER LYTTLETON." ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES —Patrick Murphy, a young man, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday charged with assaulting P.C. McDonald, and resisting P.C. Sisson in the execution of his duty. The evidence showed that at half-past eleven on Saturday, the 10th inst., the constables had two prisoners in custody for being drunk and disorderly in Widnes-road. The prisoner kicked Sisson on the knee, and then ran back amongst the crowd which had collected. Afterwards he struck McDon- ald a blow on the back of the head, felling him to the ground. The prisoner, who pleaded guilty to striking Mc- Donald, was sentenced to a fortnight's hard labour on each charge. ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—At the Petty Sessions an Thurs- day Joseph Newell, a boy, was convicted of stealing a bottle of cider, the property of Thomas Kinchlev, la- bourer, of 17, Wellington-street. He was ciuglat walking out of the house with the bottle in his possession. He was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod.—Julia O'Brien, a young woman, was charged with stealing a coat worth 10s, the property of John Donnell, from the dwelling- house of her mother, Caroline-street, on the 20th April. Donnell was a lodger in the house, and the coat was missed. Subsequently the prisoner pawned it with Mrs. Jameson, pawnbroker, Ann-street. The prisoner was sent to a month's hard labour.

DESERTION OF FAMlLY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. F. H. Gossage at Widnes Police Court on Thursday John Connolly was charged with deserting his wife and two children. Mr. S. H. Hartley represented the Guar- dians and Mr. Scannell proved the case. It appeared that on the 31st October Mr. Scannell found the prisoner's family imperfectly clothed and without food, and they were removed to Whieton Workhoupe, where they remained for some time. The prisoner when he left the town was in re- ceipt of 35s per week, and could well maintain his family by his family by his exertions. He had, however, been a great source of expense to the Union, as his family bad been in- mates of the Workhouse on nine occasions, and he had twice been committed to gaol for his neglect. The Bench sentenced the prisoner to three months' hard labour. ASSAULTING A GRANDMOTHEIL AT WIDNES. Michael Connolley, a young man, was charged with as- saulting Jane Tooley, his grandmother, aged 75, who lives at 9, Moon-street. On Monday evening the prisoner and his uncle were having a quarrel. The old woman attempted to separate them, when the pri- soner struck her several times on the face with his fist. Complainant, at a previous hearing, said he kicked her on the forehead, but now denied that statement.—Dr. MacLen- nan said he examined the old woman, who was suffering from a black eye and a lacerated and contused wound over the right eyebrow, and a small incised wound over the left eyebrow. They were serious wounds, and he had to stitch one of them up. A clog such as that worn by the prisoner might have caused the wounds. The prisoner was sentenced to two months' hard labour. DEATH OF A WIDNES JOURNALIST.— It is with regret that we record the death, after a prolonged and painful ill- ness, of Mr. J. P. Morewood, journalist,Widnes-road,Widnes, who was the representative of the "Liverpool Courier "and "Express "in that town. The deceased, who was 48 years of age, had a wide and varied experience as a journalist. Trained as a printer in one of the publishing houses in the metropolis, his tastes being literary, ho secured a situ- ation as a reporter about 25 years ago. The vicissitudes he had to experience during that long period formed an enter- taining topic of conversation amongst his confreres. At one part of his career he was proprietor and editor of a newspaper in Radcliffe, near Manchester, and was on the highway to prosperity; but in an unfortunate moment he was induced to become surety to a large amount for a per- son with whom he bad intimate relations.. The usual story of avoiding liability by the person most interested followed, and Mr. Morewood was the poorer by a thousand pounds, and his business prospects were ruined. Subsequently be held the position of editor and manager on several news- papers, about four years ago taking charge of a Widnes journal. He had made numerous friends in the chemical , town, through his ability and bonhomie, and his demise is the cause of widespread regret.—" Express." He leaves a wife and six children to mourn his loss.

CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The third annual concert by members of the singing classes, which have just concluded their season's work, was held on Monday evening, in Elles- mere-street school-room. The choral pieces, which are the chief feature of these concerts, were efficiently rendered by a well balanced choir of forty voices. The pieces were of the usual interesting character, and the audience showed their appreciation ot them by their heirty applause Seward's "With laugh and song" was especially well ren- dered, the choir entering into tbe spirit of the composition, and it was re-demanded. Mrs. Newall sang "Angels ever bright and fair," from Handel's "Theodora," with taste and feeling. Miss Cuizon gave an efficient rendering of the two songs allotted to her, her vocalisation of "I built a bridge of fancies," in the second part of the programme being es- pecially noticeable for purity of tone and distinct articula- tion. Miss Hammersley received a well deserved encore for her tasteful interpretation of " The mother's prayer." Miss Jones sang the old ballad, " Poor Bessie was a sailor's-wife." Handel's "Lord, remember David" was well interpreted by Mr. Holford, who gave in the second p..rt a vigorous rendering of "Ti's Standard Bearer." Mr. Scott took the place of Mr. A. Fox, and sang Gonnod's "Nazareth." In the second part he brought down the house by his rendering of "Peter Piper," and in response to a clamorous encore sang "Woman, lovely woman" in capital style. Mr. John Leathwood gave a pleasing version of "Thy gentle voice." Mr. Joseph Hatumereley received an encore forhis efficient rendering of "Three acres and a cow," and Messrs. Howard and T. Fox acquitted themselves well in the execution of the duet "David and Goliath." The concert was undou- btedly a success from a musical point of view. The audi- ence, though select, was of smaller proportions than the quality of the concert merited. In the session just con- cluded the classes have been very successful, and the results in the examinations have been quite satisfactory. This is a matter for congratulation to Mr. Holford, the conductor and teacher.

SIR RICHARD CROSS. We understand that ar- rangements are being made for a meeting of the Conservative party of the Newton Division. It will be held in the Viaduct Instkute, Earlestown, and will be addressed by Sir Richard Cross. DARING BURGLARY AT GOLBORNE.—About two o'clock on Friday morning Mrs. Martha Harrison, pawnbroker, Heath-street, Golborne, who lives alone, was awoke by hearing someone moving in her bedroom. She rose in bed and saw a man, who walked out of the room on seeing her sitting up. She got up and knocked on the bedroom wall to awake a neighbour. A constable happened to be walking the street, and hearing a noise went up to the house and could hear someone coming down- stairs. Immediately•afterwards a man came out of the door, carrying his clogs. The officer failed to seize him, but caught. him after a sharp chase. Meanwhile Mrs. Harrison raised her window to shout for assistance, and saw the man in the officer's custody. The officer entered the house and found that goods to the value of £5 had been moved from their places. The prisoner, whose name is John Johnson, was brought up on Saturday at the County Magistrates' Office, Warrington, and remanded to Newton Sessions.
MEDICINES, ELASTIC STOCXINGS, CHEMICLLS, DRUGS, /cc., by parcels post, under 11b., 3d. _. Kay, Brothers, Eltockport.— Advt.

/ MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEADIEN.—A. concert NHL be given by the band of the training ship Indefatigable, in Runcorn Public Hall, on the evening of Tuesday, the fourth of May. FOOTBM,L.—On Monday afternoon next a footi,4lt match will be played between Runcorn and Widnes on the ground at Irwell-lane. The kick-off is AC three o'clock. DEATH OF THE OLDEST LANCASHIRE MAGISTRATE. —On Monday the Rev. Richard Moore, vicar of Lund, died, aged 93, at the vicarage, near Kirkham. The deceased was the oldest but one clergyman of the Church of England, and was the oldest justice of the County Palatine. He conducted service up to about two years ago. MR. RYLANDS AND HIS CONSTITUENTS.—Mr. Peter Rylands, replying to telegrams and letters from Burnley, expressing disapproval of his having at- tended Wednesday night's meeting with Lord Salis- bury, writes—" I shall now restrict my opposition to the measure of Home Rule and Irish Land Pur- chase as far as may be to my votes and speeches in the House of Commons. I shall act mainly with Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Trevelyan and other Liberal members, who, though antagonistic to those measures, will not in any other way unite with the Conservatives in promoting party views." RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.—Tte monthly meet- ing was held on Monday, Mr. W. J. Shore in the chair. The Librarian reported that during March there had been issued from the lending department 1,873 books, being an increase of 420 over the cor- responding period of last year. The receipts amounted to .£1 16s 7d. Numerous gifts of books had been made to the Library during the month. The Librarian stated that since the Library was opened in 1882 the sum of £269 had been spent in the purchase of new books. It was decided to call a special meeting to consider the question of additional accommodation to the reading room, VISIT OF SANGER'S Cincus.—By our advertise- ment columns, it will be seen that John Sanger and Sons' Hippodrome, Circus and Menagerie -is about to pay a visit to Warrington and Widnes, being timed to appear at the latter place on May 7th, and at Warrington on May 6th, At Widnes the circus will be erected on ground adjoining the Grapes Inn, and at Warringtoa on the va- cant ground near the Post-office. There will be what are termed free novelty processions, which, being attended with much "pomp and circumstance,' will no doubt be witnessed with interest by large numbers. Sanger's establishment is one conducted on a large scare, and claims to be five times larger than any other exhibition in England. It is favoured with extensive Royal patronage, and its bill of fare is of such a nature as to attract all classes. No doubt many will take advantage of the visit, and give themselves the treat which the circus affords.

ARRIVAL OF THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER.— Bishop Moorhouse landed at Dover on Monday morning, and proceeded in the afternoon to London, where the right rev, prelate will consult with the Committee of Selection as to the choice of his suc- cessor at Melbourne. In the course of a conversa- tion with a correspondent the Bishop, referring to recent well-known disputes in the diocese, expressed his determination to ignore all former quarrels and to act as if they had been simply non-existent. The new Bishop and Mrs. Moorhouse will, upon their I arrival in the diocese, be the guests of Mrs. Fraser, rat Bishop's Court, Higher Broughton. It is gene- rally understood that the Bishop will eventually take up his abode permanently at the episcopal residence selected by his predecessor. So far, the Bishop has promised to preach at St. Peter's Parish Church, Bolton, on Sunday morning, May 9, and at St. Chad's Parish Church, Rochdale, on Sun- day, May 16. LOCAL CASES AT LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS. —The General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the Hundred of West Derby commenced in the Sessions house, Islington, on Tuesday morning. The Earl of Derby presided, and there was a full bench of magistrates. The following local cases were dis- posed of :—Arthur C. J. Bennett (31), draughtsman, for stealing, at Warrington, on the 13th March, two photographic lenses, the property of Henry Newton and Company, five years' penal servitude. James Bibby (14), labourer, for stealing, at Bold, on the 11th March, a mare, the property of George Fox, three months' imprisonment, with hard labour. Mary Holland (40), for having, at West Leigh, on the 13th March, stolen 21b. butterine, the property of Ralph Hague, three months' hard labour. Wm. Kennedy (34), for stealing, at Rainforo, on the 11th March, the sum of £55, the moneys of Andrew Murdoch, six months* hard labour. Patrick Haverty (49), labourer, for having, at Parr, on the 20th ult., unlawfully and maliciously wounded Bridget Haverty, six months, with hard labour. On Wednes- day the following cases were dealt with, viz. : Anthony Canavan (21), labourer, for having, at War- rington, on the 4th April, unlawfully wounded Thomas Murray with intent to inflict grievous bodily harm, was sentenced to four months' impri- sonment. Joseph Hampson (20), labourer, for hav- ing, at Eccleston, on the 20th February, knowingly uttered two base half crowns, was sentenced to eight months' imprisonment, with hard labour. Jas. Salmon and Michael Hanley were each sentenced to three months' imprisonment for having, at 'Vin- die, on the 21st March, feloniously broken and en- tered the warehouse of Thomas Sanders, and stolen 180 oranges and 121 b. weight of apples. Michael Kenny (30), glass blower, was sent to gaol for six months, with hard labour, for having, at Windle, on the sth April, indecently assaulted a girl named Ada Clisham, aged eight years. James Thelloe (28), collier, for having, at Sutton, on the 21st March, fel- oniously and indecently assaulted Ellen Brennan, I was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment.

ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The annual meeting of Widnes Local Board was held yes- terday afternoon week. Present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. F. H. Gossage, E. Carey, T. Handley, W. W. dossage, J. Mid. wood, R. Cook, F. Heyes, J. Taylor, H. Gaskell, junr., .1. Houghton, S. Sadler, and J. T. Allen (clerk). APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN. Mr. Carey had much pleasure in proposing that Mr. F. H. Gossage be requested to take the chair for the ensuing year.—Mr. T. Handley seconded the motion. They had had four years' experience of Mr. Gossage in the chair, and he (Mr. Handley) thought he had proved his fitnegs to preside over the deliberatLons of the Board.—The motion was carried unanimously.—The Chairman then took the chair which had been occupied pro tern by Mr. Allen, and thanked the members for that mark of their confidence. If they could work together in the en- suing year as they had done in the past two years, he thought the business of the Board would be carried on effi- ciently and without undue loss of time. (Hear, hear.)—The Clerk said he had been searching the records of the Board and he found that Mr. Gossage had been a member continu- ously since 1869, and during the last four years as chair- man. Mr. Gossage had served the tocvaship longer than any person who had over been on the Board. THE COMMITTEES —The following committees were ap- pointed: Finance—Messrs. Handley (chairman), Heyes, Brown. Cook, Midwood, and Wright. Health : Dr. O'Keeffe (chairman), Messrs. Cook, Heyes, Houghton, Hus- band, and Midwood. Highway—Messrs. E. Carey (chair- man), Houghton, Husband, W. W. Gossage, Sadler, and Taylor. Gas and Water Committee Messrs. Gaskell (chairman), Brown, W. Gossage, Taylor, Sadler, and Wright. General Purposes—Consists of the chairman of each com- mittee with the addition of Messrs. Wright, Sadler, and Heyes.
TENDERS.—It was decided to advertise for tenders for the erection of the infectious diseases hospital and the public library.—There was no other business.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffeulkes. UNSUCCESSFUL SUITORS.—Mr. J. 0. Jackson, grocer, Bridge-street, Runcorn, sued John Dawson, of Bridgewater- street, Runcorn, formerly a shopkeeper at Weston Point, for £4 lOs for a firkin of butter sold and delivered. Mr. Lake appeared for the plaintiff. The defendant appeared in per- son, and denied the delivery of the butter. The plaintiffs carter failed to prove that he had delivered it, and judgment was given for the defendant —Thomas Unsworth. labourer, Five Crosses, was sued by Samuel Peacock, shoemaker, Frodshatn, for lie money lent and repairs to shoes for de- fendant's daughter. Mr. Burton appeared for the defendant, who denied having borrowed any money, and said the shoes were repaired for a married daughter. Judgment for the defendant.

CONTEMPT OF COURT.—Samuel Peacock, shoemaker, Frodsham, sued John Antrobus, of Ship-street, Frodsham. for 13s 9d for repairs to shoes and several articles of fur- niture. His Honour gave a verdict against the defendant at 5s per month, whereupon the defendant's daughter, who is barmaid at the Queen's Head, High-street, Runcorn, shouted "He can't pay any such sum. He can only pay half a crown." His Honour ordered the woman into c us- tody. At the conclusion of the business of the court she was brought before the judge, and apologised for her con- duct. His Honour said she must behave herself in a court of justice, or she would be sent to gaol. She was dis- charged.

ICLOAN TRANSACTION.—An action was brought by Archibald Dutton, blacksmith, 48, New Egerton-street, Run- corn, against George and Elizabeth Thompson, Luton-street, Widnes, Joseph Jameson, Mersey-road, Widnes, and James Dutton, Church-street, Runcorn, to recover the sum of £26 18s 6d, being the amount of a contribution due in re- spect of a loan. Mr. Cartwright. solicitor, Chester, ap- peared for the plaintiff, Mr. T. J. Peters for Thompson and his wife, Mr. J. W. Knowles for Jameson, and Mr. F. A. Lake for James Dutton. Mr. Cartwright said the plaintiff was induced in an unfortunate moment to become surety in a loan transaction made by George and Elizabeth 'I homp- son. The sum of £25 was advanced by the Union Loan and Discount Company. to Thompson and his wife for Jameson, and aprontissory note dated the 3rd July, 1852, was signed by Joseph Jameson, James Dutton, Mehl.

bald Dutton, as sureties, besides the Thompsens• The Thompsons did not pay a single shilling on account of the loan, and on the 6th March, 1884, a writ was issued against Archibald Dutton as the most substantial of the sure- ties, and judgment was signed and execution levied upon his effects. Dutton made arrangements with the company, by which he paid the sum of £2B 103, and the company agreed to give further time for the balance of the judgment, and upon he and his cousin James Dutton giving a promis- sory note for £l5 lOs 81. James Dutton made a payment, and reduced the amount to £lO 93, which had been subse- quently paid. The plaintiff now sued to recover a contri- bution from each of the defendants. After hearing the evi- dence his honour gave judgment against Thompson for the full amount claimed, and against Jameson for £7 10s.. A non-suit was entered in favour of James Dutton and Mrs. Thompson.

PRESENTATION TO P.S. WALLEY, OF FRODSHAM. Police sergeant %Valley, of Frodsham, formerly of Run- corn, was the recipient of a handsome testimonial to the esteem in which he is held by the inhabitants of Runcorn. on Wednesday evening, when many of his friends and a number a tradesmen in the town assembled in the Drill Hall, to do him honour. Daring his ten years' residence in Run- corn Sergeant Walley, through the faithful and intelligent discharge of his duties, won the favour an goodwill of all the law-abiding citizens, and on his removal to Frodsharn, several months, ago, it was determined to recognise his public services in a substantial manner. Messrs. P. Smith, S. Yarwood, and F. C. Price commenced a subscription list, and quickly had in band a considerable sum of money. A beautiful double-cased gold watch, gold albert, and a purse of gold formed the pteient, and the watch bore the following inscription : Presented to Sergt. Philip Walley by the magistrates and tradesmen of Run- corn, as a token of esteem for the urbanity shown by him in the discharge of his numerous duties during ten years service. March, 1886. P. Smith, treasurer." Superintendent Leah, who made the presentation, said he had the utmost pleasure in testifying to the ability of Ser- geant Walley. When he (Superintendent Leah) came to Runcorn a perfect stranger two years ago, he found Ser- geant Welley on the spot where he had been stationed for some eight years, and he was net long before he found out his worth as a police sergeant. (Applause.) His assis- tance to him • as a straneer was very valuable He was certainly gratified that his efforts had tieen so much appreciated by the respectable inhabitants of Runcorn. He had the greatest pleasure in handing the gold watch, guard, pendant, and a nurse of gold to Sergeant %Valley. tie trusted that he would long live to enjoy the use of the gift, and that it would enceurage him to be a protector to law-abiding people and a terror to evil doers. (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Hankineon said, as an inhabitant of Runcorn, he begged to convey the expression of his goodwill towards Sergeant Walley. He hoped that in his new sphere of duty Sergeant Walley would succeed in winning the respect of the public as he had in Runcorn. (Applause.) Sergeant Walley said he was exceodingly grateful for the very handsome present of which he had been the recipient ; but while he valued that, he cared more for the feelings which had pPoropted the gift. He was not a speaker, and if he filled to express his thanks in words, he felt none the less sincerely the great kindness of his friends. He felt proud that the inhabitants of Runcorn had ever thought that he was deserving of such a handsome present, and gratified to receive it from their hands. It was his chief aim to do his duty honestly and straightforwardly, and be hoped to succeed in carrying out that object. He thanked the subscribers to the fund, and begged to ac- knowledge the efforts of the promoters for their very great and unexpected kindness. (Applause.) Mr. P. Smith, in moving a vote of thanks to Supt. Leah for making the presentation, to Captain Haziehurst for the use of the Drill H• 111, and to Mr. Player for his services, said the fund had been subscribed to by 90 persons, whose subscriptions averaged a half-guinea each. He hoped he would long live to wear the watch and guard which had been presented to him. (Applause.) The metion was carried and the company separated.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Present— Mr. T. 6. Timmis, J.P. (chairman), the Rev. Fathers Pine. can, and Clarke, Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon, Imison, Robinson, Glover, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Danby (clerk). PROSECUTIONS.—The District Education Committee re- ported that during the month of March (five weeks) there were 118 applications for the piyment of school fees. and 332 parents appeared before the committee for contraven- tion of the Ediacation Act. Fees were recommended to 13, paid in 108 cases, and 26 persons were convicted by the magistrates.

FINANCE.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to. £944 8s 10J, and repor- ted that the receipts for the month were school fees for Sitnm's Cross .L 54 93 7d, Warrington-road £22 17s 6d, West Bank 1:,44 Bs. The minutes were passed on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

ALLEGED BREACH OF HONOUR.—After some discussion as to the propriety of putting such a question, the follow- ing letter addressed to Mr. Glover by the Rev. Father Fine- gan was read :—"At the list meting of the School Man- agement Committee Mr. liaison brought forward an expres- sion of yours that the committee had better let the affair of Mr. Danby's drop, as a friend of his (Mr. Imison's) was concerned in the matter. As it appears you have infor- mation on this subject which the committee does not possess, I am requested, as chairman of the committee, to ask you for an explanation on the subject."—The Chairman re- marked that be did not think the time of the Board should be taken up with discussing matters of opinion which mem- bers had expressed outside. He did not wish them to de- generate into a vestry. (Laughter.)—Mr.Glover submitted that the public ought to know where and when he used the words attributed to Eim.—Mr. 'unison : At the foot of the stairs after the last Board meeting.—Mr. Glover sai 1 he es- teemed it a very serious breach of the laws of honour to drag before the public anything that bad been said in pri- vate and in a friendly way. That had been done that after- noon.—The Chairman; You admit that you used the expression.—Mr. Glover said he could not swear to any words that he used. So far as the first part of the remark attributed to him went, that it was time the committee let this affair drop, he was decidedly of that opinion that day. —Father Finegan: So am I, too.—Dr. O'Kteffe: As Father Finegan and Mr. Weyer have said they would let the matter drop, is it not better to let it drop ?—Mr. Brock: I quite agree with you, Dr.—The Chairman concurred, and added that in the action they had taken with regard to the affair, the committee ha) been actuated with a desire to serve the Board and the public.—Mr. Imison said it was not a conver- sation he had with Mr. Glover. He thought it was not fair that he should be under that imputation.—The business then concluded.

div.head: SAILING MATCH ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: SAILING MATCH ON THE MERSEY.

Yesterday afternoon the 10th Warrington Annual Handicap Sailing Match took place on the river Mersey. It is usually held on the Saturday follow- ing Good Friday, but this year, it is stated, the tide would not allow of it being held on that day. The weather was gloriously fine, and several thousand spectators lined the banks on both sides of the river. The boats started from Runcorn, sailed round a boat moored at Six Acre, near Walton Bridges, and completed the race at newest end of Thewlis's wall. The names of the boats entered were Achilles, cap- tain, Robert Warburton; Black Jack, William War- burton; May, E. Gleave; Annie, T. Duckworth ; May Fly, J. Davieson; Red Jack, J. Leigh; Plough Boy, J. Emery; Queen, 11. Warburton, junr. ; Chuck°, W. Weldon; Primrose, S. Spencer; Jumbo, J. Hatton ; Deerfoot, T. Skelhorn. As ' the boats neared the winning post it ' became evident that the contest for first place lay between Chuck° and Primrose, who sailed close together for some distance, each occasionally taking a slight lead. Chucko succeeded in getting in a short distance ahead of Primrose, but we under- stand an objection was made on account of a foul. After the race the crushing on the narrow path near Thewlis's wall was very great, and a boy who was apparently exhausted fell from the road into the mud at the side of the river. A young man jumped down to the assistance of the boy, wlio was uncon- scious. Although so many people were congre- gated, good order was preserved throughout. the afternoon. During the afternoon a rumour gained ground that a boat containing several people had been upset a distance up the river, and that one of the occupants was drowned. On inquiry it was.ascer- tained that three men, whose clothes bore evidence of their having been in the water, and who ap- peared to be somewhat under the influence of drink, reported to a Lancashire county policeman at Sankey Bridges that they had been in a boat which capsized, but up to last evening no con- firmation of the report that a man had been drowned had been received.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, April 17th, 1886.—The mean temperature was 44.1 Fahr., and therefore about the same as the preceding week. The maxi- mum temperature 53 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 16th inst., and the minimum temperature. 30 Fahrenheit, on the 11th inst. The rainfall measured .08in. The general direction of the wind was N.E. During the week, which was the 16th of the current year, 44 births and 21 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 23.5 per 1,000, against 19.3 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 22.9. the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from measles, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from acute rheumatism, 4 from phthisis, 3 from old age, 4 from brain disease, and 2 from lung disease. One case of diptheria and four cases of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parlianient.—JNo. U. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health. div.head: GOOD FRIDAY AT RUNCORN AND
div.p: GOOD FRIDAY AT RUNCORN AND
WIDNES.

Good Friday was celebrated yesterday in the usual fashion. Service was held in the morning at the churches of the Establishment and at the Catholic chapels. The service at Ditton Jesuit Col- lege was very solemn and impressive. The weather was beautifully fine, a hot sun tempered by a cool breeze causing people to be early astir. All day there was a constant stream of pedestrians across Runcorn Bridge, their destination being Overton Hills, Halton, and Chester. All the conveyances in the town were fully engaged, and the " wheelmen " having brightened and oiled their machines, went abroad to view old scenes and places. The railway station at Runcorn was closed as on Sundays, the only train departing during the day being a special to the Welsh watering places. The passengers on both lines of railway atWidnes were numerous, and special trains were run to Blackpool and Southport and were fairly well patronised, but Liverpool, Hale, Lymm, and other pleasant places nearer home came in for most favour. In the evening the Primitive Methodists of Hutchinson-street held their annual Sunday school tea party, and the Welsh Wesleyane had their usual concert. At Runcorn the Primitive Methodist Band of Hope concluded the session with a tea party, and a tea meeting was also held in con- nection with the United Methodist Free Church.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S FOOTBALL.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S FOOTBALL.

EARLESTOWN V. LOWER DARWEN.—These teams met at Earleetown on Good Friday, and a very fast game resulted in a victory for Earlestown by four goals to one. HAYDOCK V. LANCASHIRE CLOWN CRICKETERS.—The Lancashire Clown Cricketers visi;ed Hp.ydock on Good Friday, and played one of their amusing games with the Haydeck (late Temperance) Club. The result was Haydock 3 goals, Clown Cricketers one. WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS. AN EXCITING GAME.

' The meeting of these teams at St. Helens on Good Friday excited the greatest interest in local football circles, and the surroundings of the game were considerably enhanced by the beautifully fine weather. Prior to the tie in the competition for the West Lancashire and Border Towns Rugby Union Challenge Cup, the two teams had not met during the season just drawing to a close, but as unusally exciting games had been played in former years, a renewal of the close games was anticipated. The supporters of the St. Helens team expressed their con- fidence in the ability of their " pets " to defeat the Warringtonians, but the latter administered a most de- cisive defeat upon the St. Helens men. Notwithstanding this the then vanquished have since held—or rather hoped —that they would be able to turn the tables on their cppo- Bents if they could secure theiripresence on their favourite ground at Denton's Cireee-lane, and an opportunity for their exertions in this respect. was provided on Good Friday. The match had been the topic of conversation in St. Helens dur- ng the week, and as the day for the match was observed as a general holiday, there was an immense attendance. Be- tween 4,000 and 5,000 persons were present. The weather was beautifully fine, and from the commencement the play was of a most exciting character. The cuphelders arrived from Warrington in a four in hand, and that team first made its appearance on the field. They and the St. Helens men were received with much cheering. The Warrington captain won the toss and Bortherick, the St. Helens captain, kicked off. Play was confined for a considerable time to Warrington territory. Barnes made a gallant attempt to run, but could not effect his purpose and a scrimmage resulted, the ball being driven into the Warrington twenty-five. Some strong forward play was then shown by St. Helens, who registered a touchdown, and shortly afterwards they registered a similar point. Imme- diately afterwards Povey rushed through, and was strongly supported by the Warrington forwards, who played well up. The ball was passed to Hayes, who attempted to run, but he was collared by Bortiawick and another scrimmage took r place. St. Helens then did some nice passing, but H. Boardman seized the halt, a good scrim- mage took place in St. Helens territory, some good play being shown by the visitors' forwards, who carried the ball to the home goal line. Barnes kicked well into touch, and he also dribbled nicely, but Borthwick suc- ceded in getting the ball, and he ran, but Buxton seized the ball and made a nice return. Jolley made a run and Tickle nearly collared him, but failed to stop his progress. St. Helens now registered a minor, which was followed shortly afterwards by Walsh making a try, which he succeeded In improving upon, amid applause, making the first goal for Warrington. The St. Helens captain aeain kicked Off, and the ball was carried close to the home goal line. Boardman, while endeavouring to run, was thrown and rather badly shaken, but he continued to play. The St. Helens forwards now worked the hall to the twenty-five flag, and Boardman relieved by a kick in touch, Some nice play was then exhibited, Jolley and Gilbert showing up well. The St. Helens captain tried a run but the ball was taken by the forwards, and Boardman saved by a very nice screw kick. Half-time was called with the ball in St. Helens territory. Shortly after tbe beginning of the second half St. Helens gained another minor. A good rush was afterwards made by the Warrington forwards, and the ball was again worked into St. Helens territory, Alec. Molyneux dribbling nicely. Boardman and Jolley nicely passed, and the latter seizing the ball, was collared by Finney, but Nevins played rather badly in failing to pass. Buxton and Jolley next showed some good play, and they were supported by Bux- ton, who made a good run into the St. Helens twenty-five, but the St. Helens forwards grandly saved. E. Foreman now showed play, but he was thrown, the result being that his head was rather badly cut. Tickle kicked well and forced Buxton to touchdown. Haselden kicked by a pass from Borthwick, and another minor was registered for St. Helens. An exciting loose scrimmage next took place, and Fair Turner saved well. Grice. one of the St. Helens for- wards, succeeded in securing a try amid prolsmged ap- plause, but Haselden did not improve upon it failing in hie shot at goal, though the opportunity for securing a major point was an easy one. Pennington got a free kick and an exciting scrimmage took place near the visitors' goal line. Some sharp play was witnessed, the ball being ultimately played into St. Helens territory by Davies, but Grice knocked it back to the visitors' goal line. The play became fast and furious, the ball being worked rapidly, but neither side succeeded in adding to their score. Tbe St. Helenites worked the ball to half-way and Haselden kicked into touch. The play then became very sharp and was taken into Warrington territory, and Davies made several good attempts to force the ball back. At the call of time the score stood :—Warrington one goal and two minors, St. Helens one try and six minors. It must be remarked that Warrington were minus several ef their best men, namely, Speakman, Rigby, W. Dillon, T. Dillon, Massey, Warren, and Hough, or the result might have proved still more decisive.. Davies and Povey played splendidly for the 'visitors, their efforts being fre- quently applauded. St. Helens played one man short, one getting hurt shortly after the commencement of the game. For St. Helens Girice and Foreman played a fine game. Mr. James Hickson, Salford, acted as referee, and Mr. T. Barnes was umpire for Warrington and Mr. McLaughlin for St. Helens. The teams were as follow :—Warrington: J. Buxton, full back; J. Jolley. T. Barnes, and H. Boardman, three-quarter backs; E. Gilbert and T. Walsh, half backs; H Ashton (captain), Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, T Davies, R Littlewood, Walter Povey, A Molyneux, W Heyes, and W Nevins, forwards. St. Helens: A Tickle, full back; B Pennington, E Foreman, and W Haselden, three-quarter backs; C Anders and A Bortlawick (captain), half backs T Green, W James, R Twist, T Pennington, VC Arnold, James Grice, T Finney, L Kershaw, and J Basnett, for- wards.

The "Daily News" gives a new turn to the statement, and says :—" We believe it will be found, when the case appears on the list, that the name of Sir Charles Dilke is struck out, and that the Queen's Proctor refers to the case under the title of q Crawford verso Crawford.'"
OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. What Mr. John Morley bitterly styled the " so- called holidays" are not permitted to interfere with the rush of interest in political events. Parliament being temporarily closed, public meetings are opened, and the clang of controversy rings through the land. Hitherto the Conservatives have taken the lead in this direction. Their meeting at the Opera House, Haymarket, has been followed by others based on similar lines in various parts of the country. The word has gone forth that meetings are to be held at which prominence and, wherever possible. presidency is to be given to the Liberals. That is a very astute policy and directed the arrangements at the Opera House. But it has not the wide success anticipated for it. Even the Opera House triumph had its disadvantages. Lord Har- tington does not conceal his conviction that he made a fatal error in taking part in the proceedings. It has done more to alienate him from the Liberal party than anything that has happened in his political career.' AO reproaches were current when he declined to join Mr. Gladstone's admini- stration. That was a matter of conscience, of the propriety of which lie was the sole judge. But there is obviously scmething different in the act of appearing on the platform of a packed Tory meet- ing and lifting up his voice against the policy of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Chamberlain was too shrewd to be caught in the trap. Lord Hartington has been caught once, and has paid dearly for his experience. As for Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., whose harmless vanity was adroitly played upon by Lord Randolph Churchill, there is something comical in his con- trition. "Please sirs," he writes to his constituents, "I will never do it any more." lam not quite sure that these personal defections have not had the effect of working to Mr. Gladstone's advantage. They have raised the spirit of Liberals in town and country, and urged them to counter demonstra- tions. These will increase as the days pass, and the one thing, hitherto lacking to Mr. Gladstone's sue- ce•ss with his bills will be forthcoming. He has always in his struggles for high purposes been backed upby the popular voice. Hitherto a strange but not inexplicable apathy has surrounded the people on the question of doing final justice to Ire- land. That is now being stirred, and the multitude of the Liberal party, having had time to think the matter over, are declaring loudly on the side of Mr. Gladstone.

A smart American pressman is over here just now engaged upon• a very systematic mission of inter- viewing. He makes his way into the inner cham- bers of eminent men, and with remarkable success induces them to confide to him their views on cur- rent events. He gains his way in quarters where "The Pall Mall Gazette" has ignominiously failed. Mr. Parnell is one of the most reticent men in public life; yet this indomitable American has got at him, and glea'ned his view of the probable effects of Mr. Chamberlain's controversy with Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Parnell talks with his customary common sense and judgment. He does not think Mr. Chamberlain's action will prevent the Home Rule Bill passing a second reading. "Mr. Chamberlain's influence on members of the present House," he says, "is very small indeed. In fact, I know of few men who have been so long in Parliament as Mr. Chamberlain who have less influence with their fellow members, or who are less looked up to for authorita- tive guidance." This is quite true. Compared with his wide influence in the country, Mr. Chamberlain's personal influence in the House of Commons is sin- gularly small. Mr. Parnell thinks the Lords will hesitate before they reject the scheme should it pass the Commons. An appeal to the country would, in Mr. Parnell's opinion, leave the balance of parties pretty much as it is. Seventy seats, 119 believes, ' the Irish vote gave the Conservatives at the last ' General Election. These would now go to no Liberals, but the issue being Home Rule a corres- ponding loss would be incurred by the Liberals throughout England generally. The only danger Mr. Parnell sees ahead is the possibility of the failure of Mr. Gladstone's health.

The Abbe Lizst has gone home a little tired. His stay in London has been a prolonged excitement not without its danger to a man of his age. One advantage the Abbe has enjoyed is his inability to speak English. German and French are his only languages, and people who could speak neither were debarred from converse with him. This cut off by tens of thousands the lion hunters who would have bored him to death. Just now London society is without a lion. But the wind is tern- wed to the shorn lamb. Society is actually out of ton, having fled before the prospects Of Good Friday and Easter Monday. It will come back again early in May like a giant 'refreshed, and will then seriously enter upon what is known as the season.

It will be very difficult to repair the loss the House of Commons has sustained by the retirement of Sir Erskine May. His presence in the chair at the table was assurance that things would be carried forward in accordance with constitutional princi- ples. In times like the present, when the Irish are on their good behaviour, things go forward well enough. It is when obstruction is rampant and mutiny prevails on the benches below the gangway, that the presence of men of Sir Erskine May's know- ledge and personal position is invaluable. I remem- ber how, one all-night sitting, Sir Erskine May crouched for hours behind the chair of Sir Lyon Playfair, momentarily advising him as further developments arose. A gross injustice was done to Sir Erskine when Lord Cranbrook inducted his son-in-law into the fat living of Clerk of Parliament in the House of Lords. Sir Erskine said nothing about it. But he felt the slight and the injury deeply, and there is no doubt that it has influenced his rMilmdLeeenanttintcte .yrtami, alitpvtnheiael ‘trtihsti roaor. nbneLlasetllpiocoeayfer tetitttil reooetruotif throbyeouemrst teuhh,tmahelt oemsiuust raecsyr:spemisecasereons pure otsuitftoroe mention oilrryn: in- vention, of which he first made the acquaintance in , the columns of the newspapers. To be one of the ' clerks at the table of the House of Commons is an honourable and desirable position. But it would be scarcely a promotion from that Mr. Lucy now holds. Mr. Russell Lowell is in London once more, and receives warm welcome from his many friends. Mr. Lowell is a stout patriot and would shrink from open admission that there was any country in the world equal to the United States. But he is strongly suspected of a secret preference for London. He has certainly taken an early opportunity of return- ing hither after quitting it upon his recall from Ministerial duties. We are looking for another eminent and popular American. "The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table," to wit, Oliver Wendell Holmes has long talked of visiting England. Now he has actually made preparations and will be here with the flowers in May. He is certain to meet with a hearty reception. Very little hope is entertained of the recovery of Lord Redesdale. Though well advanced in years, he was of remarkably sturdy constitution, and seemed likely to last almost as long as the House of Lords itself. But he counted too much upon his strength. He had a great contempt for most things, including the weather. To put on an overcoat was a sign of weakness that ill became him. Accordingly he went out in whatever weather without an overcoat. and has at last come to grief. His disappearance from the House of Lords will complete the removal of the landmarks that has been going forward with such remarkable regularity during the past year. If we take Captain Gosset, Sir Erskine May, and Lord Redesdale together, we have three names most familiar in relation with Parliamentary work during the last half-century. Captain Gosset resigned his post last session, his retirement being speedily fol- lowed by his death. Sir Erskine May has with- drawn from the table for the last time, and Lord Redesdale is not expected back again at his old place at the table of the House of Lords. It is curi- ous that these personal incidents are coincidental with the beginning of the work of a newly reformed Parliament.

There is to be a new crop grown on English soil, and travellers crossing the country by rail will be puzzled to see strange plantations with which they are much more familiar than they suppose. The Lords of the Treasury are going to allow an experi- mental cultivation of tobacco, but the necessary permission is not to be had for the asking. If a farmer plants an acre he must enter into a bond of .£lOO to secure his undertaking that all the leaves shall ultimately pass through the hands of the revenue officials, who will weigh them and deter- mine the duty to be paid. Good judges maintain that the experiment will be a certain success. The soil of England, and more especially the soil of Ireland, they say, is admirably adapted for the growth of the commoner kinds of tobacco. The crop will be large and reliable, though the quality may be coarse. In the meantime the social ques- tion will be largely influenced. England is one of the few countries in which you can get a good cigar at a not unreasonable price. The number of very cheap cigars sold in this coun- try ia almost inconsiderable, because_they hare a

double tax to pay. The exporting country tare them and our revenue taxes them also, so trade is scarcely possible. The poor smoke pipes, and on the whole, don't lose by the necessity. In Germany the churchwarden is unknown. You do occasion- ally see a pipe of a highly complex and cumbrous character, that looks more like some wind instru- ment; but cigars are the general rule. Cabmen, porters, soldiers, railway guards, all smoke cigars in Germany, and it is the same in Italy. The reason is that tobacco in that form is as cheap as in any other form, and much more convenient. You get a " Minghette" cigar all over Italy for a penny, and. a " Trabuco for three half-pence, and three cigar- ettes for less that a penny. If the new experiment succeeds it will be attended with the disappearance of the pipe and possibly also with a variety of fairly good imported cigars and a rise in price of the best. The poor man will be the gainer, and the loss will fall on the consumers of the sixpenny cigar.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, Councillor Greening, and Mr. John Fair- clough. DRUNICENNESS.—Winifred Conway was charged with being drunk and disorderly. The case was adjourned for a month on la, isoner promising to take the pledge.—Michael Duffy, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dol- man's-lane, was reprimanded and dismissed. William Dolan was fined ss, including costs, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-street on the previous night.—Thos. Gaynor was fined ss, including costs, for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street.—Mary Garritty, for being drunk and disorderly in John-street and Clare-street, was fined 5s and costs. MISCELLANEOUS.—Martin Lyons and Thomas Oates were charged with playing at pitch and toss in Cloth Hall-yard. They were dismisied.—Catherine Heesom was tined 103 and costs for keeping lodgers without having her house regis- tered.—William Farrell, for stone throwing, was fined lOs and costs, acd John Macdonald, similarly charged, was dismissed. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNICENNESS.—Mary Coyne was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, and fined 103 and costs.--Catherine Connolly and Bridget Lally were each fined a similar amount for being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street. SLEEPING OUT.—Thotnas Ward, for sleeping out in a closet in Lower Bank-street, was sent to prison for seven days. THCRSDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) Alder-

man Burgess, and Major Litton. MISCELLANEOUS.—John Burke, charged with using threat- ening language to Ann McGarry, was discharged.—Mary Mannion was tined for drunkenness.—For playing pitch and toss Richard Bally, William Langley, and John Smith were each ordered to pay is—John Smith, charged with throw- ing stones at Bank Quay, was ordered to remain in custody until six in the evening, and to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSION'S. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Rylands and Mr. James
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSION'S. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Rylands and Mr. James
Marson.

DRUNK ON' LICENSED Paaansas. William Leighton, Timothy Taberner, Bridget Ann Welsh, and John Addison were charged wi.th being drunk on the licensed premises, the Chapel liouse Inn, Buttonwood, on the 10th inst.—Ser- geant Cairns said that he visited that house on the after- noon of the day in question. He found the defendants drunk in the vaults; Leighton was asleep and the others were staggering about.—The Bench fined each defendant 53 and costs. TRAVELLING WITHOUT TICEET.—ThOmaS Caldwell and Henry Daintith were charged with travelling on the Cheshire Lines from Urmston to Padgate with intent to de- fraud the company. Defendants alighted from the train at Padgate and told the ticket collector that they had given up their tickets to the stationmaster, which, however, was not the truth.—Thev were each fined lOs and costs. A PUBLICAN FINED—John Hayes, landlord of the Stocks Inn, Padgate, WAS charged with having his house open dur- ing prohibited hours on the afternoon of Sunday. the 11th April. Mr. Jenkins defended. Four men named Frederick Evans, William Waterfield, George Watson, and William Burrows were charged with being on the premises. The question resolved itself into one of whether the defendants were boner fide travellers, and Mr. Jenkins also submitted that the men were allowed into the house by a young ser- vant without the knowledge of her master. Watson and Burrows, it transpired, came from Sankey and were entitled to refreshment.—They were therefore discharged. Evans and Waterfield were each fined 5s and costs, and Hayes, the landlord, was fined 103 and costs, the license not to be en- dorsed. A NUISANCE.—Robert Mercer was charged with allowing a nuisance at a ditch adjoining four houses at Poulton, Fearnhead.—The case was adjourned. GAME TRESP/US.—Michael Finerty and Joseph Blower were charged with trespassing on land at Buttonwood in search of game on the 11th inst.—They were each fined 103 and costs. A VIOLENT WOMAN. Sarah Ellen Wilkinson was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the highway at Great Sankey on the 15th inst., and with doing damage to telegraphic insulators to the amount of ninepence.—She re- ceived a bad character and was sent to prison for two months.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Blfore Mr. T. H. Gbssage and Mr. John Brock. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Each of the following per- sons was fined 58 and costs for drunkenness :—John Wal- lace, Patrick Riley. Patrick Brady, and John Maley. Patrick McCreese, a young man, against whom InsAector Wood produced a long black list, was bound over to be of good behaviour on a charge of creating a breach of the peace by shouting and kicking at the doors of houses in Waterloo-road on Sunday evening.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY—Before Mr. George Pilkington. MISCELLANEOUS.—John Smith, Elijah Seddon, Catherine Delavey, Elizabeth F. Welsh, Thomas Swale, were each fined for drunkenness.—Mary Malarkey and Bridget Barrett were convicted for breaches of the peace and bound over. John Lightfoot and Walter Atherton were each fined is and 4s 6d costs for per- mitting the chimnies of their dwelling-houses to be on fire.—Michael Allen, Thomas Boscoe, and Joseph Don- nollev, youths, were each fined 2s 6d and costs for playing pitch and toss in Pleasant-street on Sunday, the 11th inst. —James Gargon, for assaulting Elizabeth McHugh, a young married woman in Chester-street, was tined 5s and costs, lOs 6d, ot 14 days' bard labour.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. Mosnay.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. F. Rigby. ASSAULT.—Ann Weedall, alias Baker, was fined 51 and costs, 16s, for having on the 19th February, committed an unprovoked assault upon her sister-in-law, Sarah Ann Evans.

WRECK ON TUE GOODWIN SANDS.—A Deal telegram says the Norwegian barque Angust Lierman Francke, from Krageroe to St. Sebastian, with ice, was wrecked on the Goodwin Sands, on Tuesday during a fo;-t% The captain was saved by the lifeboat, but the rema!nder of the crew

(six) were lost. THE PIMLICO CASE. The trial of Mrs Adelaide Bartlett was brought to a close on Saturday even- ing. When the court assembled in the morning the Attorney - General (Sir C. Russell). commenced his reply on behalf of the prosecution. Taking it for proved that the deceased man died from the effects of some irritant poisoning, he said the question was reduced to two points—whether the posion was taken by the de- i ceased with suicidal intent, or administered by some one else with criminal intent. He argued that all the circum- stances pointed to the utter improbability that Mr. Bar- tlett would take his own life, and said that if the poison was administered by anyone else that person could be nobody hut the prisoner. In summing up Mr. Justice Wills re- marked that but for the acquaintance with Mr. Dyson Mr. and Mrs. Bartlett might have been now living happily to- gether. His lordship severely criticised the conduct of Mr. Dyson. Dealing with the evidence, he pointed oat that there was no difficulty in the deceased in his restless craving for sleep getting the chloroform and himself taking it. The jury were out of court considering their verdict for upwards of two hours. On their returning they said they had found a verdict of not guilty. Although they thought there was the gravest suspicion attaching to the prisoner' they did not consider that there was sufficient evidence to show how or by whom the chloroform was administered. The prisoner fainted on hearing the verdtct. Since the verdict has been ' given a member of the jury has stated that their long deliberation arose through the opposition of yonanths b';deevt. only one of the twelve. The Rev. ST. HELENS RECREATION v. Weeemme.—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and after a very fast game Walkden won by two goals and five minors to a goal and three minors. The Recs. were without J. Gregss n, T. Rankin, and W. Taylor. Sr. HELENS V. LivEnroan OLD Boys.—This match was played at St. Helens on :Saturday, and resulted in a draw. St. Helens scoring one goal, two tries, and six minor points, and the Old Boys one goal, two tries, and three minor points. Anders, Pennington, and James got the tries for the home team, while for the Old Boys Crawford, Edmund, and Munn scored. WIDNES RECREATION V. WIDNES " A " TEAR —These teams met on the Widnes ground on Saturday, and after a hard-fought game of two 35's the" A "team were declared the winners by two tries and five minors to one try and four minors. Widnes were best represented by Harding and Bingham, of the first team, while all the forwards worked hard, especially A. Brown, Hughes F. Wright, and S. Wil- kinson. The Recreation bad to play some of their second team men, through Grundy, Summer, and McGurl not Peing able to play ; but they, however, tried hard to secure the victory. They were best represented by Parkinson, Broome, and Bradshaw behind, while of the forwards, who all played a good game, Currie, Noon, and Brannon were, perhaps, the pick, especially the latter. Teams :—Widnes (".e " team): Full back, T. Wilkinson ; three-quarter backs, Bingham, Harding, and Wright; half backs, Rimmer and Howard; forwards, Brown, Hughes, Wilkinsdn, Woods, Spencer, Beddows, F. Wright, J. Keyes, and J. Hampson. Recrea- tion : Full back, T. Wailing; three-quarter backs, Broome (captain), Parkinson, and Barber; half backs, Bradshaw and Norris; forwards, Charles Farrell, Currie, Shaw, Bran- non, McCririe, Hewson, Noon, and G. Wright. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. WARRINGTON ROVERS.—ThiS match came off last Saturday at the ground at Lodge-lane, in the presence of a fair number of spectators. The ball was kicked off about 3-30, two 40 minutes being the time to play. The Bangers played with a 'slight wind and down hill in the first half, and scored 6 minor points. On resum- ing play at half time the score stood—Rangers 6 minor points Rovers nil. The Rovers now thought they could l win, playing with the wind and hill in their favour, but they were mistaken, for by hard and steady play 3 other ' minors were put to the score, and shortly afterwards a try was obtained by Foster, the kick at goal failing. On resum- ing play the Rangers scored another minor and then an accident occurred. Rovers kicking down the field with the ' wind sent the ball past the-full back, who, on coming up to it, fell on it over the line. Fair of the Rovers coming up at the same time, the ball slipped from under the full back land he claimed a try, which neither of the umpires agreed I to, but the referee over-ruled. Nothing of any importance occurred after this, and when time was called the score stood—Rangers 1 try 11 minor points to Rovers 1 try. Teams:—Rangers: Full back, P. Hastings; three quarter, Mather, Edwards, Marshall; half, Minchell, T. Bate ; forwards, Robinson (captain), Boyle, Cook, J. Hill, Buckley, W. Hill, J. Monks, Foster, and W. Bates. Rovers: Full back, Brown; three quarter. Allen, Bellian, Handles; half, P. Fair (captain), Graham; forwards, Mclntyre, Horden, Braide, Bibby, Hackett, Savage, Woods, Barlow, and Allton. RUNCORN V. WAVERTREE.—This fixture was played on Runcorn ground on Saturday, instead of on the Wavertree ground, as previously arranged. The Wavertree captain won the toss, and decided to play with a strong wind blowing in his favour. Joule started the ball, the which Lamble re- plied, and the next move of note was a dribble by Andrews, which Dodd stopped by dropping on the ball. After the scrimmage Davies ran nicely, and Wainwright kicked well into the Wavertree half, and a touchdown was soon regise tered. Speakman made an effort to force his way by a strong run, which Gatley followed with a good dribble. H. Hughes, being close in his wake, picked up, and ran in close to the posts. Faulkner took the kick at goal, which failed. Shortly afterwards from the throw out Joule secured the ball and dashed over the line, gaining the second try by a good piece of play. Lewis failed at goal. Play now en- sued on the home line, the Wavertree forwards, Wilcock, Singleton, and Bryant, played a hard game. Two dead balls were quickly scored by the visitors, after which some good loose play was shown by Wright, who got on a nice dribble, followed by W. Hughes, who contributed a good run. Lamble and Morton tackling well prevented him scoring. From a line out Wainwright got the ball smartly, and ran over the line. The try was objected to on the ground that Davies had been in touch previously. The referee not see- ing the point the Runcorn captain gave way. From here Lamble made tracks for the home goal, but was soon stop- ped. Wilcock followed and made a good effect, and Woods being pressed kicked to touch in goal. The play soon merged on the Wavertree line. Clarke, Hofflana, and Dolan gained headway frequently from the lines out, and the play eventually got close to the line, Andrews giving Speakman a good chance, but he failed to take the pass, and Wilcock and Dodd got back to centre, from which H. Hughes put in a dodgy run. The whietle sounding for half time, the hall lodeed in the Wavertree half. After the usual interval Wavertree started the ball from centre, and soon a scrimmage was formed in centre. The ball coming out, Wainwright ran and passed to Davies, who got in, the try being ruled back. However, the play still ledged in the visitors' half. H Hughes quickly gaining his second try, but Lewis failed at goal. The ball was again restarted, and after some smart play Andrews eluded the Wavertree backs in an easy fashion, gaining the fourth try, Woods placing a goal. A start was again made from centre, Lewis making a good retarn, which Woodward for Wavertree responded to by a clever dodgy run. This Wainwright followed by a run, administering a parting kick over the Wavertree backs, and getting on the ball again got the fifth try close to the touch line. W Hughes took the place, and by a splendid kick sent the ball over the bar. Lewis returned the ball, which was again sent to Woods, when by a long kick and the poor play of the Wavertree backs the ball rolled dead behind the goal line. Rousing up a little the play got to the home line, but the ball did not remain long here. Davies ran and kicked on the visitors' half, and after some loose play H Hughes gained his third try, Woods being again successful at goal. A start was again made from centre by Wavertree, and during some loose scrambling play on the home line Singleton got a try for Wavertree, which Dodd, however, failed to convert itsto a goal. Wright and Andrews were the means of getting the ball into the visitors' quar- ter, Speakman scoring. and Woods again kicking a goal. The assault on the Wavertree lines was maintained by Wright, Lewis, and W. Hughes, but only a minor point was scored, the game closing in favour of the Runcorn men by four goals, three tries, four minor points, to one try and three minor points. Davies, Hughes, and Andrews played an excellent game for the winners behind the pack. In the pack Hoilland, Lewis, Clarke, and Dolan did a lot of push- ing, Joule, Wright, and Wainwright being prominent in loose play: The Wavertree backs were of very little use save Dodd and Lambda. Among a good lot of forwards were Wilcock, Singleton, and Bryant. Teams :—Runcorn : Woods, back; Davies, W. Hughes, and Speakman, three- quarter backs; Hughes and Andrews, half backs; Wright, Joule, Lewis, Lewis, Clarke, Hoffi end, Faulkner, Dolan, Oat- iey, and Wainwright, forwards. Wavertree : Rowe, back; -tenable, Woodward, and Moreton, three-quarter backs; Dodd ,1 and Spedding, half backs; Wiicock, Howden, Grierson, I Bingle:on, Bryant, Parry, Hoyle, Morton, and another, for- wards.

WARRINGTON V. WALTON.—During the past week the excitement in football circles has somewhat abated, but still on Saturday last some 2,000 spectators witnessed the above match. The committee of the Warrington club had offered one third of the gate to bring down a good team, but they somewhat failed in this respect, only turning up with thir- teen men, substitutes having to be found to make up the required number. Warrington, on the other hand, were minus the services of Ashton, Warren, Massey, Bigby, and W. Dillon, but still they could do almost as they liked with the Waltonians, who were defeated easily, the score being Warrington four tries and four minors to Walton nil. The reround was in good condition, and the weather very favour- able. The 'bus from the Griffin was once more called into requi,ition to convey the teams to the scene of action. The ties in the second round of the competition for the Wellington Challenge Cup were played on Saturday after- ;loon.

EARLESTOWN (HOLDERS) V. HAYDOCK RAMBLERS These teams met on the ground of the St. James's Club, at Haydock, in the presence of a considerable number of spec- tators. For the first time since their defeat in the Liver- pool cup contest. Earlestown was represented by its fall team, though Dagnall (centre) officiated as goal-keeper, Apppleton, the usual custodian, taking his place, while J. Green (back), and T. Sidieley (left wing) exchanged posi- tions. The Earlestonians had the best af the game through- out and during the first half against the wind scored four goals. In the second half they added five more, one of which was scored by Dagnall (goal-keeper), and Earlestown thus won by nine goals to none. Earleatown team :—Dag- nail, goal; R. Green and T Siddeley, backs; Duxbury, Whalley, and Bowker. half-backs; Rich and Ellison, right wing; Appleton, centre ; Sims and J. Green, left wing. _

HAYDOCK ST. JAMES'S V. ST. HELENS ST. MARE'S.— Played en Saturday afternoon, and resulted in a victory for the St. James's team by two goals to none. EARLESTOWN ROVERS V. ASHTON RECREATION (2ND.)— These teams having been ordered to replay their tie in the first round, met on the Havdock St. James's ground on Friday night, when the Rovers won by two goals to one.
EARLESTOWN ROVERS V. MILLFIELD ROVERS. These teams played on Saturday afternoon on the ground of the latter. The visitors won by three goals to one.

STEIIISIIAW CROSS WANDERERS -v. Sr. HELENS ASSOCIA. TlON.—This match was played at St. Helens and resulted in a win for Stubshaw Cross by six goals to three. At half time the score stood two goals each. On re-starting, the Wanderers began forcing their opponents, and qiickly re- gistered their third and fourth goals. St. Helens after a sharp scrimmage, managed to score their third goal, but the play from this point was all in favour of Stubshaw Cross.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday the Liverpool Old Boys sent a team to St. Helens and effected a drawn game, whilst Warrington easily defeated Walton. Wigan went down before Swinton, anti Tyldesley succumbed to Leigh. For three years in succession the final tie in the Lanca- shire Challenge Cup competition has taken place on the North End ground at Peepdale, and on each ef these occa- sions the Rovers has been one of the competing teams. Before Saturday they had on each occasion to face their own townsmen, the Olympic, but this year the battle had to be fought against the Bolton Wanderers, and all who witnessed the game agreed that it was the poorest ex- hibition that had ever been seen in Preston in a final tie. Prior to the commencement of operations the majority of the spectators sided with the Wanderers, but the fame of their opponents debarred almost all, when they bad seen the constitution of the Bolton eleven, from hop- ing for their success. But before the game had progressed a quarter of an hour it was evident that the Wanderers meant winning, and support came accordingly. The strong north-easterly wind which almost from goal to goal did mach to spoil scientific play, but, so far as really scientific combination went, the teams were about evenly matched. Neither side went in for a passing game, the only occasion on which combination was observable being when for about the space of a quarter of an hour after changing ends the Rovers pressed their opponents. The Rovers certainly were without Arthur, but if the Inter- national custodian had been in his place it is extremely doubtful whether the result would have been any different, as the shot which defeated Mac. Was a bad one to spoil. On the other hand, it must be borne in mind that the Wan- derers had four of their second team doing duty, so that, taken altogether tho association cup holders ought to have been able to have upheld their previous week's reputa- tion.
A report of a complivaentary banquet given to the War- rintton team in recognition of their success in winning the challenge cup will be found in our columns. It was a very enthusiastic gathering.

div.p: A LAMPLIGHTER IN LUCK.

The Bridgwater Mercury publishes the following in- teresting facts :—John Manley, of Bridgwater, is a happy man. His good fortune deserves to be made public. Hav- ing lived Along us all his life and held the position of lighter for over twenty-nine years, his name and face are familiar to everybody in Bridgwater. He is liked by all. and it is safe to say one may go here, there, or yonder, and whether he meets this, that, or the other person, anywhere within the limits of our town, he will be sure to find a well- wisher of John Manley. While his life has, generally speaking, been aa uneventful one, he has, nevertheless, dur- ing those twenty-nine years, met with some strange experi- ences. In nightly furnishing light for us all, as it were, he has weathered many a storm and wintry blast. The cause of his present rejoicing is best explained by quoting his own words, and we will only add that being familiar with the facts of the case, we gladly make public the statement, which is as follows:

" Ever since I first got my appointment from the Gas Company, in 1857, I have made it a rule to let nothing in- terfere with my duties, and for seventeen years I scarcely missed a day. I was proud of my record and resolved not to spoil it ; but one night just twelve years ago, I was obliged to get a substitute or let the people of Bridgewater wander about in darkness. Having been exposed to a spell of very bad weather, I was stricken down with a terrible attack of rheumatism, which completely disabled me, so that for weeks I could not move my arms nor do my work. Although used everything that was recommended to me, Ito get rid of this ailment, I have ever since been a martyr Ito it, and for weeks at a time have been unable to attend to my duties. In those twelve years I endured more suffering than words can express, and I began to regard my case as chronic and altogether hopeless. When I was recently taken down again by a fearful attack of my old enemy— rheumatism—and one of our lady citizens sent me part of a bottle of a remedy which she said was a dead shot for that fearful disease, as she had found out from personal experience, I felt it hardly worth while trying the article. I was persuaded, however, to make a few aoplications, and to my astonishment and delight the pains and swelling not only left me, but E have been free from them ever since and able to do do my work as well as ever I could in my life. I have not felt as well in twelve years, and I do not mind saying that I, and all those who knew of my frequent dis- ibled condition, regard St. Jacobs Oil, which is the thing I

She said that the defendant Club. made a great "ado" when he knew that she was to receive the £l7O, and he proposed that he should give up his situation, and that she should enter into business. She talked of getting a divorce from her husband, but the defendant said he would not spend a single penny upon such a course. When she came to Runcorn she did not like the Mariners' Arms, but the defendant took the house upon his own responsibility. After this she took up her resi- dence at the Mariners' Arhas. The defendant intro- duced her as his sister. She intended to get a divorce from her husband and to marry the defen- dant. She had lost between £7O or £BO altogether, through her connection with the defendant. She became dissatisfied the first week she was at the Mariners' Arms. The defendant was in the habit of bringing women to the house, and it seemed that he wanted her for a bad purpose. She told him that she was not going to put up with that kind of thing. The defendant " larked " and "carried on " before her with women he brought to the house, and when she pro- tested he said it was good for business. She told the defendant that she must save something for the children, and as she was a good needlewoman, she intended to get her living by sewing. The defen- dant was all right when he could get money out of her, but he had made her look very little and low. She had a good character before she came to Run- corn.

_ Cross-examined by Mr. Davies: She was 34 years of age. The defendant told her when she first met him that he was 25. He did not say that he was only 21.—Mr. Davies: Didn't you ask him. at the Orange ball to come and stay at your house? Plaintiff: Me ask him ! No. How could you say so ?—Mr. Davies: But did he as a matter of fact stay in your house? Plaintiff: He came and stayed a certain time.—Mr. Davies: How long? Plaintiff: Longer than he ought to have done.—Mr. Davies: And your three children were at home at the same time? Plaintiff: Yes.—Mr. Davies: Now did you ever try to persuade this young man to come and live with you in Runcorn? Plaintiff: Never in my life.—Mr. Davies: Didn't you beg of him to come and live with you and marry you? Plaintiff: I begged of him to give it up.—Mr. Davies: Didn't you tell him that you were a widow? Plaintiff: ; I told him the candid truth.—Mr. Davies: Why didn't he marry you? Plaintiff: I found out that my husband was drowned, but the defendant would not marry me because of the women coming to the house.—Mr. Davies: When he stayed at your house on the night of the Orange ball did he not remain until seven or e;ght in the morning? Plain- tiff: I cannot say. He has proved a scamp to me.— Further cross-examined, the plaintiff denied that she had lived with him as his wife. She would not have married the defendant if she could. He did not say he -would marry her if he dare, but that would make her guilty of bigamy. The defendant had since married another woman who had been divorced from her husband. She had seen and ex- perienced a " lot " since she knew the defendant. His Honour said it was quite evident that the relations of the parties had been of a very improper character. The evidence of the plaintiff herself was quite enough to convince him of that. It seemed that the money had been spent with her sanction, and he must give a verdict for the defendant with costs.

VERY IMPORTANT CONSIDERATION. A most important consideration for all at this season of the year is how best to rid the system of tte diseases induced by the trials of winter. In many cases it seems as though the seeds of consumption had been planted in the system by the trying weather we have gone through.
