GENERAL ItEWS.

It is officially announced that her Majesty's birthday will be kept on Saturday the 20th May. Arrangements were made on Wednesday for Lord Har• tington to address his constituents at Rawtenstall on Mon- day. The Ven. Archdeacon Darby, D.D., is to be installed as Dean of Chester at the Cathedral on Thursday, the 29th instant. The death of the Right Rev. Dr. Cotterill, Bishop of Edinburgh in the Scottish Episcopal Church, is an- nounced. It is stated that negotiations are progressing for the establishment on a large scale of a shipbuilding yard at Preston by a Glasgow firm. Announcement is made that from the sth May the rates for televains to the principal stations in the United States and Canada will be reduced to pd. per word. The Duke of Cambridge, as Commander-in-Chief, was en- tertained at a banquet given by the Lord Mayor of London at the Mansion House on Saturday evening. Alderman Sir Thomas Baker died on Saturday, at the age of 75. He was Mayor of Manchaster for two years, from November, 1880, to November, 1882. On Tuesday morning a fire occurred at Skinners' Alms-houses, Mile End-road, London, owing to the over- turning of a spirit lamp, and Mary Willey was burned to death. A large number of cotton operatives at Great Harwood have asked for an increase of nay whilst engaged in the pro- duction of certain classes of goods, and threaten to strike in a body if the request be not granted. A Noiwegian brig was wrecked on the Goodwin Sands on Tuesday. Some hours elapsed before a lifeboat reached the vessel, and then only one man, the captain, was saved. Five other men and a boy were drowned. EARTHQUAKE. —About twenty minutes to one o'clock on Sunday morning, a distinct shock of earthquake was felt at Cornrie, Perthshire, and in the neighbourhood. The vibration was also felt at St. Fillan'a, on the shores of Lock Earn. The new villa residences in Kilburn, near London, which were all but completed, fell on Monday morning and buried a number of workmen in the lower rooms. Three of the men were seriously injured, and others sustained minor hurts.

THE LIVERPOOL EXHIBITION. Mr. F.. 1. Leslie lectured in the Public• Hall, War- rington, on Monday evening, on the "Liverpool In- ternational Exhibition . and what there will be to see in it."---The M..i-iron (Alderman Harrison) pre- sided, and said that 16 trusted that the result of the exhibition would be.to stimulate very Much that technical education which many people thought was so essentiallynecessary in order to maintain their commercial supremacy. The exhibition would,: he believed, be of an educational character.—Mr. LESLIE took his'audience on an imaginary visit to the building now in course of construction in Edge- lane, showed them on, each side of the entrance the Royal apartments ;.- and then entering the main building, on the left the foreign section, in front of which would be Belgium, Prance, and Italy, which had all appointed. State Commissioners, and were organizing theivown National Courts, and ,at. the back would be the exhibit's of Russia, Germany, Austria, Holland, America, and almost every other country in the world, even including Hayti and Chili. On the left of the entrance, the south trail- Sept would , be devoted wholly to British com- merce and manufacture. Looking down the main nave from ' the entrance, the visitor would be able to get a perspective view of a broad span of glass and iron crowded with exhibits from every nation of the globe, extending right down to the Concert Hall, nearly.a quarter .of a mile away. Models, drawings, and pictures would be .there, to show the entire history of sea travelling. The lee- taxer then proceeded to give a brief sketch of the history of navigation from the earliest times, as it would be exemplified in the. exhibition. This ac- count, illustrated with numerous lantern views, was most interesting. . An unique collection had been arranged of the travelling carriages of India and China, and the animals used to draw them. Allud- ing to the exhibits in the railway section, Mr. Leslie said it was intended to bring out with singular pro- minence the remarkable development of railway construction during the past half century.7-A warm vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer on the proposition of the MAYOli,and the proceedings then terminated.

THE SOLICITOR-GENERAL.—Having failed to obtain a seat at Ipswich, Sir tiortiee Davey is desirous to resign the Solicitor-Generalship. In view of prospective contingen- cies, however, it is possible that Mr. Gladstone may not accept his resignation. The speeches of council in the action by Mr. M'Lachlan against Messrs. Agnew and other gentlemen terminated on Wednesday, and the referee will now have to prepare his judgment. It is expected that this decision will be given about three months hence. Some tenant farmers who met at Ballinacragay, near Kildysart, county Clare, on Saturday night passed a resolu- tion disapproving of the Land Purchase Bill. They had expected, it appeared, not a "Landlords' Relief Bill," but a bill which would bring themselves relief. STABBING A BAILIFF.—A sheriff's bailiff was seriously stabbed on Thursday morning while making seizures f-r rent at Rathrnore, about ten miles distant from Killarney. He was accompanied by a force of police, but a large crowd bad assembled, and made a violent attack upsn him. Two arrests were made. FIRST MANX ELECTION UNDER THE BALLOT ACT.—The election of a member of the House of Keys for Garff Sheed- ing took place in Ramsey Court house on Tuesday. The returning officer at one o'clock declired Mr. Allen returned. This was the first election under the new Ballot Act, and was remarkably quiet, especially as compared with the last one under the old system. REMARKABLE DEATH FROM BLOOD POISONING.—Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at Southport, on Tuesday, on the body of Edmund Parkinson, aged 73, Who died on Saturday. On March 19th, decased was in the poultry run attached to his house, when a cock flew at him and scratched his thumb. It swelled, and he went to a doctor, but notwithstanding his efforts the unfortunate man died from blood poisoning. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. PRESENTATION TO LORD ROSEBERY. Lord Rosebery who is at present staying at The Durdans, Epsom, was on Wednesday morning presented with a handsomely illumina- ted and bound address by a deputation representing Liberals of the Epsom Division of Surrey, congratulating him on his acceptance of office as Foreign Secretary. His lordship briefly acknwleaged the presentation, but made no refer- ence to political matters. The proceedings were conducted in private. GREAT FIRE IN LONDON.—A fire was discovered about two o'clock on Tuesday morning, at Messrs. Braden cis Com- pany's steam flour factory, Bermondsey. The main portion of the premises on the river side, containing valuable ma- chinery, was wholly destroyed. The fire also communi- cated with the premises of Messrs. Jordan and Co., drug grinders; Messrs. Hartman, Roll, and Co., coffee merchants; and Messrs. Sharp and Co., tanners, and coesiderable dam- age was done. GREAT MAIL BAG ROBBERY.—At the Mansion House, London, on Tuesday afternoon, a well-dressed man, aged 40 years, giving the name of Henry Andrews, was charged with receiving three Russian hundred rouble notes and other securities, value £4,000, which were stolen from a registered letter bag, on the Bth instant, while in transit from London to the continent. The accused had presented the notes for payment, and when they were recognise said they had been paid by another man for a bet. He was remanded. BOTANIC BEER.—At Nottingham Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. Buszard, Q.C., Deputy Recorder, upon an appeal by the Inland Revenue authorities from a decision of justice, held Summer's botanic beer, manufactured from fer- mented sugar and water and flavoured with herbs, to be beer within the meaning of the Inland Revenue Act, 1885, and to retail which necessitates the holding of an Excise license. This decision affects every description of beer containieg over.two per cent. of proof spirit, and is considered exceed- ingly important. ALLEGED WIFE MURDER.—A gas-stoker named John Halpin is in custody at Rochdale charged with murdering his wife, who was found lying in the street on Satarday night in a dying state. She accused her husband of having kicked her violently about the body, and the police surgeon who examined the woman believed that death was caused by hemorrhage from internal injuries probably caused by kicks. Halpin was on Wednesday discharged from custody by the Rochdale magistrates. A coroner's jury had decided that the woman died from the effects of injuries accidentally received. OUTRAGE ON A WOMAN.—The Brynmawr magistrates were engaged until late on Monday investigating a charge of assault committed upon Mary Morgan on August sth, 1884. The prosecutrix lived in an isolated house on a mountain, and at midnight William Walters, with a gun, knocked at the house door. Prosecatrix, thinking it was her husband, opened the door, when the prisoner walked in, and threatened to shoot her if she resisted him. A terrible struggle ensued. The evidence against the prisoner was of the most conclusive character. The Bench committed him to the assizes for trial. THE VACCINATION QUESTION.—A deputation waited upon Mr. Stanstield, on Monday, at the office of the Local Government Board, to ask that relief from penalties should be granted to conscientious objectors to vaccination, and that a " conscience clause " should be submitted to Parlia- ment. Mr. Stansfield stated that his opinion bad always been that there was no advantage in making martyrs of people, but he had considerable doubt whether the House of Commons would grant any concession upon this subject. i Unless there was a probability of obtaining support, t was not for the Government to propose a measure to Parliament. He suggested that an endeavour should be made to get an inquiry into the subject, either by a commission or a com- mittee. RAILWAY SERTANTS.—A meeting of railway servants was held in Manchester on Sunday afternoon, to consider the action of the Directors of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company, who have decided to commence next month to pay a large number of their employes on .what is known as the "trip" system. Under this system, which is already in operation on the London and North-Western and the Midland lines of railway, guards and others wall not be paid by the hour, but will receive so much for the journey. Complaints were made that under this system men would suffer for blocks and delays for which they vr!ile in no way answerable ; it was also stated that the probability was that the men in their anxiety to get their work done would often expose themselves to great danger. A resolution express- ing' regret at the action of the Directors of the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire Company was carried, as was another in favour of Mr. F. A. Channing's Railway Regula- tion Bill. THE CLARET VINTAGE OF 1883.—The period having now arrived when it is possible to form a definite idea of the quality of the Claret Vintage of 1883, it may be well to point out that in their annual report on the 1883 Vintage Messrs. Gilbey, who have done much to popularize Claret in England, and who speak with a certain amount of au- thority, as owners of Chateau Loudenne, one of the largest Bordeaux vineyards,. expressed an opinion favourable to the vintage, at that time lust completed. This opinion the quality of the 1883 wines, which are now coming into con- sumption in England, appears to endorse, and to the large class of consumers who use Claret as a beverage at their meals, the wines of 1883, when selected with care and judg- ment, offer characteristics of flavour, elegance and cheap- ness which are all important to the English consumer, while lollNl._ornTihnge polling Post, at such is as from one shilling to two shanties per Apiarich2elseti,ecltBiBaGa. of a bottle it is difficult to conceive of better value being obtain- ablemoney—The'Ecr .member for the Central division of Bradford in place of the BRADFORD fr,r E late Mr. W. The missions which have been going on in War- rington during'the last three weeks closed last' Sun- day.- A very large congregation assembled at St. Albans, Bewsey-street, to hear Father Richmond, the eloquent father of charity, for the last time. The mission at St. Albans has been very -well attended throughout, numerous Protefotants attending night after night. The Fathers of Charity have been pre- sented with different presents -from the congrega- tion, and also from • the children of the schools in acknowledgment of their good work amongst the people, which they have well deserved. Father Richmond left for Rugby last Monday morning. At the Catholic Church of St. Mary, Buttermarket-st., last Sunday being Palm Sunday, High Mass was celebrated at eleven o'clock by Father Sumner, the parish priest of St. Mary, the palms being blessed and distributed amongst the congregation. The gospel of the day was read in English by Father Whitehead, 0.P., whilst the Celebrant of the Mass was reading it in latin: At three o'clock in the'afterrioon the last instruction to tho Children was given, and in the evening thin large church Was crowded by people anxious to witness the closing service of the mission. Rosary was recited by Father Cyril Bunco, 0.P., who also gave a short instruction. The ser- mon was preached by Father Philip Limerick; 0.P., of London, orte of the ablest preachers of the Dora- inican Order. After the sermon the renewal of ' baptismal vows took. place, and the scene was very striking, with the hundreds of tapers burring, held in the hands of the congregation. Father Limerick thanked all those Who had in any way helped to ' make ,the mission such a success, including the hard-working perish priest, Father Sumner, who ' had done so much for St. Mary's during the time he has been in Warrington. He also thanked the or- ganist and choir for their services, and the Sacristan of the church who had been so obliging to them -during, their stay. The magnificent High Altar of St. Mary's was illuminated with innumerable candles and flowers. Two of the missionaries left town on Monday for London, and one will remain. at St. Mary's until next week to help the priests 'during this Easter Sunday. • On Friday week the Rev. Father Richmond was presented by the boys ' of St. Alban's School, King-street, with a sum of money, a silver-mounted umbrella, suitably inscribed, and an address, of which the following is a copy :

To THE REV. FATHER Rini:mom). Dear Rev. Father,—We, toe boys Lf St. Alt an's Roman Catholic School, wish to te,der to 'sou our heart felt thanks for the nice mission you so kindly gave us durineyour first week In Warrington. We feel assured that the greatest pleasure we can give you IS to promise, by God's grace, to faithfully follow the course of life you have hid down for us, viz, following in the Divine footsteps of our blessed Lord, and becoming worthy members of our mother Church

That we may not forget your teaching, nor the attention we have paid to it, we request your acceptance of this small token as an acknowledgment of your labours amongst us, and re- quest your prayers for our welfare, particularly during the months of May and Povember. We must also thank our good and kind priests for bringing you amongst us; and praying G‘al you may live long to con- tinue in your ho!y work of inlssions —.We remain, dear rev. father, your devoted chtidreo In Christ, THE BOYS OF ST .ALBAN'S ScaooL. Signed on behalf of the children, GEORGE G. BROWN, O.' .B , Manager. JAMES hTNESs, Bead Master. JOHN LAWTON,' Schwan • The present consisted of a silver m tun ed umbrala, with the Inscription "To the Be". J. R. Richmond. Front the boys of lit. Alban's School, Warringtcn, 1886," and a bum of money.

SHOCKING BRUTA At the Borough Court, on Tuesday, a young man named Walter Gourke, a puddler at Dallam forge, who lives in Walker-street, was brought up in cus- tody on charges of assaulting his wife, using malicious threats to her, and cruelly ill-treating a dog. The parties have been married twelve months. On Saturday evening prisoner came home, and at the time his wife had on her knee a silver-haired Skye terrier, which had been given to her by an uncle. He seized the dog, threw it up against the ceiling, and then cut its throat with a knife. He afterwards assaulted and threatened his wife under circumstances related by Chief Constable Hunt. Prisoner was remanded until Thursday.- Prisoner was brought up at the Borough Court on Thursday morning, when he was defended by Mr. A. Browne. —Mr. Jenkins appeared for the complainant, and stated the case to the Magistrates. He was instruc- ted to say that in consequence of the violence of prisoner to his wife she could not live with him, and to ask the Magistrates for a separation order Complainant said that she had been married about 12 months. On Saturday morning prisoner went out and did not return until seven o'clock in the .even- ing, when he was a little under the influence of drink. He threatened to cutler b-- throat, and she left the house with her baby and went to her father's. He followed and wanted her to come out, but she refused. As she was sat down he struck her on the side of the head. She would never live with him again, as he had so many times threatened her. In answer to Mr. Browne complainant denied that she had annoyed her husband by taking a cer- tain drug. She had never thrown his wages in his face because he took a shilling for himself. They had never had a quarrel about the dog. She had been a good wife to him and had properly attended to his wants.— Complainant's father-in- law said that on the Saturday in question his daughter came into the house. Defendant followed soon afterwards and said "Come out of this, you," to his wife. He struck his wife a hard blow on the ear, knocking her against the scullery door. ness next day got the dog out of a raintub in pri- soner's yard; its throat was gashed.--A little girl, sister of the complainant, said that she saw the dog in the yard; it was bleeding from the throat, but was alive and wanted to shake hands with her. She was crying, and the dog was screaming. She also spoke to prisoner's assault on his wife.—P.C. Chantler said he went to prisoner's house on the Sunday, and found the floor and wall were spattered with blood. He found the dogin the yard dead, with its throat cut right across. There was blood about the yard, as though the dog had been running about. —lnspector Spinks said that he arrested prisoner on the three charges. Prisoner replied "I was in drink and did not intend to hurt the dog." Witness cor- roborated the statement of P.C. Chantler regarding the state of the house.—Mr. Browne said that he could net deny that prisoner did cut the dog's throat. • The defence was that he was drunk.—The Mayor: No defence at all.—Mr. Browne said that prisoner was aggravated and taunted by his wife,

who would have the dog against his wishes. Tri,": goner .alsbialleged that the dog bit him on the hang —Mr. Browne urged that prisoner's assault on Ws wife was not a serious one.—The Mayor said tlit the Bench- had concluded to convict- prisoner was a great pity that a young* man like him shou-19: have degraded himself 'by such an exhibition 01 brutality towards the clog and his Wife. Se Would be fined 20s and costs for the assault on his wife,' and 20s and costs for the cruelty to the dog. , should also decree a judicial separation, prisonor to pay his wife lOs a week.

It was not exactly a "dry locality " that he had Visited, and he arrived home slightly exhilarated. He kanaged, by describing several erratic rather than geomet- tlcal lines, to get to his bedroom and into a chair. Then he called to his wife in a stage whisper : "I can't get my boots et" "What's the matter with your boots?" " Nozzin'," le a faint whisper. "What's the matter with your hands, then," she cross-examined. " Nozzin'." "Why don't you Poll your boots off, then ?" "Maria, I've forgot the com- bination ?" , Cow ED !—At a place called Prickwillow a man was driv- gig some cows from one farm to another, and one of the cows bolted, and climbed a bank. Against this bank, and built with a sloping roof below it, is a blacksmith's shop. At the moment that the cow got on to the bank a Conserva- tive politician was in the shop haranguing the blacksmith, a Radical, on what he was pleased to term "Radical lies alad false promises." "You've returned a Radical for the county," said the Tory; "and now where's your cow and t„hree acres? I suppose you expected them to fall through l'ee roof!" At that moment there was a crash, and through Lila roof there fell, at the foot of the Tory disbeliever, a real ve cow. The politician gave a wild yell of terror and Asa.

THE CHESHIRE RAILWAY MYSTERY. On Monday afternoon, Mr. J. Tatlock, Chester coroner, held an inquest on the body of Lizzie Davies, who was found terribly injured on the Chester and Warrington line of railway. Mr. Fennah, of Chester station, watched the pro- ceedings on behalf of the London and North-Wes- tern Railway Company. Edwin Davies deposed that deceased, who was twenty-six years of age, was his daughter. She had been engaged as a domestic servant by her aunt, who was a provision dealer and named Mrs John Chesters, of 19, Castle Foregate, Shrewsbury. John Dobson, a platelayer, stated that, about half- past five o'clock on the morning of the 14th inst., he was proceeding to his work along the line, when he , observed deceased lying on the North-Western Bridge, half-way between Norton and Daresbury station. She was lying on the outside of the up- road, meaning the road to Chester. Her right foot was nearly off, and there were marks on the right side of her face.—By a Juror : The ulster which de- ceased wore at the time she was found was only half-buttoned. There was no sign of a struggle having taken place. He produced a railway ticket from Exchange Station, Manchester, to Chester General Station, which he found on the roadway near deceased. Henry Franklin said that he was guard of the train leaving Manchester at 10-40 p.m. on the 13th April, and noticed deceased in one of the third-class compartments. The door of the compartment was fastened, but not locked. Deceased was missed at the Chester ticket stage on the arrival of the train, the door of the compartment being loose. Dr. W. Lees, acting house-surgeon at Chester In- firmary, said deceased died from injuries sustained to the brain. In the pocket of her dress he found a purse containing 3 lOs in gold, 98 in silver, 10d in copper, and a few other articles. Mr. Franklin, the guard, was recalled, and said that the train waited at Warrington about seventeen minutes, and it was impossible for anyone to enter the compartment in which deceased was, without his seeing. No one could pass from carriage to car- riage whilst the train was travelling at such a pace between Norton and Daresbury. The jury returned a verdict of "Found on the railway suffering from wounds which caused death; and as to how she came by them there was no evi- dence to show."

THE HOME RULE QUESTION. In a speech which he delivered at Bradford, on Saturday evening, Mr. Shaw Lefevre said there were people who thought a Parliament could not be granted to Ireland without the unity of the Empire being destroyed. He had no such fear. In his opinion there was far greater danger to be appre- hended from a policy of coercion than from the establishment of a Parliament in Ireland which should deal with purely Irish affairs. On Saturday night Mr. Brand, M.P., who is to move the rejection of the motion for the second reading of the Irish Government Bill, addressing his constituents at Stroad, explained why he opposes Mr. Gladstone's measures. A resolution approving of Mr. Brand's views was carried, though an amend- ment expressing unabated confidence in the Govern- ment received very considerable support. Sir John Gorst, M.P., speaking at Hastings on Saturday night, said Mr. Parnell would in time be supplanted by other agitators with greater demands. Mr. F. Hardcastle, M.P., and Mr. F. S. Powell, M.P., attended a meeting at Westhoughton, and an that they would offer strenuous opposi- tion to the Government's Irish policy. Mr. Chaplin, M.P., at Sleaford, also denounced the Ministerial proposals. On Saturday, at a meeting of the Executive Corn- mittee of the Lancashire Union of Conservative and Constitutional Associations, resolutions were passed expressing strong condemnation of the proposals, and urging upon all the associations in the Union the desirability of calling public meetings "to protest and 'petition against Mr. Gladstone's scheme." Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth, whose seat for the Clitheroe division had become vacant by his accept- ance of the post of the Chancellor of the Duchy, was on Wednesday re-elected without opposition. It is asserted in the " Pall Mall Gazette" that Mr. Bright continues to be very hostile to Mr. Glad- stone's Irish scheme, and that his objections are likely to lead him to abstain from voting for the second reading of the bill. Mr. Chamberlain in a letter to a Welsh correspon- dent says the first step in his Federation proposal would be the creation of Provincial Assemblies, empowered to legislate only on subjects delegated to them, and leaving all Imperial questions to the united Parliament at Westminister. If, however, Wales and Scotland do not desire such extensive local government, he sees no reason why the experi- ment should not in the first instance be confined to Ireland. From London it is reported that the Conservative leaders will not, generally take any active part during the recess in the controversy on Irish go- vernment. Their only prominent representative, as now arranged, will be Sir M. Hicks-Beach, who speaks at Gloucester. On the other hand, a great number of meetings have been convened by the "Loyalists " from Ireland, and on the Liberal side the recess will be well occupied with important public meetings. Two of the Conservative members for Sheffield—Mr. Howard Vincent and Mr. Ashmead-Bartlettr--atten- ded a meeting held on Monday in the historic Para- dise-square to protest against the separation of Ire- land from Great Britain. A resolution condemning Mr. Gladstone's propo- sals was adopted at a meeting of Conservatives held at Oldham on Monday evening. Mr. McLean, M.P., who was the principal speaker at the gathering, expressed his belief that the proposals would not be accepted by Parliament, and that if they were they would prove unworkable. Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, speaking at Macclesfield on Monday even- ing, denounced the Premier as " traitorous and treacherous" to England in respect of his Home Rule proposals. The quarterly meeting of the Glasgow Chamber of Commerce on Monday adopted by a large majority a resolution declaring that the passing of the Government Home Rule measure would be pre- judicial to the commercial interests of the United Kingdom. Large numbers of representative Liberal meetings have passed resolutions expressing unabated con- fidence in Mr. Gladstone. Lord Salisbury, on the other hand, is confident that Mr. Gladstone's "desperate scheme" will fail. Addressing a crow- ded meeting in Glasgow, on Wednesday, Mr. Davitt said the Irish people would accept and loyally stand by Mr. Gladstone's proposed Constitution in spite of the restrictions, in full belief that a few years of peace, contentment, and progress in Ireland would induce the Imperial Parliament to further extend the power of self-government in the Irish Legis- lature. The Easter political campain was inaugurated on Wednesday by great meetings of Liberals at New- castle-upon-Tyne, Birmingham, and Glasgow. Lord Spencer and Mr. John Morley were the principal speakers at Newcastle. The latter in a very uncom- promising speech declared that he adhered to that part of the Home Rule scheme of the Government which provided for the exclusion of the Irish re- presentatives from the Imperial Parliament at Westminster. At Birmingham, • Mr. Chamberlain, in his speech, declared that no settlement of the Irish question would be permanent that did not satisfy the demands of Mr. Parnell for legislative independence. LYMM.

GOOD FRIDAY.—As usual on Good Friday, large num- bers of people belonging to Warrington. Manchester, and ether neighbouring towns yesterday visited Lymm, and doubtless with such beautiful weather enjoyed their outing. In addition to the very large contingent who came by train, vehicles of almost every description were utilised by the excursionists, and the accommodation at the hostelries seemed to be taxed to the utmost. In the village itself the holiday appeared to be generally observed, though judging from the number of labourers engaged in the surrounding 'fields the farmgrs were loth to lose so favourable a day for agricultural purposes.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD.

The annual meeting of this body was held at the office of I the Board at Lymm, on Friday evening. There were present Messrs. H. Cameron, Forster, Hall, Thomason, Woolly, Gibbon, and Ride-way (clerk). Ericrtorr OF CHAIRMAN.—Mr. Thomason proposed that Mr. Cameron be appointed chairman. In him, he said, they bad a chairman who had well fulfilled his duties in the past, and who was worthy to take the position again.—Mr. Woolly seconded the motion.—Mr. Hall proposed as an amendment that Mr. John Dewhurst be elected chairman. He stated emphatically that he had no feeling personally against Mr. Cameron, but he thought that Mr. Cameron's appointment was wrong, because he he'd a position under a member of the Board, Mr. Dewhurst. Suppose anything occurred by which some large ependiture of money had to be incurred on the property of Mr. Dewhurst, and the Board were equally divided on the subject. The chairman would have to give his casting vote, and he asked them as sensible men which way would he give it? Ninety-nine out of a hundred would say that he would give it for the benefit of his master. He (Mr. Hall) did not say so, but he thought the position of chairman might lay Mr. Cameron open to temptation. He then spoke against the present system of polling for Local Board elections, and in favour of vote by ballot.—There being us seconder to the motion, Mr. Cameron was elected.—ln returning thanks, he said that Mr. Dew- hnrst's engagements were such as to render it inconvenient to accept the post of chairman. He referred to statements said to have been made in reference to him by Mr. Hall out- side the Board, and expressed his determination to act firmly as chairman it necessary, at the same time wishing that the business should be amicably conducted. ELECTION OF CO3IMITTEES —The following committees were elected :—Building and Fire Engine, Messrs. Appleton, Hall, and Woolley; Finance, Messrs. Dewhurst, Hall, Brazen- dale, and Woolly; Gas, Messrs. Thomason, Dewhurst, and Brazendale; Road, Messrs. Dewhurst, Forster, and Gibbon; Sanitary, Messrs. Hall, Brazendale, and Thomason; School Attendance, Messrs. Appleton, Thomason, and Woolly; and Sewage Farm, Messrs. Appleton, Forster, and Gibbon. This was all the business.

div.head: iCritea to tin Editor.
div.p: iCritea to tin Editor.
THE LIBRARY QUESTION.

Sir,—lt is gratifying to see that practical steps have at last been taken towards making our library " free " in reality as well as in name. The deputation which I see has been formed to bring the matter before the powers that be ought to have an easy task before them. The treating of all alike in connection with a rate-supported institution like a public library is so obviously the right and only jus- tifiable thing to do that it is hard to imagine what can be urged against the arguments which no doubt the deputation -will use. That the funds at the command of the Library Committee are limited cannot be regarded as a valid argu- ment against freeing the library, or if it can it is an argu- ment utterly fetal to the setting up of a free library any- where. The funds at the disposal of every Library Com- mittee in the kingdom have a hard and fast limit some- where, but that fact has not prevented the opening of num- berless free lending libraries. All it has led to is t'..e estab- lishment of libraries of different degrees of magnitude so to speak. In Liverpool and Manchester they have free libraries on a scale commensurate with their means, and in smaller towns things are managed in the same way. It would be an insult to the very excellent Library Committee of Warrington to suppose that they could not do what the committees of other towns, large and small, have done. READER.

div.head: PARTY VERSUS PUBLIC.
div.p: PARTY VERSUS PUBLIC.

Sir,—l should think that all who feel the least interested in the way the poor law affairs of this union are managed would be heartily glad to learn that the Board of Guardians had paid so handsome a tribute to Mr. Darbyshire as it did at its last meeting. It is not very easy to believe that the public good is the first consideration of those people who strove se hard to tarn Mr. Darbyshire off the Board of Guardians. I must say I was rather surprised to find that Major Pickmere was one of the nominators of Mr. Dartv- shire's opponent. I remember that when the major lost his qaaliiication as a voter at the last revision of voters' lists in Warrington an attempt was made to get up some righteous indignation against the Liberal party. We were told that the disfranchised alderman was one who always nut party considerations aside when the good of the public was in Q a esti ea, and that it was carrying party action to a vicious extreme to object to the vote of a man of that kind. Ido not know whether all this was correct or not, but if it was I should think this model alderman would have a bad quar- ter of an hour of it when he read what was said about Mr. Darbyshire's serviccs to the public by members of the Board of Guardians of both shades of pslitics. He could hardly come to the conclusion that be bad been setting party considerations aside for the public good when he gave his influence against a man like Mr. Darbyshire.—_ V ours, Ake , LATCHFORD.

ELECTION OF GUARDIAN FOR GRAPPENHALL. Sir,—With reference to Mr. Darbyshire's and his friends' utterances as to the above. I venture to assert that he has no legalnr moral ground for complaint, and I beg to place before the public the following facts :—Twopennyworth of newspaper literature has not been given on behalf of Mr. Woods to the Grappenhall voters as stated. The newspaper distributed on the day of voting only cost one half-penny, and as to the same newspaper sent out previously, although on this occasion it cost a penny, only a few copies were distributed, and each paper was marked purposely to render it quite unsaleable. But admitting for the sake of argn- inent that three halfpennyworth of newspaper literature was Circulated, can any reasonable man call it "Bribery and cor- •ruption," considering the close and hard fought nature of *he contest and the fact that Mr. Darbyshire distributed -during his -canvass printed statements expounding his vir- tues and advocating his claims. Mr. Woods has not paid zor will he pay for the newspapers or anyelectien expenses, As to the conduct of the election, Mr. James Ashcroft who distributed the voting paper -i did not attempt to influence any voter, and there was no impropriety either in distribu- tion or collection. The person who accompanied Ashcroft had a perfect legal right to do so, as he was appointed for that duty by Mr. Woods to ensure every ratepayer getting a Voting paper. The counting of the votes was conducted in perfectly fair and legal manner as regards Mr.Darbyshire, in feet Mr. Sutton argued every point with me from his side, and disallowed several of Mr. Woods' votes for the slightest defects. The result of the counting was not known either to Mr. Woods or myself until after the last four votes had come in and the voting was closed, and even then we were only told that the numbers were about equal. The election was not affected in the slightest by the c,eunting being commenced before the pen bad closed.—Yours, H. J. LONGTON. Warrington,2otl2 April, 1886.

GOOD FRIDAY AT WARRINGTON. Yesterday seemed to be all but universally ob- served as a holiday by the various classes of War- rington. The beautiful spring-like weather invited to out-door enjoyments, and in the afternoon par- ticularly the town had almost a deserted appear- ance. Special and the ordinary trains as on Sundays were run from the different stations, and by these immense numbers left the town for Blackpool, Frodsham, Lymm, and the various other popular resorts. In the afternoon still more seemed to pour out into the lanes and bye-ways around the town, and a considerable assembly gathered by the river side at Bank Quay to witness the annual handicap sailing match. Good Friday is evidently regarded as the initial day of the bicycle and tricycle season, and the number of cyclists who passed through, the town was something remarkable, of the number being about thirty members of the St. Helens. Cyclists Club on their way to Altrincham. Services were held in most of the churches in the course of the day, and in the evening congregational gather- ings were held. Late in the evening the returning , excursionists gave the streets an animated appear- ance, but, it is pleasant to record, everything passed off quietly, there being a commendable absence of drunkenness and anything of a disorderly char- acter. .

div.head: SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY.

Yesterday the Salvation Army celebrated the third anniversary of their work in Warrington by holding special services, which were well attended. In the afternoon the members, with their band, pro- ceeded through various parts of the town, and held open-air meetings. T. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, BUTTERMARKET-

STREET. Passion week has been celebrated here very be- comingly. The church was draped in purple and all the images covered up. The chapel of repose w4s splendidly decorated with candles and flowers. Great praise is due to the people who decorated the altar of repose, including Mrs. Fox and the others who brought beautiful flowers. The services of Holy Week commenced on Thursday morning, when the Church was filled with a large congregation. The procession of the Blessed Sacrament to the altar of repose took place during the mass, and all through the day numbers of people could be seen watching before the lighted al ar. At eight o'clock in the evening, prayers were recited before the side altar, and after the service many stayed until the church was closed for the night. The service for Good Friday commenced yesterday morning at ten, o'clock, Father Fishwick officiating at the Mass of the Presantified. The large church was over- crowdeir. The sermon was preached by Father Bunce, 0.P., cne of the missioners who is staying at St. Mary's during the Holy Week services. The people then walked to the altar rails to kiss the feet of the Crucifix. The procession of the Blessed Sac- rament from the altar of repose to the chancel then walked round the church, headed by Cross bearer and torch bearers, Father Fishwick carrying the Sacred Host. The choir of the church sang the "Stabat Mater," during the Mass, without the organ, and with excellent effect. The six large candles upon the new altar were then lighted, and the Mass concluded. In the afternoon at three o'clock the church was filled. The Devotion of the Way of the Cross was recited, the procession going round the church, stopping and meditating at each statio7 of Christ's journey to Calvary.

div.head: MISSIONARY MEETING.
div.p: MISSIONARY MEETING.

The annual missionary meeting was held at Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel last evening, when the commodious building was nearly filled. Mr. Bennett, of Leeds, occupied the chair, and amongst those on the platform were the Revs. J. McTurk, J. 11. Jones, G. E. Cutting, F. J. Sharr, and T. Waugh. The meeting commenced with singing and prayer. after which Mr. Wright read the balance sheet. It stated that there had been a slight decrease in the Warrington collections, but, taking into account the depressed state of trade, it was considered very satisfactory. —The Rev. G. E. Cutting read the annual general report, detailing the work of the Missionary Society in different countries.— The Chairman then -delivered a long and eloquent address, in the course of which he referred to the opium traffic, and condemned the action of the Government in sanctionirg it for the sake of adding to the revenue.—The Rev. F. J. Sham in an inter- esting speech, referred to missionary work in Spain, Italy, and China, and, remarking on the opium traffic, said that it was doing almost as much mis- chief in China, as the missionaries were doing good. The opium traffic was a disgrace to a people calling themselves Christians. He did not know how it was, but no matter what Government was in office—Conservative or Liberal--it was always the same, but they hoped to arrive at some way of grappling with this question.—The Rev. Waugh, ex- pressed himself more in favour of home missions than foreign missions, believing that if England and America were Christianised the whole world would soon be the same.—The Rev. J. H. Jones proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, and to the gentle- men who had attended as a deputation, and the resolution, on being put to the meeting, was carried with enthusiasm.—lt was announced that the col- lections amounted to £32 Bs, being £lO in advance of what was collected last Good Friday. LA.TCHFORD BAPTIST CHAPEL.

The annual tea and meeting in connection with the above chapel were held last evening. Above 200 per- sons sat down to an excellent tea in the schoolroom, the tables being presided over byMesdames Wilkin- son, Jones, Pearson, W. T. Wilkinson, Fairhurst, Adams, Dutton; Misses Smith (2), Riley, Wilkinson (2), Hankey, Gee, Yarwood. Albinson, and Light- foot. The after meeting was held in the chapel, there being a large attendance. The chair (in the absence of the Mayor through indisposition) was taken by the Rev. Mr. Varley, the pastor of the church, and there were also on the platform the Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. E. Moore, Rev. G. Rigby, Messrs Davidson, Wilkinson, and Naylor. The Rev. J. Yonge having engaged in prayer, a s,,iitable address was given by Mr. Naylor, in the course of which he mentioned the fact that it was now over a quarter of a century since that place of worship was opened, and that he attended all the annual meetings,with few exceptions during that time.—The Rev. E. Moore said they had been hoping they might have had that day as they had the previous Good Friday, the presence of their esteemed Mayor of Warrington. It spoke very well for the catholic and liberal spirit of his worship that he again con- sented to take the chair at the Baptist tea meeting, and they all regretted sincerely that indisposition had prevented his worship from carrying out his good intention. In connection with the promised visit of the Mayor he had been thinking how very different were the times in which they lived now to what they were many years ago. English history re- minded them that at one time it was a very serious matter—it would have been at all events if it had been possible, which it was not—for the Mayor of a tciwn like Warrington to be present at such a dreadful outrage and offence against all the laws of God and man as a Nonconformist meeting. (Hear, hear.) He dare say it would have cost his worship his head, and certainly it would have cost him his office. He (Mr. Moore) might also remind them that in those days their friend, Mr. Varley, would not dare to show his face there as a Baptist parson, and his congregation would have been scattered to the four winds of heaven before it dared to worship God according to the dictates of their conscience. the owuht o fore t or (Hear, hear.) There were many of their forefathers hindrance privilege that w o u dh e 3- cheerfullyt o ay enjoyed have given ith- their life's blood. Therefore, he said, let folk talk as they like about the good old times, he was thankful they were gone and right-down thankful was he to live in these days. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He hoped it would never come that English people, and especially English non-con- formists, would cease to value and be truly thank- ful for the inestimable blessing of liberty of con- science. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the Established Church, he said they found that to-day Ritualism and Popery were making great strides, and he thought he was correct in saying that a large ma- jority of the bishops on the bench at the present time were largely committed in the direction of Popery. They could not view things like these with indifference. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Moore con- cluded by urging them as non-conformists to care- fully and earnestly consider the bearings of all the great social questions that were brought before them, and when they had made up their minds what 'course to take to take it with all the earnestness of which they were capable. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. Yonge also expressed regret for the absence of the Mayor. Few Mayors they had had, at all events whilst he had been in Warrington, had shown themselves so willing to obey the calls that were made upon them and to make things pleasant all round. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Yonge) was always glad to come to that meeting, for one thing because they always got some good music. The Latchford Baptist Choir had a reputation which no doubt many other choirs envied. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to say they lived in days when there seemed to be some promise

div.head: rcl,F, EXAMINER, SATURDAT, APRn, 24, 1886.
div.p: rcl,F, EXAMINER, SATURDAT, APRn, 24, 1886.

of spring time amongst the denominations—more. warmth, a more genial bearing, and more brotherly love. He rejoiced to know that next month, in London, the Baptist Union and the Congregational \Union were to have a day's joint session. He thought that was a sign of the times for which they all ought to be thankful. (Hear, hear.) He never could since he began to think about things at all un- derstand why different views about the question of baptism should keep Christian brethren apart at least so widely and so sternly as they kept apart in the years that were past. Surely the joint meeting of the two unions would be productive of vast good to all the churches, and would send a thrill of new life among the congregations that the Baptist Union and the Congregational Union repre- sented. (Hear, hear, and applause.)—Short addresses were delivered by the Rev. G. Rigby and other gentlemen, and in the course of the evening several anthems and songs were admirably sung.

ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.—Particulars of a sale of 1 work to be held next Wednesday in connection. 1 with this church will be found in our advertising columns. SUDDEN DEATH. Eirly yesterthy morning a child named Lucy Eleanor Young, six months old, I whose parents reside in Manchester-road, died very suddenly. She wits put in bed apparently in her usual health and was found dead early in the morning.

PRIM-ROSE DAY.—On Monday primroses were 1 generally worn in Warrington in commemoration 1 of the death of the Earl of Beaconsfield. Many I Liberals, as well as Conservatives, wore buttonholes of the pretty flowers. In front of the balcony of the Conservative Club was placed a wreath of prim- roses, centred with the letter "B," which had been worked by Mrs. Speakman. LATCHFORD CRICKET CLUB.—The opening day of this club was Saturday last, when about 30 members picked by the captains of the first and second teams took part in a match. The weather throughout was favourable, and, owing to the desire to allow all members present to have a chance of playing, there were too many on each side to allow of the game being finished, which consequently re- sulted in a draw. THE LENDING LIBRARY.—The . deputation ap- pointed to wait upon the Library Committee with the object of urging that the Lending Library should be made free to the public have been in communication with the chairman of the corn-

mittee (Mr. Beamont). It has been arranged for the interview to take place at the next meeting of the Library Committee, which will be held on the 14th of May. " ECCE Homo.--- On Thursday evening a service was held in Holy Trinity Church, at which was per- formed the sacred cantata "Ecce Homo" which we recently noticed, the words of which have been selected and arranged by Mr. John White, and the music composed by Mr. Wm. Johnson, both of whom ' are Warrington gentlemen. The principal soloist was Miss Riley, who was very successful in her parts. The same cantata was also rendered last evening at Christ Church, Latchford. WARRINGTON MUSEITNI.-A temporary addition to the attractions of the Art Gallery has been made by the hanging of 16 pictures lent by Mr. William Long, J.P., of Thelwall Heyes. The collection includes works by Ward, R.A., Cooper, R.A., Herbert, R.A., Piot, Beavis, Duverger, A. Bonheur, Weber, and other artists. Mr. Long has set an example which it is to be hoped will be fol- lowed by other gentlemen who have works of art which the public would be delighted to see. VEGETARIANISM.—We understand that the Vege- tarian Society are making arrangements to provide a Vegetarian Restaurant at the Liverpool Exhibi- tion similar to the one which was so successful at the London Health Exhibition. Our townsman, Mr. W. 11. Chapman, whose management gave much satisfaction at "The Healthenes;" is again to be entrusted with the management of the Vegetarian

Restaurant, and we need liardly say that w antici- pate that he will be as successful in Liverpool as he was in London. BANK QUAY SUVSCRIPTION BOWLING CLUB.—The opening main of the season took place yesterday, ,when there was a good attendance of spectators present, and the green was in excellent con- dition. Thirty-two members competed; and the playing throughout the first round was of a good character, especially the game between J. Gleave, jun., and the veteran Ball, which the former won. In the second round James Shaw cleverly defeated R. Stringer, and afterwards proved successful in gaining the first prize, the vice-president (J. Taylor) being second. A CHILD SCALDED TO DEATIL—Mr. W. T. Hus- band, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Crown and Sceptre Inn, Buttermarket-street, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of a child named Wil- liam Farrell, the son of a bundler, who died at the Infirmary from injuries received on the previous Friday. The child was living with its grandparents in Cloth Hall rard, and on the afternoon of Friday was walking backwards when it fell against a pan containing boiling water. The pan was upset and the child was severely sc.ilded. The jury returned a verdict of "Accident 4 De%th." LORD BEACONSFIELD AND PRIMROSES.—The fol- lowing tit-bit is from this week's " Truth " :—" I shall give the vacant thistle to Lord ," said Lord , Melbourne. "If you do," replied Lord Palmerston, "lie will eat it." If anyone had offered a primrose to Lord Beaconsfield, it may fairly be presumed that he would have yearned to devour it, for there is only one allusion to this flower in all his works, and that is in " Lothair," where, at a spring picnic, one of the characters rather ridicules his wife for bursting iuto ecstasies about the primroses, atd remarks, " lhave heard that they make a capital salad." SAD DEATH OF A CHILD.-31r. J. Hesketh, painter and decorator, has had two children taken suddenly and seriously ill. The elder, a girl of nine years of age, died, we regret to say, on Monday evening under circumstances which lead the medical gentlemen who were in attendance to suspect that both children may have absorbed some poisonous matter in sweets which they had eaten. No inquest was deemed necessary, but there has been a post-mortem examination, and further inquiries are being made. The younger child, it is satisfactory to state, is recovering. 1.0.G.T., WESLEY LODGE, 400. The usual monthly popular entertainment of the above lodge was held in the Mission Room, Academy-street, on Monday. It was in aid of the lodge choir, and there was a good attendance. Mr. F. Monks occu- pied the chair. An excellent programme was gone through, including cornet solos, songs, glees, reci- tations, and a humourous sketch entitled "A Sprig of Holly." The items were contributed by the fol- lowing ladies and gentlemen :—Bro. Smith, Mr. J. S. Johnson (Liverpool), Mrs. Waring, Miss Wilcox, Sister Davenport, Mrs. Littlewood, Mr. Nash, Sister Ashworth, and Bro. Sheath. Mr. Crossley -officiated as accompanist. After the usual vote of thanks, a very pleasant evening was brought to a close by singing the Doxology. SAM HAGUE'S MINSTRELS.—This talented troupe of artistes visited the town during the past week, , and for three nights drew good audiences at the Public Hall. The programme is undoubtedly the most excellent of its kind presented out of London, judged both as to the items themselves and the man- ner of their performance. Each and every member of the company contributes his quota to the enter- tainment in a finished and pointed style, and the whole of the funisracy and unflagging. The mixture of solo singing and conversational witti- cisms which forms the feature of the first part is thoroughly enjoyable. The second part is given up to miscellaneous drolleries of the most side-splitting character. By those whom a couple of hours' diversion is better than any tonic the visit of this minstrel troupe will be hailed with pleasure. The heartiness of the applause showed also that the enjoyment of the programme is general as well as particular. But for the drawbacks of the Lenten season, Mr. Hague's entertainment would doubtless have been attended by crowded audiences. THE CEYLONESE EXHIBITION AT PO3.IONA. There is now open at the Pomona Palace, Manches- ter, a very interesting exhibition somewhat on the model of the Indian and Japaneses villages which have attracted so much favour in London. Carl Hagenbeck, a well-known entrepreneur on the Con- tinent, has brought over to this country his Ceylon- ese Exhibition, which has been presented in many of the leading towns in Germany, Austria, and Hungary, and is now for the first time exhibited in England. The leading interest of the exhibition is of course in the Cingalese people who, to the num- ber of about severity, have been brought over. These people, with materials provided for them, have built for themselves housesin. the Agricultural Hall, and here their home life and religious per- formances are to be seen. In addition to the people there are a large number of very fine elephants, some old and patriarchal, and one as little
as six months -old, _ and 'a number of Zebus,

or oriental cows, which are used as beasts of burden, and also as cobs and hacks. The exercises of the people are quaint and curious. We see snake charming, some very clever juggling, and much dancing. The Devil Dances, of which two examples are Oven, are semi-religious func- tions in frequent use amongst the superstitious natives. At the close of the entertainment portion of the exhibition is a very imposing procession of a religious character, and it is a feature of the ex- hibition which should not be missed. The exhibi- tion which opened on Wednesday will remain open for three weeks.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

HIGH MAss.—Solemn High Mass will be celebra- ted at St. Mary's Church, Buttermarket, to-morrow (Sunday) morning. The preacher will be the Rev. Father Cyril, O.P. STRANGE BEHAVIOUR OF A YOUNG WOMAN.— On Thursday morning a young woman named Mary Bostock, of Stockton Heath, near Warrington, was observed walking on the bank of the river, oppo- site the Bank Quay Soapery, evidently in a state of excitement. Some men on the Lancashire side of the ' river saw her take off her hat and jump into the water. Three of the men procured a boat and brought her to the Lancashire side. She was con- veyed to a public-house near by and attended to, and was then taken by a county constable to War- rington Police Station. Thence she was taken home in a cab. The woman's demeanour has of late been strange, and it is believed that her conduct is attri- butable to a love affair. THE TRAINING COLLEGE.—The result of the local competition for designs for the chapel intended for the use of the students connected .with the War- rington Training College has been made known. The Committee of the Church of England Training College invited. the local architects to furnish designs for the new structure, which is to be erected in close proximity to the college,and their decision has been in favour of those presented by Messrs, Pier- point and Adams, of Bold-street, Warrington. The work, it is understood, will be commenced at an early date. But for certain circumstances, over which the committee had no control, the erection of the building would have been taken in hand at a much earlier date. In addition to the chapel, a scheme for providing increased practising school accommodation has been under consideration by the committee. THIEVES AT LARGE.—A shop in Bridge-street was on Sunday night entered by thieves, who had got in by means of a cellar grating. Nothing of value, however, was taken. Of late a number of depredations have been committed under circum- stances which lead to the belief that an organised gang of thieves is at work.— At the Borough Court, on Wednesday, Chiet Constable Hunt informed the Magistrates that there had been about five places broken into within the last seven nights, the object evidently being to secure money. On Tuesday night the clothing shop, in Winwick-street, of Mr. Morton was entered and some property taken. The place of Mr. Fairhurst, corn factor, Mersey-street, was broken into on Saturday night, and a man was seen on the premises. He, however, succeeded in escaping with about £3 in cash. Mr. Fairhurst was away from home. On Sunday evening the boot shop of Messrs. Freeman, Hardy, and -Willis, in Bridge-street, was entered and about _E4 worth of property taken. He wished the Press to take notice of the matter, so that tradesmen might be warned to keep a sharp look out; they would do well to take care that their cash was securely placed.—At the Borough Court on Thursday morn- ing a young man named Edward Percival, alias Foy, was charged with breaking into the warehouse of Edward Whitehead, Eagle and Child-yard, and stealing various articles to the value of ss. Chief Constable Hunt said he had reason to believe that prisoner was concerned in other robberies, and a remand for a week was granted to enable inquiries to be made. LOCAL SINGERS IN SCOTLAND.—TWO of the prin- cipal artistes at a rendering of the oratorio, "Judas Maccalmeus," at Dunfermline, Scotland, last week were local vocalists, Miss Wallington and Miss Monks: The two Warrington ladies are repqrted as having sung with great intelligence and an expres- sion which showed evidence of careful and matured study. Miss Wallington's voice is regarded as pure in tone and very flexible. The florid passages, with which her part abounded, were as a rule performed with great ease; her phrasing being also remarkably good, and her rendering of "Pious orgies" was marked by much devotional feeling; but it was in the air "From Mighty Kings "that her singing created the deepest impression, which was in every way admirable, and whether in feeling or execution left nothing to be desired. Miss Monks, who took the contralto solo music, sang her part with culti- vated taste and care, and with much intelligence. In the air "Father of Heaven" she was very suc- cessful, and imparted a right feeling to the words. The recitative "Oh, Judus, 0 My Brethren," and "From Capharsalama" was delivered admirably well, with considerable dramatic force. Miss Monks was also very successful in the duet with Miss Wal- -ington, "0 lovely peace," which was exquisitely rendered by both ladies,:and received a well merited encore.

CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. The 101st quarterly meeting of the members of Warrington Co-operative Society was held on Monday evening in the Co-oper- ative Hall. The president, Mr. T. Birchall, occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of mem. - bers.—The President, in a few opening remarks, said he was glad to report that the past quarter had been one of the most prosperous the society had ex- perienced. In addition to again paying the large dividend of 3s in the X they were adding £•00 to the reserve fund, which he thought was a desirable thing to do in these depressed times. He also mentioned that they were paying at the rate of £6,800 a year to their members. (Hear, hear.)—The balance sheet was read by the Managing Secretary (Mr. A. H. Rathbone), and showed that the sales during the past quarter amounted to a total of £10,014 2s 2d. The Secretary also reported that 127 members had joined the society in the past quar- ter, whilst there had been 68 withdrawals. The Management Committee submitted to the meetin,g, a proposal by the local Cambridge University .Ex- tension Movement Committee that the society should undertake a second course of lectures during the ensuing season in connection with that move- ment. After some consideration, however, it was decided that it was not desirable that the society should incur the responsibility involved in such an undertaking. Mr. J. Shaw Green, the newly ap- pointed auditor, gave a satisfactory account of the financial affairs of the society, and highly compli- mented the managing secretary on the manner in which the books were kept,. REVIVAL SERVICES.—On Sunday the Rev. Thomas Waugh, Conference evangelist, conducted the first of a series of revival mission services in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel. At seven o'clock in the morning the services were commenced with a prayer meet- ing, and at half-past ten Mr. Waugh preached in the chapel from the words, "The promise of my Father," Luke xxiv, 49. Ile solicited the sympathy, prayer, and interest of the people, and asked them to do their best to promote the success of the mis- sion. In the afternoon a service for young people was held, the older scholars from the three Wes- leyan schools being present. The sermon was based on the words "Suffer little children to come unto me," Luke :UHL 16. From 30 to 40 young men and women gave their hearts to Christ, as well as a number of children. In the evening the chapel was crowded, and forms were placed in the aisles for thel convenience of those who were unable to obtain ' seats elsewhere. .The subject of the address was "Excuse," and the text "And they all with one con- sent began to make excuse," Luke xiv, ,18. Mr. Waugh referred to the excuses made in the present day by people when pressed to become Christians, including—first, "The inconsistency of professing Christians ;" second, "The fear of falling away ;" and third, "There's plenty of time," and to each ex- cuse Mr. Waugh referred at length. At the close of the address, the congregation bowed in silent prayer, after which Mr. Waugh asked all who wanted to become Christians to stand up to be prayed for, and from 60 to 70 persons responded to the request, the congregation still kneeling. A short prayer meeting was held, after which those who wished to give their hearts to God were accom- panied into the inquiry rooms by the mission Workers, and from 50 to 60 men and women, in- cluding several soldiers in uniform, professed to have given themselves to the service of God. The mission services so far have been a success. div.p: Jules Fame was charged at Jersey on Thursday with negligently causing the death of Louisa Journeaux, with whom he went out in a boat. He was di:charged on account of insufficient evidence.

- TWICE TRIPLETS —The Cologne Gazette announces a case of almost unexampled fruitfulness in the family of a Rhine- lander named Naveack, residing at Niebl. Within eleven months the wife of Herr Naysack has twice presented him with an addition to the family, consisting each time of a trio of infants. The mether and six youngsters are thriving as well as can be expected in the cottage of a poor day labourer.

div.head: PRESCOL
div.p: PRESCOL

FAIR.—The usual fortnightly fair was held at Prescot on Tuesday. There was a moderate attendance, and several head of stock exchanged hands. CONCERT.—On Saturday night a concert was held in the Assembly Hall, Kemble-street, when Mr. andiMrs Power and other ladies and gentlemen took part, and the Whiston Brass Band gave selections at intervals. RUN OVER—On Saturday, a child aged two years, son of Mr. Thomas Haworth, of the White Hart, Prescot, was run over by a passing trap. On the doctor seeing it he found no bones were broken, and the child is now progress- inkfavourably.

-CONFIRMATION.—On Monday a confirmation service was held in Prescot Parish Church by the Bishop of Liverpool. There were present about 80 candidates, male and female. The Rev. H. A. McNaughten, vicar, and the Rev. F. N. Lee took part in the service.

MAD DoG.—On Wednesday, some excite.nent was caused in Prescot by the appearance of a mad dog, which unfor- tunately bit the child of Mr. F. Anderten. Victoria Place. Tbe animal was finally run down and shot in Derby-street by Mr. Ainsworth, of Warrington-road. INDEPENDENT ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS.—A meeting of the district was held on Saturday night, to consider the desirability of joining the Liverpool district in forming a procession on the occasion of Her Majesty's visit to Liverpool. It was unanimously agreed to join the above district.

PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—The first meeting of the mem- bers of the " new " School Board was held on Monday night, when there were present Messrs. W. L. Evans, J.P., W. Goldsworth. J. B. Sanders, and H. Cross (clerk).—The Clerk read the certificate of the returning officer (Mr. S. H. Hartley), that the whole of the members of the old Board had been re-elected for the ensuing three years, viz. : Messrs. W. L. Evans, H. Fogg, W. Goldsworth, J. T. Hall, T. P. Hewitt, J. B. Sanders, and C. Spenceley. On the motion of Mr. Goldsworth, seconded by Mr. Sanders, Mr. Evans, J.P., was elected chairman; and on the motion of Mr. Sanders, seconded by Mr. Goldsworth, Mr. C. ipenceley was elected vice-chairman of the Board. Miss Oldfield, teacher of the infants' school, applied for a new desk and platform, and the matter was referred to the clerk and Mr. Sanders, who were instructed to obtain the necessary tenders and purchase the required desk. The Board decided to close the schools on Gocd Friday and Easter Monday for the Easter holidays. The clerk submitted his estimate of pro- posed expenditure for the half year ending 29th September next, which amounted to £250. The estimate was approved, and it was decided to make a "call" for that amount upon the overseers.

div.head: TRADES UNION MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. A DISABLED WORKMAN PRESENTED WITH £5O.
div.p: TRADES UNION MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. A DISABLED WORKMAN PRESENTED WITH £5O.

A meeting of considerable interest to local working-men I was held in the large room of the Wellington Inn, Earle- 4 street, on Monday night, when a public meeting, under the auspices of the Earlestown branch of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, was called for the purpose of present- ing Mr. John Wilson, an injured member, with £5O out of the accident fund. The chair was occupied by Mr. Samuel Woods, miners' agent, of Park Lane, and there was a very good aaendance. Representatives were present from the the following trades :—Pattern makers, steam engine makers, moulders, boiler makers, railway servants, /cc. The Chairman remarked that he considered that society had been the pioneer of all other workmen's societies, and alluded at some length to the various grants made by the Engineers' Society towards the benefit of the miners in dis- putes with their employers. He said the gifts had been given out of pure good feeling, with the object of benefit- ing men not in their own trade, and seined perhaps as they were in a particular branch of industry, but men who had to risk their lives down in the deep mines amidst dangers which no ether class of workmen had to contend against. They had felt it their bounden duty to make during the last ten years no less a sum in gifts than £1,709. (Applause.) Considering those facts it would have been an act of in- gratitude on his part not to have accepted the invitation which had been given to him to preside over that meeting. He hoped they would have an enjoyable meeting, and that its result would be long remembered by all present, in- cluding their unfortunate brother who had had the mis- fortune to lose the sight of one of his eyes.—Mr. D. Williams (the local branch secretary) then made a 'state- ment with respect to the society, remarking that they were always prepared to assist in making the path of labour smoother and more pleasant than it had ever been, and their generosity, as the chairman termed it, had net been con- fined to the miners. He thought they might certainly con- gratulate themselves and call themselves a real benefit so- ciety. He pointed out the great benefits derived by the members of that society, and remarked that during the present year they had expended £2Bll 133 5d in that branch. If they went fully into the benefits of their organisation and their critics well knew the conditions of their lives in the workshop, their opponents would modify their opinions and say such organisations were necessary under the altered can- ditions of life and labour. Owing to excessive, competition, the greed for gain, and the speed at which machinery was running, and the consequent physical exhaustion, it was necessary their organisation should both provide for and protect its members, that it should be an ark of safety, a refuge for the weak and oppressed, and a comfort to the afflicted. (Applause.) Speaking of the objects of Trades Union organisations, he said, they did not want all wages fixed at one rate, but they wished a minimum rate to be fixed, which he did not think was an injustice to the em- ployers. He believed the periodical depressions in trade would be immensely modified if working-men were better united, and he did hot see how men could better participate in the fruits of their industry than by joining such a society, sticking to it, and improving it. (Applause.)—The Chair- man followed with a lengthy speech on Trades Unionism, urging that Trades Unions had conferred the greatest bene- fit upon this country. Their first object was to recognise the equal rights of employers and employed, and they wished workmen to have fair pay and wages for their labour. He denied that a trade organisation was a conspiracy against the employers, but one of its objects was to assist their unfortunate brethren, and not only express their sympathy with words, but in a practical manner. (Applause.) They also aimed at a better repre- sentation of labour and trades in the House of Commons, and he hoped the time would come when every trade union and every branch would be associated together in one strong combined organisation. (Applause.) Notwithstanding the depression in trade he was pleased to notice the Engineers' Society was increasing, and remarked that while they had 45,472 members in 1878, they had 51,277 members last year. He urged that over-population was one of the causes of the depression in trade, and after the question of how to deal with the population for whom they could not find em- ployment the land question of this country,would have to be dealt with. He did not see any relief from the depres- sion unless they had a drastic measure of land reform. (Applause.) The Chairman afterwards said he had to present to a dis- abled brother the sum of £5O to which he was entitled as a member of the Engineers' Society. Their brother John Wilson had the misfortune, while following his work, to lose the sight of one eye, and he (the chairman) trusted the sum he was receiving would prove a blessing to him and his family, and that be would never seed the assistance of others. He thought it was a blessing to Mr. Wilson that he was a member of the society, and he was sure the gift was accompanied with the good feelings and wishes of every brother. (Applause.)—Brother John Wilson appropriately ; responded, and remarked that he was not now going to turn his back upon the society, but would continue a member in the future, and so keep his wife and family from going to a pauper's grave. He advised all young men to join the society as soon as they possibly could. (Applause.)—Mr. Wm. Davies said if it was not for such societies as that the ratepayers and Guardians would have to do considerably more than at present with the view of assisting the working classes. During the last ten years that branch of the Engineers Society had paid £34 Os 10d as the ccnting- ent fund for strikes and disputes; £1,697 7s 4d as donations to members out of work; £574 3s 3d as sick pay; £273 9s superannuation: £lB3 for funerals; and £3OO as benevo- lent grants to members in distress. During that time the contributions, fines, and levies amounted to £3,907 15s. Every ratepayer ought to be proud they bad such organisa- tions in their midst, and he was not aware that any of their members had ever had cause to apply for parish relief. ( Applause.)—Mr. George Ratcliffe, one of the township similar tie, andiaenese,iseaiedhe fullyfom ape weeks egtedto aheet a meetingffortsoft ebatf and the Board of Guardians be expressed himself in favour of the I establishment of accident funds at various works. He be- lieved such societies relieved taxation. He was proud he bad been again elected a Guardian, and said he should do his utmost to meet the requirements of the situation, and he would act according to his conscience. (Applause.)—On the motion of Mr. H. Roberts, seconded by Mr. Seddon, and supported by Mr. W. Gilmour, a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, and the meeting concluded.

CRICEET.—L. & N.-W. C. T. ECCLESTON C. C. This match was played at Sutton on Saturday, and resulted in a draw. Score: Eccleston, 115; L. and N.-W. C., 16 for four wickets. CONFIRMATION.—On Thursday week the Bishop of Liver- pool held a confirmation at St. Thomas's Church, Ashton. T present were the vicar (the Rev. H. Siddall), the vicar gyveilcearror St. . James's Haydock (the Rev. A. H. Kearney), and the curate of St. Thomas's. The candidates numbered about 180 in all, 110 of which belonged to St. Thomas's, and the remainder to St. James's. At the cenclusien of the , confirmation service the Bishop delivered an earnest ad- dress to the candidates. In the afternoon the confirms were entertained to tea at St. Thomas's Schools by the vicar, and in the evening a special service was held at St. Thomas's Church, at which there was a very good congre. gation. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A BEAKESMAN.-0131 Monday after- noon, lUr Rowbettom, coroner' held an inquest at the Wigan Infirmary, touching the death of Samuel Aspinall, 22 years of age. of Downall Green, Ashton, who died on Friday last owing to injuries received earlier in the day whilst follow- his employment as a brakesman at the Garswood Col- , liery. The deceased was riding on a train of waggons' and whilst jumping from one to another he caught his head against the girder of a bridge, and the blow knocked him backwards between the waggone. The whole of the front part of the train passed over his arm. There was a large wound on his forehead, and deceased became insensible soon after. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
LATEST NEWS.
Several volunteer:regiments arrived at Colchester on Fri- day, and went into camp. Others are expected to bring the. total up to 3,000.
_ Lieut.-Colonel Sir Henry Edwards, Bart., C. 8., died on Friday morning at his residence, Halifax, in his 74th year, after a protracted illness.

LAND PURCHASE IN IRELAND.—The trustees of Mr. Nathaniel P. Byrnes, an extensive landowner in the West- port district, county Mayo, have offered to sell his tenants their holdings at twelve years' purchase calculated on the present poor-law valuation.

- Tim Home RULE QTJEST. lON.—The Liberal Executive Council at Goole, on Friday, unanimously agreed to urge Sir John Ramsden, M.P., to support Mr. Gladstone in his endeavours to settle the Irish difficulty. It is stated that the hon. baronet's attendance at the Opera House meeting has caused considerable dissatisfaction amongst his con- stituents.

ARREST OF A SUPPOSED MURDERER:A man named John Neill was arrested in Cavan yesterday by the local constabulary on suspicion of being the man who murdered Daniel Neill, at Knocks, on the high road between Clona- killy and Dunmannay on the 3rd inst. by shooting him through the bead with a revolver. It is stated that pri- soner's appearance closely corresponded with the descrip- tion of the murderer as circulated by the police. The pri- soner will be conveyed to Dunmannay forthwith.

ANOTHER STRIKE 1N BELGIUM. BRUSSELS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—At Gramont, this morning, a strike of match makers took place. Reinforce- ments of gendarmes were telegraphed for, and on their arrival were received with showers of stones. Several arrests were made.

FIGHTING IN UPPER BURMAH. The Press Association has received the following from the India Office :—The latest intelligence received from the Vicerov of India states that a report had been received from Mr. Bernard that a detachment pf two hundred men was despatched by General Norman from Bhamo against a Kachin chief who had raided on some neighbouring villages. The enemy occupied the top of a hill. Two stockades were carried successfully, but Wace, the commander of the party, and another officer, Lyle, were wounded, besides seven men. The jungle in front being very difficult, further ad- vance was considered imprudent, and our people returned to Bhamo.

WAKEFIELD CORN, THURSDAY.—The market to-day is quite of a holiday character, very little business being transacted. Wheat is very firmly held, and where sales are made last week's prices are insisted upon. There is little demand for other articles that prices cannot be quoted, but the small retail demand or barley shows an advance on last week's prices.
