FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION. A case of some importance to Warrington' tradesmen was heard at the Borough Court on Thursday morning. John Cross, butcher, Golden' Square and Corporation-street, was summoned for creating an obstruction by allowing meat to projees over the footpath. Mr. Whittle (deputy town clerk) appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Jenkins IQ- peared for defendant and for the owners of the Pr°-- perty.—Mr. Whittle said that the proceedings we instituted under the Police Clauses Act of 1847. On the 14th inst. Mr. Cross had a table placed outsig?• his shop in Golden Square, and in consequence was almost impossible for people to pass on the footpath, which at that point was very narrla Meat was also hanging outside the shop, e" pedestrians were forced to go into the roadwasc--_,. Inspector Spinks then gave evidence. He said thaN. on the morning in question he went to Goldenh ! Square, and in front of the defendant's shop, wh,„ic "' was managed by his son, he saw a quarter of ,"t projecting 15 inches over the footway, whie""_.A.s - that point was barely two feet wide. There also a table about four feet long and two feet I'7ll on the footpath. Four carcases of sheep weL. hanging over the table. Defendant told witness would put the. meat out as long as he liked---5 defence, Mr. Jenkins contended that Mr. Cross bit, a right by vested interest to place a bench, bloc• or table in front of the premises. • His second eelli tention was that there was no footway in front 00 the premises in question, and that there had bee ,/ no dedication to the public of such space for 11-„4le. such purpose. He was instructed to watch the csio. , on behalf of the owners of the property, tolvilo it was a point of some interest. It might a'-l'" ecl fl affect other property owners in the town. He aslt--h that the most serious consideration of the Belie; should be given to the matter. It was his intent,e,': !to prove the title to the property, and that t.n; ! owners enjoyed the right to place the table oatslhue • the shop. He urged that the shop, prior W passing of the Market and Improvement •,'`'s ! which incorporated the Town's Police Clause/ ,! Act, was in existence, and that the right placing a table or block outside was not interfer,v,:, with.—Witnesses were called stating that, the tau'ay had been placed in the position complained of for long number number of years, and lengthy legal argumen.,..., iwere entered into.—The magistrates retired to OA Isider their decision. On returning the Mayor sts! ! that they had come to the conclusion that it ! not necessary, or, at all times, wise, to give reaso. for their having arrived at a certain concluslti They had arrived at the conclusion that there undoubtedly been an obstruction, and that the,. should be obliged to inflict a penalty. - Breakfast table. Father of family reading: 'There is a cat in Manchester that drinks beer." Daughter (fourteen) : "Pa, she must be a Maltese cat." "Do you enjoy Meyerbeer ?" she asked him as they were sitting at a concert recently. " Well, to tell you the troth," he answered, "I don't know that I ever drank any," and then sat still and listened. In a small village not a hundred miles from Inverness which boasts of a school and schoolmistress, and also a goodly number of juveniles, the mistress was rather annoyed by one of her pupils, a young lassie who was blind of one eye, bringing on the Monday morning only one-half of the sum (twopence) she charged for weekly instruction. Deter- mined to know the reason why, she sent her home on Mon- day morning to tell her "mither" that she wanted another penny. After the lapse of a reasonable time, the school- room door was rather unceremoniously opened by a red- headed Highland woman, who, leading the little girl by the hand, advanced towards the mistress in a manner that would have made a stouter heart than hers tremble, and vociferated in a voice of thunder, "800 daur ye chairge tuppence for a lassie that's only getton as e'e?" IN NO HURRY FOR CONVHRSATION.—A well-known family up town has au eight-year-old urchin upon whom a revival at one of the churches has made a deep impres- sion. He astounded his good Mother the other night by saying " Mammii, lam going to church to-night to be converted." "Converted, Jimmie? Why, you do not understand what that means." "Yes, I do, and Jam going to join the church, and be a Christian hereafter." "If you do that, yon must give up dancing add going to the museum." "What is that? Must I quit going to the museum." "Oh, yea." "Then," after a minute or two of earnest reflection, "I guess I'll go down and see the four-legged woman just once more before I am converted."—lndianopolis Journal.

iwould be accepted with its present restriction as only an instalment towards complete separation. As to the Land Purchase Bill, he was convinced on reflection that Mr. Gladstone's reduction of the amount of Consols to be issued to fifty millions was illusory, and that ultimately the amount must be be one hundred and fifty millions. He was afraid his opposition to the Land Purchase Bill could not be met. The bill was a bad one, and he would sooner give up politics than pledge the future capi- tal and earnings of the country in order to gratify the Irish proprietors. His objections to the Home Rule Bill, he said, would disappear if representation , of Ireland at Westminster were maintained, and he , would be glad to concede to Ulster a separate As- sembly. At the Glasgow meeting the Duke of Argyll was the principal speaker. Mr. Labouchere, M.P., presided on Thursday even- ing at a mass meeting held at the St. James's Hall, London, in support of the Government of Ireland Bill. Mr. Howell, M.P., moved, and Mr. J. Leices- ter, M.P., seconded, a resolutioh congratulating Mr. Gladstone on his endeavour to give effect to the principle of allowing the Irish to legislate on all domestic matters, and expressing the hope that the bill will become law with such modifications as will place it in complete harmony with Radical desires. Mr. 11. W. L. Lawson, M.P., Mr. Pickersgill, M.P, Mr. Howard Spensley, M.P., and the Hon. B. Cole- ridge, M.P., supported the resolution, which was carried with enthusiasm. On the motion of Mrs. Besant, seconded by Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., the chair- man was authorised to sign a petition to the House of Commons on the subject.
